Whose good designs Are all their boast! For words are dew. 7.: They do the most Whose lives possess The sterling stamp Of righteousness; For deeds are tree. And if the heart Be pure and good -- The life will be Just what it should— Not dew, but true.

THREE SONNETS• V....--CTSIC TO PONT. Had. YOU been wise, you never had been poor, Or knocked unanswered at a Christian door. Why did you not in youth add store to store? Knowing how fame by wealth is made secure; How genius even with fame is never sure Of being statued upon any shore; How ragged virtue is a thing impure; And guineakss piety a saintly bore? Go to! your honesty's a blank; your nurk Is penniless; your feet and back are bare. Since you have earned but blows from Fortune's rod, Die like a Iran, and leave the world your curse-! Heavens 'I how you start, like any king! and glare With glorious eyes, as if you were a god! li.—Porr To cYN-lc. What voice is this that counsels with a sneer, To end a life that fails to gather pence? Surely in poverty is no offence? Surely in'mintage is no magic gear To buy salvation in another sphere, Where only grace and worth make competence? Bare feet, bare back! Not these, but this, I fear— 7j Naked of heavenly knowledge going hence. Who,lives on less than little may be rich; An empire's revenues o'erspent make poor: 'Tis not the crown, but the king's heart, is king, And rears him high or rolls him in the ditch. At councils of the gods I sing secure, And all the stars sing with me as I sing. 111.-SAGE TO CYNIC AND POET. Patience, brave friends! though hard it is to wait 'The crowned event you wish that never comes, While rude souls blow their trumps and beat their drums Over DI2BII trophies at a brazen gate, Where supple knees slip down on new estate. Rather be poor, good hearts, than rich with sums 'Earned by no deed of worth. Sweet are life's crumbs To him who hungers through an honest fate! Hope still remains though far behind we pace In the long progress led by dancing plume And glancing spear, adown the jubilant wind. 'Something there is to give us heart of grace . The proud must serve the Moulder of their doom; 'God serves the humble-true, though halt and blind. —Wilma* Plumage, in Gtod Words for April.

"How often does the ferry-boat start?" asked the lady. " Ivery fifteen minutes, mum." "nor long since the boat left here?'" " Tin minutes, mum." Lady waits ten mindtes, and then says, "Didn't you say the boat starts every fifteen minutes?" "I did, mum." "Well, I have waited here ten minutes since you said the boat had gone ten minutes." "Yes, mum." "Then how do you make out that it starts every. 15 minutes?" "Why, you see, mum, it starruts from this soide wan 15 minutes, and from the Wier soide the nixt." . Lord Kaimes, in one of his circuits as a Lord of Jus- ticiary in Scotland, having crossed the ferry to King- horn, the boatman, to his Lordship's surprise, refused to take any money for the service he had rendered him, in consequence of their being old acquaintances. On be- ing desired to explain, the boatman observed that his name was Torn Clark, and that he and his wife Bett had both been tried for sheep-stealing, and had it not .been for his Lordship's jaw, both Bett and himself had either been hanged or transported. His Lordship, smiling, bade him be more honest in future, as the consequence might be fatal to him, should their acquaintance ever be renewed. A VALUABLE HINT.—" What are you buying now ?" sisked Ned Steven ion of Andrew Powell on meeting the latter in Bell's iewelry store. "I am looking for some vresent to give my wife on her birthday. I tell you, making presents costs a heap of money." "Why don't you do as I do? I have never failed to make my wife a present on her birthday every year for 25 years, and I am not out a cent thus far." How do you manage it ?" "It is very simple. After we were married, when her birthday came round I gave her a 20 dollar gold piece. When my birthday, came around she gave me the 20 dollar piece back, and we have kept that up ever' since, and neither of us are out s cent." Ma. DLIINVIN AND TRH DWI 011 ARGYLL—In the last year of his life Mr. Darwin did me the honour of calling upon me in my house In London, and I had a long and very interesting conversation with that distinguished., observer of nature. He did not profess to be a theologian ' or a meta-physician; it was his work in the world to record facts, so far as he could see them, faithfully and honestly and to connect them with theories and hypothe- ses, which were constructed, at all events, for a temporary convenience, as all hypotheses in science must be before being proved. But in the course of that conversation I said to Mr. Darwin, with reference to some of his own remark- able works on the "Fertilisation of Orchids," and upon " The Earthworms," and various other observations he made of the wonderful contrivances for certain purposes in nature—l said it was impossible to look at these with- out seeing that they were the effect and the expression of Mind. I shall never forget Mr. Darwin's answer. He looked at me: very hard. "Well, that often comes over me with overwhelming force; but at other times," and he shook his head vaguely, adding. " itseems to go away." This is exactly the language which we have expressed in a remarkible passage in the book of Job, in which that truth is expressed which every Christian holds— that in nature we cannot see the Creator face to: face, and that • there are difficulties and veils between Him and the visible methods through which He works. "Be- hold I go forward, but He is not there; and backward; but I cannot perceive him; on the left hand where He cloth work—but I cannot behold Him; He hideth Him- self on the right hand that I cannot see Him. '—The Duke of ARGYLL, in Good Words. A SENATE OF ONE.—In 1866, previous to the passage of the Reconstruction Act, the Legislature of Arkansas assembled in what hecame known as the rebel session. EaPecting trouble, the "rebel session" adjourned in M„arull, with a view of meeting again 011 the Ist May. In lac meantime General Ord received instructions to pro- hibit the reassembling of the men who, under the Con- stitution of the United States, had no right to enact laws. Nearly all of the members yielded to the military mandamus, but a few headstrong statesmen, knowing that the country demanded their services, convened upon the arrival•of the proper time. The State House was surrounded by soldiers, but the determined Legis- lature met in General Newton's law offiCe. John R. Fellows, now a prominent lawyer of New York, and assistant-district attorney of that city, was the only Senator present. Entering the little room set apart for the Senate, Mr. Fellows took his place behind the desk, struck the board with a horse-shoe, and said, "The Senate will come to order. As the chaplain is not pre- sent, Mr. Fellows, you will please offer a prayer." Then Mr. Fellows Prayed. "Mr. Fellows," said r. Fellows, "you will please act as sergeant-at-arms." "Yes, sir," answered himself. "As the secretary is not present, Mr. Fellows, you will have to discharge the duties of that officer." All right, sir." "Read the proceedings of the last day's session." Mr. Fellows read, and then moved that the journal stand approved. "Any objec- tions, gentlemen ?" There being no objections, the journal was approved. "Mr. President," said Mr. Fel- lows, "I see that the janitor is not present. We need a bucket of fresh water. "Mr. Fellows " said Mr. Fellows, "I will appoint you to discharge the 'duties of janitor." Mr. Fellows brought a bucket of water. "Now, gentle- men, we are ready for business." Just then some one looked in and said, "Come on, John, let's get a drink." "Second the motion," said Mr. Fellows, and then, turning with the gravity for which he is noted, con- tinued :—" It is moved and seconded that the Senate ad- journ and take a drink. All in favour of the motion will say aye:" "Ave !" “ Contrary, no. The ayes have it, and the Senate will adjourn." A. few moments later the Senate was again called to order, and the transac- tion of business began in regular form. The com- inander of the post, hearing that the Legislature had met in violation of his orders, sent a file of soldiers with orders to arrest the members and bring them to head- quarters. The Lower House, consisting of five mem- bers, hid adjourned when the soldiers arrived, but the Senate was still in session, deep in a discUssion pending the passage of a bill amending the revenue laws of the State. Mr. Fellows was arrested and taken before General Ord. "'Who are you ?" asked the General. "The Senate of Arkansas." " A member of the rebel Legisla- ture, eh? Captain? {There are the other members ?" fins was the only one we found. General. He had as- sembled and organised himself into the Senate, and was discussing a bill when we arrested him." "Have you got the bill ?" "Yes, sir, here it is," producing the do.niment. The General, after reading .the bill, said, "A very. good idea, Mr. Seitate. Now, sir, what is your opinion; do you think it would have passed ?" "1 tirnk that its chances were good," replied Mr. Fellows. "You are no doubt a wise legislator. By the way, Mr. Senate, do you ever drink anything ?" Mr. Fellows said that his most intimate friends had known him to drink. "Captain," continued the General, "pull out that jug. Drink, sir, and then we will go down and pass the bill." Severalyears afterwards, when reconstruction had been effected, Fellows's bill was taken up, passed without trouble, and is now a law. A pair of slippers—Two eels. The most formal of flowers—The primrose, "The oldest inhabitant is usually a man," says an ex- change. But it needn't be soil women would only stand up to their ages. Franklin, on hearing the remark that what was lost on earth went to the moon, asserted that there must be a deal of good advice accumulated there. A benevolent Quaker took a tract to a starving, sick man. "Friend, I bring thee something good to read, but so that thou can'at -understand it better I give thee five shillings." "Have you heard Miss Simpson sing since she took lessons?" "Several times." "Do you think she has im- proved?" "Very much." "In what particular ?" "She doesn't sing as much as she used to.' A witty lady says of the people of a New England town :—" They are very pleasant, very intellectual, very delightful in a distant sort of way, and talk to you like so many books; but when you approach them socially I they all climb into their genealogical trees as though they were frightened." Admiral Lee, when only a post captain, being on board his ship one rainy and stormy night, the officer of the watch came down to his cabin and. cried, "Sir, the sheet anchor is coming home." "Indeed !" says the captain, "I think the sheet anchor is quite in tho right of it. I don't know what would stay out such a stormy night as

this." TROOPING THE COLORS.—The ceremony originated with William, Duke of Cumberland, colonel of the Cold- streams, and afterwards of the Ist Foot Guards, who, scandalised at the unsteadiness of officers scarcely re- covered from their midnight potations when they ap- peared at early parade, devised the manceuvres known as trooping," which requires each officer and non-com- missioned officer to march 'slowly and solitarily in a straight line to his post.—W. H. E. FRENCH Gaixairray.—When the Gaul performs a gal- lant act, he extracts all the honey that is to be got out of it. If he gives up his seat to a woman, he takes off his hat and points to the vacant place as if he were sur- rendering an empire and inviting a queen to enthrone herself thereon. If he hoists her umbrella, it is as if he were spreading out the canopy of heaven over her head. If he picks up a fallen glove, he offers it to the owner as if he were placing his sword and honour at her disposal for the rest of his life. If he quits her at the foot of a stairway, he looks after her as a chamberlain of the Court might do when her Majesty mounts the throne. All this makes him happy.—Monsieur at Home. AT WORK AMONG SCHOOL BOARD BEFAITLTERS.—Let us take, then, a morning in November. The largest and most convenient public school in the district is selected. One of the principal rooms is appropriated for the re- ception of parents and children, and four smaller rooms for the hearing and consideration of the various cases. One or sometimes two members of the Board preside in each room, and one case at a time is brought in. To- wards eleven o'clock, there may be teen converging hither from all points of the compass and from all the streets, lanes, and alleys of the district, a downcast poverty-stricken company of men, women, and children, but chiefly women and children; the men being for the most part at work, while the women are generally ac- cepted as the more suitable for being dealt with. . And thus in panoramic succession for two or three hours each week or fortnight are the circumstances of about eighty families, more or less, laid bare. Stern reproof and warning are as frequently required as advice and sympathy. The knowledge that the Board has power to bring defaulters before the sheriff exer- cises a wholesome influence upon the manner in which the reproof is accepted, and, as a rule, the warning is' found to have the desired effect. Prosecution and punishment are only resorted to in cases of hardened offenders, and are looked upon as affording an occasional necessary example, rather than with much hope of per- manent good. Where through unfortunate necessity father or mother are sent to prison by the sheriff it is the custom of the School Board to make inquiry into the circumstances of the children, so that steps may be taken for their relief. It not unfrequently happens, when the father is incarcerated, that the rest of the family enjoy more quiet and comfort than usually fall to their lot, and would be quite willing that the imprison- ment might be years instead of days. In a larger num- ber of cases it is the pleasing duty of the Board to coun- sel and direct the parents towards agencies, ways, and means which they had not previously thought of. They are thus enabled to see that a little more earnestness and diligence on their part might often help them to over- come difficulties and obstacles which weft not so insur- mountable as they had believed. Many honest parents have come to the meetings downcast and sorrowful who have gone from it cheered and hopeful—" a little word in kindness spoken" goes a long, long way in evoking the sympathies and stimulating the flagging resolves of poor down-hearted fathers or mothers.—" Twelve Years' , Dealing with Neglected Children" in" Good Words." STORIES ABOUT ANIMALS.—The smallest bird of prey found in England is the merlin, which is remarkable for the cunning it displays. A railway engineer has for several years observed the tactics of one of these birds,. which frequently attended him on his journeys. It usually followed the train, sometimes partly hidden by the smoke, watching for the small birds which the train frightened as it passed. The merlin swooped toward them with incredible speed-while they were scattering in their panic, and when it missed its prey returned to continue its flight in the wake of the carriages. Though the train might have a start of one hundred and fifty to two hundred yards, it came up to it in a second or two, watching the rising of a bird from one of the hedges bordering the line. Another story of animal instinct is told by a Scottish sportsman. He had taken a "shoot- -Ing box" for the hunting season in Yorkshire, but a neighbouring sportsman's retriever annoyed him by stealing the birds that his own dogs had brought in. I The theft was stopped by the sagacity of his own re- triever, which, discovering the thief in the act of rob- bery, gave chase, punished the intruder, recovered the stolen bird, and took it back to his master. Here is an- other good dog story, told by the Rev. J. G. Woods. A dog regarded as of thoroughly irreproachable training, was charged with worrying sheep at night. The family rebutted this charge, on the ground that the dog was fastened into their kitchen at night, and was never let out until the servants came down in the morning. The farmers, however, persisted that they knew the dog well, and had seen him going from the sheepfold, though he had managed to escape them. To settle the matter, one of the daughters of the dog's owner volunteered to sleep in the kitchen and-tiatch the dog's behaviour. A little after midnight he got up, came to the bed, and sniffed about until he had satisfied himself that the lady was not awake. Then he leaped into the window-seat, lifted: the catch of the shutters, and opened them. Then ha undid the latch of the window,wluch he opened, and then disappeared. After a long interval he came back, closed and fastened the windows and shutters, and finished by licking his own feet and the marks which lie had left by springing on the floor. As soon as she heard the ser- vants stirring, the lady rose softly and slipped through the door: But the guilty dog had marked her. He sprang up and made a dash at her, for he saw that his secret was discovered. The dog was so furious that no one dared to go into the kitchen.; and at last a gun was pointed through an aperture, and he was shot dead.

NOTES ON AGIITCULTURE, HORTI- • f• OUL Wig, O. /RI ' Pnessneca'oe fleas n WATER.--A correspondent asks for a simple test whereby to detect the presence of iron in water. He needs only to keep a pint of water- in a quart bottle of white glass, and shake it up occasion- ally. If there is iron in solution in the water, it will ion become oxidised, and reveal its presence by an o.lireous colour and deposit. fliers FOR TRH Feasi.—A sharp, bright hoe is poison- ous to weels. Never spare oil on creaky and rusty axles and hinges. Brains are the cheapest fertilisers that can be employed on the farm. An abundant sup- ply of pure water is as essential to profitable swine husbandry as is an abundance of sound wholesome food. It is an accepted law of physiology that pure water is an essential article of diet for man and beast. Feed it to all animals on the farm. Trees should always be ob- tained from some responsible grower, who has an estab- lilhedputation for fair dealing and good packing. A small yof water is very useful on every farm; it will a ord a drinking place for cattle, while it can be stocked with fish and made useful in keeping ducks and geese. Every farm and garden should have its compost heap, where all sorts of rubbish that will decompose should be placed; over it throw suds, Sm.; it all goes, when mixed up, to make excellent manure. To keep a small quantity of apples for family use, carefully place them in boxes or barrels, and fill all the spaces between the fruit with cool wheat bran which has been pre- viously well dried in an oven. It has been thoroughly demonstrated by practical men that the small breeds of swine mature earlier, require less food to maintain the system, and therefore produce more pork for the food consumed, than the larger breeds. There are many reasons why black hogs are preferable to white ones, of which these are some—They are not only more hardy and vigorous as a general thing, but are less subject to disease, especially that of the skin. Tim WIRRAL AND BICRESNRHAIS Acinictrnsvese So- ciiirrv.—The prize list for the forthcoming show of this society, to be held on the 17th, 18th, and 19th of June. has just been issued. We find that all entries close on the Bth of June, and that nearly £l,OOO is offered for competition. The society's showyard is of a permanent character, and is replete with every requisite for the comfort and accommodation of the various classes of animals, he. The sheds are boarded at the sides, and the roofs are covered with stout canvas. The society's district extends to all parts within 25 miles of Birken- head Town Hall. lathe horse section some very attrac- tive premiums are offered. Two sets of prizes are being given for stallions, six for agricultural and roadster mares, foals, fillies, and geldings; two for hunters, three for leapers, four for roadsters, two for ponies, and three for harness horses, ponies, and cobs. Premiums are also offered for tradesmen carrying on business in the society's district, and to tenant farmers principally de- pendent upon farming, and residents in the society's district. A good show of cattle may be expected, prizes being offered for bulls, dairy cows, and heifers, Channel Islands cattle, Ayrshires, and for shorthorns, and in ad- dition to these premiums the President of the society offers two silver Cups, one for the best bull and the other for the best dairy cow. Handsome prizes are offered for sheep and pigs. In poultry and pigeons several new classes have been added. The dog show will be held under the Kennel Club rules. Several extra prizes are offered and challenge classes are provided for champions. For implements and machinery four gold and ten silver medals are offered. Faintnns' Arms/ex—A meeting of the Farmers' Alli- ance was held at Holborn Restaurant, London, on Tues- day, Mr. Geo. Judd, the president, in the chair. The re- solutions passed at the conference of the Scottish Farmers' Alliance and the general committee of the Eng- lish Farmers' Alliance on the 25th of February last were discussed, and the following were adopted :—" 1. That inasmuch as experience has already shown the Agricul- tural Holdings Act, 1883, to be a failure, and as no scheme of compensation short of that contained in the fourth clause of the Farmers' Alliance Land .Bill, 1881, will give to the occupiers of the soil proper security for their invested capital, it is absolutely necessary that steps be taken by legislative enactment to secure full compen- sation to the outgoing tenant for every improvement which increases the value of his holding." "2. That any new Landlord and Tenant Bill should also provide that any reasonable stability of tenure be secured to an improving and sitting tenant, by giving him a power of appeal to an impartial tribunal against any attempt to raise his rent upon his own:improvements ; and every matter of difference or dispute between a landlord and tenant arising out of such attempt shall be heard and determined by such tribunal; and such tri- bunal shall, in case a landlord, in opposition to the tribunal, determines to resume possession of the holding, have power to award compensation to the tenant." "3. That in the opinion of this conference the proposed Land Bill for Great Britain should embody the principle of free sale of the tenant's improvements, with pre- emption to the landlord." It was further resolved, on the motion of Mr. Bear--" That the Executive Commit- tee be requested to consider the draft bill already pro- visionally agreed to at the Aberdeen Conference, and, acting on the instructions of the resolutions as carried to-day, endorse or alter the several clauses, and submit the result to a future general meeting, having first learned how far the Scottish Alliance agrees with the deeesions arrived at." ' THE FARMERS' Crsin.—At the meeting of this club, on Tuesday evening, at the Inns of Court Hotel, Mr. W. Eve in the chair, Mr. Frederick J. Lloyd introduced the sub- ject of "Field Experiments." In speaking of ,the man- ner in which experiments ought to he carried on, he said a notion was far too prevalent that such experiments required land specially set apart for them, a large expen- diture of money and labour, and a considerable amount lof scientific skill. Every farmer, whether conscious of it or not, was an experimenter, every crop an experi- ment. Every farmer was, or should be, a close observer of nature. In alluding to the services of Miss Ormerod to British agriculture, he said farmers had been her con- stant assistants in her researches, and what had been done with regard to insect pests might be done in refer- ence to othei matters. There ought, he maintained, to be a closer union between the chemist and the farmer. He thought that State aid might be usefully rendered by means of information conveyed in Blue Books and yearly grants to assist in scientific experiments carried-on at central stations.—ln the discussion which followed the paper, Mr. C. S. Read, M.P., remarked that the experi- ments at Rothamstead and Woburn had been coriducted without any regard to expense. However good might be the results of experiments, the expense might exceed the value to the farmer, and Sir John Lawes and the late Dr. Voelcker might have told them that that was the case with many of their own experiments. The great thing which science had done for the farmer was the showing him the why and wherefore of successful agri- culture.—The remaining speakers were Mr. E. Packard, Mr. W. Wells, Mr. W. Sergison, Mr. T. Bell, Dr. A. J. Voelcker, Mr. Charles Howard, and Mr. Bernard Dyer, the last-named gentleman remarking that subscriptions for the carrying on of field experiments should not be confined to a single year, the only way to secure valu- able results from such experiments being to continue I them from year to year, so as to avoid the evil of arriving at premature conclusions.—A vote of thanks was given to Mr. Lloyd for his paper.] CO-OPERATIVE FARMING.—Mr, F. Fuller writes to the Land Agents' Record :—Last week I visited Radbourne Manor Farm, Southern, Warwickshire. This farm com- prises 356 acres of stiff, wet, cold, clay land, five miles from a railway station and eleven miles from a market town. The last tenant ruined himself and the farm, as after leaving it no tenant could be found to take it at ss. per acre. Mr. Bolton King, the landland, then attempted association farming by taking his late farm steward, David Johnson, a tenant farmer, together with 12 picked labourers, as associated tenants, Mr. Bolton King being not only landowner but banker. Mr. Bing found land and money, and David Johnson and his merry men found brains and labour for farm opeeations. Your readers ought now to see this farm, which only two and a half years ago was in the most wretched and dilapi- dated condition, the land, like the neighbouring land now, not yielding more than about three quarters of wheat, four or five of oats, and three or four of beans per acre, while last year it yielded , five quarters of wheat, eight quarters of beans, and nine quarters of oats per acre, and there are now on the farm 109 head of cow stock, 115 sheep, 14 horses and colts, 38 pigs, and about 400 head of poultry. One poultry house is made to travel from field to field, according as insect or other food is necessary. Eggs and butter are now producing about £6 per week. The associate labourers have 15s. per week, with 4d. an hour for overtime, extra pay in har- vest, milk every day, and a division of profits at Michael- mas, which last year resulted in some cases £2, others £3, and others 2,5 a piece. The associates paid £1 per acre rent, six per cent, on borrowed capital, and paid rates, taxes, and tithes in addition. The fame of the associa- tion reached Oxford, and the authorities of Balliol Col- lege have induced Mr. David Johnson to take their Upton Hill Farm of 400 acres, and to cultivate it on the association plan. David Johnson has now got possession ofjthe land but not of the house, and a farm in worse condition you never saw. The terms on which it is let are for the first six months nil. For the next year 10s. an acre; for the next year 12s. 6d.; and for the future 15s. per acre. The tenancy is yearly, with two years' notice to 9ult, the lessor paying for all improvements by valuation. Plenty of capital, £4,000 has been volun- teered for stocking Upton Farm at 5 per cent. On both farms your readers may see game in sufficient quanti- ties, and the association protecting/it ; they are, more- over, as proud of their game as they are of their horns, cattle, sheep, poultry, Sze. Three distinguishing features of assocjated farming are—cleanliness, thrift, and hope' all are cleanly, cheerful, and hopeful, all are industrious and all are careful of everything about them, workhouse and the jail are no longer looked upon as the only certain things besides death. The associates are, in -fact, emancipated from what they call slavish labour,. and are no longer slaves but associated workers for the common good of all parties equally. All these men are now on the high road to be cultivators of the soil on their own account.

WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL An ordinary monthly meeting of this Council was held ia the Town Hall on Tuesday evening. There were present— Tbe Mayor (Alderman Harrison). Aldermen Pickmere, Kean. Holmes, Chandley; Councillors Barker, Dixon, Brown, Broadbent, Mackie,- J. Pierpoint, Jolley, Greening, Whittle. Ridgway. Taylor, Tinsley, Marsh, Sutton, Bolton, W. Pierpoint, Fleming, Hutchinson Francomb, Wright, .; Brooke (town clerk), LOngdin (borough sur- Chorley (borough treasurer), and Whittle (deputy ark). TRH APPOINTMENT OF NEW TLAGISPRATES. The MAYOR announced that Mr. Councillor J. Greening. Mr. Edwin James Guest, Mr. Alderman Piokmere, and Mr. Cancelllor Platt had been placed on the commission of the peace for the borough, and had taken the necessary oath to qualify them to sit as magistrates. Councillor MACHIN said that he should like to ask one or
in w—n ,
Roberts
Mot), town ol

two questions in connection with the announcement made by the Mayor. If they were to have more magistrates, he did not know four gentlemen more competent to occupy the position, than those recently appointed ; but that was an occasion on which it was desirable that they should know, if possible, something regarding the appointment of magi- strates in general. He was not going to introduce the ques- tion of politics in an offensive sense, but did want to know ' the powers of the Town Council in connection with an ap- pointment of that kind, which might have had a strange and sudden connection with the quk etion of the election of an alderman, which was, as they knew, a little bit noisy. lie wished to know whether the Town Council had been consulted in the matter in any way, or whether the Mayor as chief magistrate had had any question put to him, or whether any committee connected with the Council bad been questioned. The fact that they had not, as he sup - poled, simply showed that that was one of the opportunities very properly taken advantage of by politicians on both aides, when they were in a majority, to reward their friends for services performed. fie thought that even in the history of Warrington, however, it had been the case •to eonsult the Town Council, and he did not consider that the beat plan, as his belief was that if they were to select they would be more likely to do it on party grounds. The MAYOR replied that although it was not customary for a speech to be made on such an announcement, he would, with the permission of the Council, answer the question. No communication had been made to the Town Council on the subject, but it was not an unusual way of appointing borough magistrates. It had In some cases been done by the Council's recommendation, but if the Government thought fit they could nominate others irrespective of the Council. Councillor MAME was in favour of the appointments being made by the Government, but thought the Council should In this case have been consulted to see whether there was a necessity for even four of the best men in the town being appointed. There were already no less than 17 Liberals on the borough commission and 10 Conservatives. They had added to these four more Liberals, which, with the Mayor, made in all 32 magistrates; there were 34 police officers, making one magistrate to every police officer, minus two. There were also 11 county magistrates having juris- diction in the borough. He thought that if they went mach further there would be a danger of the magistrates on 501050 occasions out-voting the bona fide members of the Watch Committee. Then there were Cheshire magistrates, who would only interfere with Latchford. Altogether they bad 47 or 48 magistrates for 45,000 inhabitants. Be thought that, if necessary, they should suggest to every Home Sec- retary as he came into power not to appoint any more magtetrates for Warrington without consulting the Town Council. The Lancashire magistracy was fall, and he did not hesitate to say that it was a wrong thing to keep a large body like the Cheshire magistratcy in such a condi- tion that in this part of the county there should be 10 of one political faith and only two of aaother. The MAYOR pointed out that the matter rested with the Chancellor of the Duchy. If the Council memorialised him, no doubt they would receive proper attention. It was not an unusual course for them not to have been con- sulted. The subject then dropped. WATCH COMMITTEE: THE TRAFFIC IN SANEHY-STRRET. The minutes of this Committee, which recommended an estimated expenditure for the ensuing half-year of £ll6B 12s 9d, were proposed for adoption by the Mason, seconded by Councillor BROADBENT. Councillor Dixon' asked if some instruction could not be given for the better management of traffic in Sankey-street on Sunday nights. Councillor .Meownt entreated the Council to give instruo- CODS to some committee to lessen the enormous crowding mentiened by Councillor Dixon. In the front of that build- ing they had a large walk from one gateto the other, which, according to a plan lately suggested, would make a capital promenade, and thus relieve the traffic in the streets. Councillor BOLTON objected to Councillor Dixon blaming the Watch Committee and the police in this matter. If there was a promenade in the town it was the main street, and the promenaders were generally respectable people who walked about irt a respectable manner. Councillor Jakhn PIERPOINT said that he should be glad when the time- arrived when they could have the's,ktil'in front of the Town Hall removed, and the walks opened to the street in such a manner that people could promenade what Was known sea public recreation ground. He thought it was time that they should have the Town Hall more open to public view, and relieve the thronging of Sankey-street. If the lamps round the promenade were all lighted there would be more walking there. Councillor Jorastr said that the question was one of s. d. His impression was that the street should be wideni.d from Craefi&d-street to Miss Garland's, which woule, however, incur some expense. Alderman CHANDLEY was surprised to hear Mr Jolley, who entered the Council with great professions of economy, speak so. (Laughter.) Having been for some years a mem- ber of the Park Committee, he might say that the suggestion had been talked about over and over again. Different plans bad been suggested and abandoned because of the cost, and, he thought, properly so. It was not a time now to incur ex- pense for ornamental purposes. Councillor BROADBENT thought it natural that people should take walks in the street where most of the large buildirgs were situate. He thought it was not their province to complain of the people filling the streets. With regard to the Town FLU grounds he thought something might be done without much expense in the shape of providing a plea- sant walk within the gates. (Hear.) Councillor HUTCHINSON thought that the sooner more I accommodation was made the better. The cost would not be much. Alderman PICIEMERR hoped that the subject would not be brought up again until the Council found themselves with sufficient money in their coffers to open up the front of the Town Hall. The minutes were then passed. MEET IMPROVEMENT, &C., COMMITTEE. This committee recommended that the sum of £B5O be paid to Mr W J Leigh for the redemption of the ground rents on the property recently purchased from the trustees of the late James Davies and Martin Cot less ; that an estimate of expenditure for the ensuing half-year of £1,590 be ap- proved, and that a number of additional lamps be provided in specified places. The minutes were adopted without discussion on the motion of ouncillor BROADBENT, seconded by Councillor GREENING.

SANITARY COMMITTEE. The minutes of this committee, which recommended an estimated expenditure of 1.4,766 for the next half-year, were approved without discussion on the motion of Coun- cillor Surrox, seconded by Councillor BARKBR.

div.head: SCHOOL ATTENDANCE COMMITTEE.
div.p: SCHOOL ATTENDANCE COMMITTEE.

The report of the Inspector contained in the minutes of this committee stated that 142 cases had been inquired into by the Board of Guardians, and school fees allowed in 128 c tees for 278 children ; that 62 cases had been taken be- fore the magistrates when fines were inflicted.in 54 cases, 6 adjourned, 1 dismissed, and 1 ordered to be whipped. The committee's estimates of expenditure for the ensuing half year amounted to £153 103. The average attendance at the different schools during the month of February was 6,691, and for the corresponding period last year 6.608; increase 83.
Councillor DIXON moved, and Councillor FLEMING secon- ded the adoption of the minntee. _

Alderman. KEAN thought the wørk of the committee was being done very satisfactorily, and they had every reason to believe the school attendance officer was doing his they to the very utmost of his power. The minutes were then adopted. MUSEUM, LIBRARY, AND ARTS COMMITTER. On the moiton of Councillor MACKIE, seconded by Coun- cillor SUTTON, these minutes were adopted.
CEMETERE COMMITTEE.

The report of .the registrar stated that the interments for the past four weeks were :—Adults. 36 ; minors, 31 ; still- born and premature, 3 ; and for corresponding period last year, adults, 30 ; minors, 25 ; stillborn and premature, 9. The committee recommended an estimate of expendi- ture for the next half year amounting to £286 121. It also recommended that Councillor Jolley be appointed a member of the committee.

THE BATHS.

The minutes of the Town Hall, Park, and Baths Commit- tee recommendtd the approval of an estimate of expenditure for the ensuing half year of £615 16s 101. The MLYOR moved, and Alderman PICIEMERE seconded, the conflrmation of the minutes.

Councillor DIXON asked if there was any report from the deputation appointed to inspect the baths at other places, and also if they were likely to have any Turkish baths. The MAYOR said steps were being taken to supply thP Council with the information required respecting the baths.

to MOO 17s. The in-come from all sources for the pas:, four weeks was £223 12s 4d. On the motion of Alderman CHANDLEY, seconded by Councillor JPiliarotyr, the minutes were confirmed.

OAS COMMITTEE. The minutes of this cenamittee contained the following recommendation :—That the tender of Messrs Newton, Cham- bers, and Company, Limited, for the supply of pipes for the Latohford supply ; that the tender of Messrs _Rough and

Son for excavating trenches for pipes in Latchford,is ac- cepted ; that temporary apparatus for the manufacture of residual products be constructed at the works at Longford, to cost about 1.120; that the tender of Messrs Joseph Whit- ham and Company for the supply of vitriol be accepted ; that the tender of Messrs Hutchinson, of Widnes, for caustio soda be accepted. Alderman HOLMES moved, and Councillor GREENING seconded, the confirmation of these minutes. Councillor Dixon thought it was quite due to the Council that they should be told how the Gas Committee proposed to spend this £l2O. The Chairman of the committee never said a word about what the £l2O was for—(laughter)—but he (Councillor Dixon) demanded to know. He also com- plained about the ligh,ing power of the gas in Warrington, and advocated that in winter the committee should en- deavour to give gas of a, good an illuminating power as possible, and in summer the gas should be made to give off as much heat as possible for cooking purposes. Councillor FRANCOMB, who did not agree with the pro- posals of Councillor Dixon, asked for information as to the amount of gas consumed by Bray's burners oomp iced with what was consumed by. the ordinary gas lamps. From what he had been told by Mr Platt he understood that Bray's burners consumed very much less gas than he had antici- pated,aud if they only burned what Mr Platt had said, be (Councillor Francomb) thought it would be wise to have more of them in the town instead of running them down as they had done in that Council. _ _

6oancallor MACKin said he highly deprecated any attempt to take away the illuminating power of gas for the sake of heat. (Hear, hear.) The great canes which those who worked in large workshops had to complain of in conneo- Lion with gas was the intense and unhealthy heat. Mr. Dixon had travelled Is Wolverhampton and Birmingham ; he (Councillor Mackie) did not know whether he had got further than that. (Laughter.) Councillor W. PillapcnNT : He's been at London. (Laughter.) Councillor MACKIE said Mr. Dixon made those two places as excellent examples with regard to gas. He himself had been in Glasgow a few months ago, and he thought the second city in the Bmpire was not to be compared as a weil-li4bted city with the little town SE Warrington. (Hear, hear.) . . . . . . .

Councillor lin-renmsow, referring to the iron pipes that had been lad along St. James-street an, Knutsford-road, said he feared that many accidents would occur there through those pipes, for which the Gas Committee would be responsible. He thought it would be better if these pipes were laid down just a few days before being wanted. (Elear, hear.) The Mason thought the pipes had been there only three or four days. Councillor HUTCHINSON said some of them had been I there a fortnight, and there had been several slight acci- dents.

Councillor TAYLOR said that last Sunday night week, after eleven o'clock. he found one of the pipes rolled across the road near to Warrington Bridge. He thought the pipes miAlat have been put on some waste land, and carted as they were wanted. Councillor W. PIERPOINT hoped Alderman Holmes would give somc. reason for their wanting machinery for the manu- facture of residual products. There had been something said about some serious bad debt the committee had made, and he wanted the ehairtnan to kindly say the amount of such bad debt. Councillor ROBERTS asked whether it was the custom of the Gas Committee to advertise for the various tenders. He knew it was the custom to advertise for the larger contracts in connection with the gasworks, but he was not sure whether it was so in reference to the other requirements, He thought it was well it should be So, in order that every- body might have an opportunity of tendering. (Hear, hear.) The MAYOR, referring to Councillor Dixon's suggestion about the gas, said it was one of the recommendations of the electric light that it did not give off heat. If that were net the case he did not think the electric light would be se popular as it is. (Hear, hoar.) With regard to the £l2O it was proposed to expend that in erecting temporary ap- paratus, so as to utilise their own residuals, and thus avoid loss.

Alderman HOLMES said the apparatus they proposed to erect would not be wasted in the now works which they should probably have to erect. It was the fractica at a I good miny gas works to manufacture their own residual , products, and it was a source of considerable profit. He ruld tell Mr Pierpolnt that there had been a loss, but what the amount of loss might be he could not tell. Councillor W PutEPOINT : I heard it was £I,OOO. Alderman Ilovuns said it would be nothing like that ; the loss they should sustain would depend upon the divi- dend paid. With regard to Mr Dixon, he (Alderman Holmes) hoped that if Mr Dixon bad suggestions to make he would make some 014 had something like a basis of commonsense about them. As to Mr Francomb's question about tbe difference between the amount consumed by Bray's burners and other burners, he thought he must re- quest to have notice of such a question. Dealing with the remarks of Councillor Hutohinson, he said it had been ex- plained that the supply of gas to Latchford and along to- wards Thelwall was insufficient owing to the gas pipes net being of suffic'ent diameter, and therefore the committee, by the consent of that Council, had gone into the question of providing a greater supply, and they should commence in the course ef a few days, making as little inconvenience as possible, to lay the pipes. I'vlr Roberta had inquired about their asking for tenders. It they wanted a particular article they wrote to three or four or half-a-dozen people from whom they supposed they could get them on the best terms, and they had done se in the cases referred to be the minutes. 1 hey had obtained tenders from one or two firrns that supplied these materials and they had aceelned one of them. Of course in large contracts it was necessary to ad- vertise for tenders, but in these small cases it was not worth while.
The minute& were then confirmed. EIRE ENOINTI COMMITTEH.

This committee recommended an estimate of expenditure amounting to £136 10s; and also that the salary of the superintendent of the Fire Brigade be increased from £l5 to 1:20 per annum. Alderman PICICHHIIII moved the confirmation of the minutes, and yeferring to the proposed increase of salary, said that Mr Turner, the superintendent of the brigade, cer- tainly deserved an increase in his salary. Councillor HUTCHINSON seconded the confirmation of the minutes.
Councillor FLtisturcr proposed an amendment that the Increase be not granted on the ground that this was an in- opportune.time to raise salaries,

Councillor BOLTON seconded the amendment, which, how- ever, after several members of the Council had spoken in eulogistic terms of the superintendent of the Fire Brigade, was withdrawn, and the minutes confirmed.

div.head: THH SHIP CANAL.
div.p: THH SHIP CANAL.

The General Purposes Committee's estimate of expendi- ture was as follows :—On borough rate account, £8943s 8d; on improvement rate account, £3B ss. The committee also recommended that the Mayor, Mr Alderman Burgess, the Town Clerk, and the Borough Surveyor be appointed to give evidence in favour of the Ship Canal on behalf of the Cor- poration in accordance with a request of Mr Adamson, the chairman of the Ship Canal Provisional Committee. There WAS also a letter from the General Post Office stating that the Postmaster-General bad received the memorial of the Council praying for the establishment of direct communica- tion between Warrington and London, but he regretted to find that the number of messages now sent between the two place would not justify a compliance with the wishes of the memorialists.
The M&YOS moved, and C.)uncillor Dixox seconded, the confirmation of these minutes.

Councillor MACHIB regretted the decision of the Post- master-General, and exp ained the method by which tele- grams were at present sent from London to Warrington. Alderman HOLIUES, referring to the minute about the Ship Canal, said he sawithat £5O was put down for the expenses of the gentlemen to be sent up to London. The IVIAvon said the expenses were not exclusively on account of the Ship Canal, as there was another deputation as well to attend the annual meeting of the Municipal Cor- porations, and also to attend with the deputation from Cor- porations and Local Authorities upon the President of the Board of Trade en the subject of railway rates and charges. . _

Alcaerman HOLMES wished to know whether the £5O was to be paid from the amount of money to be contributed to the expenses of the canal. Councillor MACKIE said that Manchester, Salford, and other towns were taking a similar course and paying the ex. penses of the deputation themselves. He trusted Warrington would not appear shabbier than those towns.

Councillor BOLTON asked how the .£5O was spent? The MAYOR: It is not spent yet. • Councillor BOLTON : Will you tell us when it .is spent? Alderman CRANDLEY ; On railway fares, theatres, itc. (Laughter.) Alderman PICIIIIERE thought they were wasting the time of the Council. That Council was really losing its dignity when they asked the Mayor how the £5O was to be spent. . _ _
Councillor BotToN thought they had a perfect right to hear all about it.
COUDCiIIOt WHITTLE objected to the payment unless it came out of the twopence in the pound rate towards the ship canal. The minutes were confirmed.
FINANCB.

Alderman HOLMES, in moving the confirmation of the minutes of the Finance Committee, said he Might tell them se a matter of encouragement that they wore making a call upon the overseers of £4,309, against an expenditure this time last year of £4,512, and therefore there WAS a reduction of rather over £2OO. The improvement rate they proposed to make was is 3d in the ,E, the rate they laid this time last year being Is GA in the £. That was a subject which he thought the Council and the inhabitants generally would feel well satisfied with. (Hear, hear.) Councillor GREENIXO seconded, and the minutes were confirmed.

TTIE ROYAL VISIT TO IRELAND.

The Prince and Princess of Wales left Ruston Station at a quarter-past six on Tuesday evening for Dublin. The special train consisted of seven carriages, and included the new saloon car made specially for the use of their Royal High- nesses. It contains drawing-room and sleeping compartment, sumptuously furnished, and replete with every comfort and oonvenience. By desire of the Prince, only private friends were admitted to the platform to witness the departure, but a large crowd assembled outside the station and loudly cheered the Royal party. The Duke of Cambridge and the Marchioness of Lorne were amongst those who attended to bid their Royal Highnesses God speed. On their journey, the Princess of Wales was presented by a lady with a magni- ficent bouquet. _

The train reached Rugby, the first stopping place, at 8-2, a minute before the time, and stayed the allotted five minutes. His Royal Highness the Prince of Wales stood in the open carriage door conversing with Lord R Grosvenor part of the time, and then took his seat. The Princess did not leave the saloon, but remained seated conversing with her travelling companion, Lady Emily Kingston. Most of the other members of the suite alighted. As the train steamed out the number of people assembled on the plat- form refrained from cheering, but raised hats, which was gracefully acknowledged. Crewe was reached at 6-48. The Prince, with Lord R Grosvenor and Mr Condit) Stephens, directors of the London and North-Western Rail- way Company, alighted on the platform and had a short conversation in the refreshment-room. Mr Webb, the loco- motive superintendent of the railway, also had a covereation with the Prince. The public were rigidly excluded from the platform.

. At a meeting of the Irish National League, in Dublin, Mr Healy, who presided, saii no act in Earl Spencer's career was more shocking than his attempt to use the Prince of Wales as a whitewash-brush for the dirty walls of Dublin Castle. Mr William O'Brien, M.P., said the great majority of the people did net care whether the Prince came to Ire- land or not, and the double object of his visit was that stated by Mr Healy, to let Earl Spencer retire in a blaze of glory and to sow dissension in the Nationalist ranks would fail in the presence of recent memories of scaffolds reddened with the blood Of innocent victims.—Mr A O'Connor, M.P., regretted that the Prince cf Wales had allowed himself to be made an instrument in the hands of an insignificant set of partisans.—Mr Leachy, M.P., believed the Royal visit would invigorate the Nationalist organisation throughout the country.—Mr William Redmond, M.P., said the visit would enable the line to be drawn in Dublin between those who were really Nationalists and their enemies. The Nationalists should note those who exhibited flags and boy- cott them as enemies.—Mr Harrington, M.P., said he regarded those who received the Prince as the same who received Sir Stafford Northcote, their loyalty arising from the convenient opportunity given of insulting the Nationalists. The Prince and Priccess of Wales, accompanied by Prince Albert Victor, landed at Kingstown on Wednesday morning, and were received there by the Lord Lieutenant, the chief military and naval officers, many of the Irish nobility, and large crowds of the people. The passage acroes St George's Channel was quite uneventful. It was happily a calm one, though a north-easterly breeze ruffled the surface of the sea a little. The sun burst out at intervals from amongst the broken clouds, and gaily played about the burnishing of the vessel, adding brilliancy and warmth to the scene. The passage was more than half eecompliehed beie'e the Prince and Princess appeared on deck, but when once there they found the prospect sufficiently bright to tempt them fre- quently from their saloon, and to prevail upon them at last to remain altogether above board. The buildings of the town and the shipping in the harbour made a great display of bunting, while the Channel Squad- ron in the bay joined in the demoustration. The landing was effected amid royal sal utesonilitary honours, and hearty popular cheering. Their Royal Highnesses received and re- plied to a loyal address from the Town Commissioners. Peoceeding by train to Deblin, a great popular welcome was there extended to them. At Westland Row Station a loyal address was presented from a body of the citizens, and replied to by the Prince in a speech in which he expressed the gratification of the Princess and himself in visiting a country noted for the courtesy and hospitality of its people, and their hope to inspect some of the Irish industries as Iw ell as share in a few of the Irish amusements. The furtherance of the welfare of all classes in Ireland, the t Prince added, was ea object dear to the Royal Family. lii driving from the railway station to Dublin Castle the Prince and Pi incess drove throueh dense crowds of orderly and. enthusiastic people, who showed every evidence of good feeling. The streets were gay with flags, and the thoroughfates were spanned by many kindly mottoes. After lunching at the Castle, their Royal Highnesses visi- ted the spring cattle show of the Dublin -Society, inspecting the prize cattle and being spectators of jumping competi- tions of horses. In their progress througn the city they were accompanied by escorts of Lancers and Hussars, and the thoroughfares were lined with troops and police. When darkness set in there was some illumination of the prin- ciple streets. Altogether the day's proceedings appear to have been of a most loyal and enthusiastic character. A general feeling of satisfaction is expressed in Dublin at the reception on Wednesday of the Prince and ?flames of Wales, and the popular gratification finds vent on all hands. Their Royal Highnesses are naderstood also to have been very favourably impressed with the warmth of the welcome extended to them, and the popularity of the Prince promisee to increase as his visit lengthens. One of those acts by which he identifies himself with the welfare of the working classes was seen on Tuesday in a visit which he paid to some of the most poor and squalid districts of Dublin The Royal party breakfasted in the morning room of their apartments at the Castle, the band of the Cornwall Regiment playing a selection of music is the upper yard. The morning was beautifully fine though somewhat cold, and a few privi- leged strangers were allowed in the Castle Yard to hear the band play. At quarter-past eleven a covered carriage was drawn up at the private exit near the Ship-street Gate of the Castle, and accompanied only by Prince Albert Victor, Lord Suffield, and Captain Hasnond, R.N., the Prince was driven away through Ship-street to Golden-lane, a poor neighbourhood, in which the houses are of the most wretched description of tenement dwellings. Here the Prince and his son entered an old and ricketty struc- ture numbered 24, which had evidently been a comparatively decent middle-class dwelling at one time, but was now in decay and disrepair. Nobody knew of the visit in the vicinity until the Prince arrived, but his advent soon became known, and a crowd of ragged women and dirty children, with such of the men as were not at work, crowded round the earriftee, and shouted their welcomes to the Prince, the poor people expressing their pleasure in some cases rather forcibly by crowding to the Prince's side in the endeavonr to shake hands with him. Cries of "Long life to your honour," Oh, he's a darlin," and "May yer honour give us some work to do," greeted the Prince as he drove off, mingled with which were the cheers of the increased crowd. From this point the Prince drove off to a group of artisans' dwellings, the Coombe, built by a limited liability company, and known as the "Coembe Area." The Prince was here followed by a large crowd in his tour through several of the neat cottages in the black. Cheers fol- lowed his Royal Highness as he drove off in the direction of Dolphin's Barn. A large block of artisans' dwellings has here been erected by Messrs Guinness, the brewers, for the accommodation of their workpeople, and Mr Cecil Guinness was in waiting to conduct the Royal party through them. This ceremony occupied about a quarter of an hour, after which the Prince's carriage was driven to the Royal Hospital at Kilmainharn, where his Royal Highness visited Sir Thomas Steele, the Commander of the Forces in Ireland. Sir Tho%.as conducted the Prince and his teen to the hall of the hospital, where the old pensioners, many of them aged and infirm, and scarcely able to fall in, were formed and received the R >yet visitors with military salute. The Prince took off his hat to them, and after a kindly glance at the line of veterans, he said "I am very glad to see you friends," a compliment which the old soldiers acknowledged by raising their caps to the prince. The Royal party was then conducted through the chapel, and afterwards left for the castle. In the afternoon the Prince held a levee at the Castle, nearly 1,100 guests attending. The Princess visited the Alexandra College for ladies in Earlsfort-terrace. In the evening a Drawing-room was held by the Princess, which was attended by nearly 800 ladies. Mr Parnell, in a manifesto published in Thursday's " United Ireland "fails to see upon whet ground the Prince of Wales is entitled to any recognition in Ireland, save from the officials, landowners, and place hunters, who fatten on the poverty of the country. He compares his Royal Highness to an electioneering agent of the Government. The Freeman's Journal states that the patent of a baro- netcy has reached Mr Richard Martin, the chairman of the Dublin Citizens' Reception Committee at Westiand-row Terminus.

DISCHARGE OF 2,000 COLLIERS.—The leading colliery proprietors in North Derbyshire have decided to join the South and West Yorkshire coal owners in descending a ten per cent. reduction in wages. At one Derbyshire colliery the men have agreed to the reduction. At two large south Yorkshire collieries negotiations are proceeding to secure an amicable settlement on a similar basis. div.head: FOOTBALL.
div.p: FOOTBALL.

Secretaries of Football Clubs are requested to note that reports of matches played on Saturday must be sent to the head office, Bewsey-street, Warrington, not later than ten o'clock on Wednesday morning.

RUNCORN V. LITHERLAND —Played at Runcorn on Easter Monday, the visitors having material assistance of members of the Welton and Bootle Football Clubs, while the home team had to draft E Lunt and W Riley from the second team to fill vacancies. The game was well played through- ' oat, and during which Richardson gained a try for Lither- land, while Speakman dropped a goal for Runcorn, a fast game ending.in favour of Runcorn by one goal, five minor points, to one try, two minor points. Teams :—Runcorn : W Hughes, back; H Speakman, E Lunt, and W Riley, three-quarter backs • Hughes and Andrews, half backs; Wright, Lewis, Joule, Dean, Barns, Hoffiand, Clarke, Roberts, and Gatlev, forwards. Litherland : Cryer, back; E R Lycett, J Williams, and J Fairclough, three-quarter ' backs; J Larkin and J Holn3' half backs; J Hulme, J Mur- phy, R Harding, J Larkin, J Houghton, J Richardson, and J McManus, forwards. BARLESTOWN T. DARWEN OLD WANDERERS.—The Dar. wen Old Wanderers, who a fortnight ago defeated Everton by seven goals to none, met Earlestown (the holders of the Liverpool and District Challenge Cop) on the ground of the latter on Easter Monday, in the presence of a consider- able number of spectators. The game was very even dur- ing the first half, and each team scored one goal ; but In the second half the play of the home team was very poor, and the Darwenians had matters nearly all their own way. They severely pressed the Liverpool cup holders, and scored five more goals while the home eleven failed to notch a single point. When time was called, Earlestown was defeated by six goals to one. The following were the teams :—Earles- town: J Appleton, goal; It Green and J Green, backs; Bowker, Whalley, and Clayton, half backs; Rich and Ellison, right wing; Duxbary, centre; Sims and Ogden, left wing. Darwen W Holden, goal; W Clarke afid J R Leech, backs; J Heiden and W A Walker, half backs; J Parsons and II Shorrock, right wing; J West and R Ashton, centre; J Norris and F Dolan, left wing. EARLESTOWN V. BLACKBURN ROVERS.—Though the first team of the Blackburn Rovers were engaged playing Queen's Park in the final tie of the National Cup Competition on Saturday, the eleven representing the Rovers' Club 'Which visited Earlestown on that day was a very strong one, and included some well known players. The visitors met the Earlestown team on the new ground in the Mesnes, and there was a good attendance of spectators. Dagnall and Ellison were absent from the ranks of the Earlestonians. The game was finely contested from the commencement, and bath goals were in turn endangered. Neither team pos- sessed any madred advantage, though at half time the Rovers were leading by ens goal (obtained from a scrim- mage) to nil. On the change of ends the home team had the ground in their favour, and for some time they pressed the visitors. The latter, however, played'a splendid defen- sive game, and rendered futile the attains of their onnomots to score. When time was called, after one of the finest games ever played at Earlestown, the Rovers were declared the victors by one goal to none, Teams :—Black- burr line-ore: W Wilson, goal; F Shorrock and R Blenk- horn, backs; P Barton, J Grayson, and 3 Walton, half backs; J Dockworth and J Hayes, right wing ; A Birt- wistle, centre • R Collins and N Walton, left wing. Earles- town : J Appleton, goal; R Green and J Green, backs; Whalley, Duxbury, and Bowker, half backs; Rich and W Pennington, right wing; W Murray, centre; Sims and Ogden, left wing. -RUNCORN V. ROCHDALE ST. CLEMENTS.—The return fixture between these teams was brought to an issue on Sat-, urday at Runcorn. The home team were very poorly re- presented, being short of five of the usual fifteen ; the visitors, on the other hand,'were string However, a good game was played, which resulted in litincorn scoring one goal, one try, four minor points, to St. Clements three tries, five minor points. Daring the first portion of the game Holt for the visitors scored, the place kick failing. In the second half Rigg and Ridaugh for St. Clements end Roberts for Runcorn scored, the attempt at goal in each case failing. A little later on Speakman got the ball from H Hughes, and taking his drop the ball glided over the bar amidst great ex- citement. A try by Roberts was disallowed by the re- feree, as was one by Speakman in the first half of the game, a capital game ending as above indicated. In the back division of Runcorn Woods, H Hughes, Andrews, and Speakman played well; in the forwards Hoffland, W Hughes, Joule, and Clarke did a lot of work. For the St. Clements Shepherd, Rigg, and Richardson, behind; Belt, Ridaugh, and Rigg, forwards, shone most. Teams :—Run- corn: Woods, back; Johnson, Speakman, and Broady, three-quarter backs; Hughes and Andrews, half backs; E Andrews, IV Page, W Mason, R Roberts, J Hoffland, W Hughes, .1 Clarke, F Joule, J Gatley, and J Lewis, for- wards. St. Clements: Shattleworth, back; Shepherd, Pratt, and Rigs., three-quarter backs; Riehardson and Ken- yon, half backs; J Holt, S Holt, Rigg, Whitehead, Rid- augh, Johnson, Holroyd, and McHugh, forwards. OLDIIAM T. WIDNES.—These teams met on Saturday afternoon, on the ground of the former, at Clarke's Field. in the presence of 2,000 spectators. The visitors won the toss, and Oldham started the ball, which was not returned, and the visitors were at once forced to touch down. On drop- ping out, the scene of action was carried on in the home team's end, and the ball was kicked dead behind the Oldham line. A series of scrimmages now took place at mid-field, ' and eventually Ripley and Barlow dribbled the ball to the Widnes end, where Barlow picked up and gair,ed a try, the II same player converting it into a goal. After re-starting I-it from centre, the Widnes forwards rushed the leather over tbe Oldham line, and forced them to save. This was sup- plemented by Farrell attempting to drop a goal for the visitors, but only a dead ball resulted, and the pressure still being kept up in the Oldham territory, a touch-in-goal was also put to the credit of Widnes. Farrell was next to the fore by a dodgy run near the home club's line' but Arm- strong gained possession, and by a splendid rush was not brought down until he had reached midfield. This brought about half-time, with the score at Oldham one goal and one minor point, to Widnes five minor points. On change of ends KenricK kicked off for Widnes, and a scrimmage was formed at centre, but eventually the visitors were forced to touch down. Goulding now retired hurt, and for the rest of the game Widnes played fourteen men. Thompson then kicked the ball over the visitors' line, a dead ball resulting, which was followed by a couple more similar points, also in favour of Oldham. Scrimmages were now the order of the day, but the Widnes representatives were twice more forced to touch down, the game eventually ending in a victory for Oldham by one goal and eiet minor points to Widnes five miner points. Widnes bad bard lines on several occasions, and Armstrong and Thompson were the pick of the Oldham men. Teams : J Murray, back; C H Barlow, J Armstrong. and J T Thompson, three-quarter-backs; J Clough and 3 R Mills, half-backs; H Court, J B Rye, W Ceoper, J D Kent, E Wood, J R Biley, J Taylor, J Smith, and R H Selby, forwards. Widnes: S Lawson, back; D Hardman, D Connolly. and J B Briggs, three-quarter-backs; T Ridgords and E Farrell, half-backs; S Li Kenrick, 1.1 Rowan, .1 H Smith, J Pervin, W Kiddie, Meagher, A Brown, T Fogg, and Goulding, forwards.

div.head: NOTES BY THE WAY.
div.p: NOTES BY THE WAY.

The Blackburn Rovers on Saturday secured their second successive victory over the famous Queen's Park Club, Glasgow, and for the second time received as their reward the only Challenge Cup open to the Association clubs of any nationaltv who like to compete for its possession, and which consequently is regarded as the emblem of the cham- pionship. Blackburn may well be proud of the successes achieved of late years, which have led to the representation of the Borough In the final tie of the competition four years together, and in the cup having a resting-place in the town for three years. There was less doubt in regard to the out- came of the match on Saturday than in either of the three final ties preceding it, The teams were well matched, it is true, and played with spirit from the start to the finish, and there was enough of exciting play to satisfy any enthusiast. The dash with which the Rovers began to attack their opponents' goal at the very outset, and the steadiness of their defence, afforded abundant evidence to justify the confidence of their supporters. Time after time they were within an ace of scoring, and only fourteen minutes had elapsed when Forrest secured the Initial point of the game. Before Brown proceeded to the pavilion to prepare to lead the Rovers into the enclosure for the match, he received the energetically-expressed adv.ce from "the Doctor " to make the play fast, and the advice received due attention. For a short time soon after the change of ends the pace slackened, but it subsequently became faster than over, if that were pos- sible, until near the close, when the knowledge that the vic- tory had been secured led the Rovers to slacken somewhat in their efforts. There is no doubt that the best team won, and fortunately there was no decision of the referee that could be disputed or leave it in doubt whether the possession of the trophy for the ensuing year was well merited. The Rovers' forwards played with the greatest dash possible, and the quickness displayed in pouncing on the ball prevented the scotch forwards from playing such a passing game as mocks the Queen's Park at their beet. On Saturday Stayeley beat Derby Midland by two goals to none, in the final tie of the Derbyshire Cup Competition; the Druids beat Oswestry by three goals to none by playing an extra half-hour, after a drawn game, in the final tie of the Wales and Border Counties Cup Competition; Middles- borough beat Acton by three goals to none; at Glasgow, West Bromwich Albion and the 3rd Lanark played a drawn game, two goals each; at Birmingham, Aston Villa beat Battlefield by two to none; at Bolton. Great Lever beat Kilmarnock by three to one; the Wanderers beat Renton by two to one; Barnwell beat Acton by three to two; in the Birmineham and District Charity Cup Competition Walsall Swifts beat Wednesbury old 'Athletic by two to one.

THE I'USSO'AFGHAN WAR.--TERRITORIAL 'MAP.

upon which a Cabinet Council was immediately summoned for that afternoon to consider the grave news conveyed therein. Sir Peter's despatch contains the information that a severe attack bad been made by the Russians upon the Afghan outposts at Penjdeh from Pal-i•Khatun. The Russian force was a large one, and the officials at the India Office believe the Russians have had men in reserve behind their outposts. Sir Peter is believed to be now at Gulran, where he will, it is supposed, remain to guard the Robat Pass on the road to Herat. His despatch was cut off at the most important point, and it is surmised by the officials that the telegraph wire which runs through Persia has been cut, this opinion being strengthened by the fact that Sir Peter had to send couriers such a long distance with his despatch that he would not have forwarded it piecemeal. Such news as was received, however, was sufficient to inform the Govern- ment that Penjieh held its own. The information in the hands of the officials dees not lead to
the belief that so many as 500 Afghans were killed ; but there can be no doubt that the affair was

no mere attack upon outposts or skirmish. The matter is lcoked upon in official circles as most serious, and as afford- ing the possibility of a CC4.9t19 belli. Seventy thousand British and Native Indian troops, divided into two divisions of 25,000 each with a reserve, are appearing on the Indian frontier to be in readiness to advance into Afghanistan.

Tiiiii-fOrce-c-o.nlY probably reach Herat in time ro prevent that place from being attacked. The chief ships of the Mediterranean fleet, numbering six of our finest ironclads, are at Malta, under Lord Hay, and these could proceed at once to the Dardanelles if so ordered. Earl Granville ar:

~..... ..... —...—.......... ..—..... rived hi London on Thursday morning, and was engaged daring most of the morning with the chief officials at the Foreign Office. His lordship has been in close communica- tion with Lord Kimberley. Great excitement is evident In

all the Government departments. R&M FIND!. APRIL 9TH, 3-10 P.Df.—A despatch from Sir Peter Lumsden, dated Gulran, April Ist, states that the Russians have attacked the Afghans in their entrenched positions at Pen jdeh, and slaughtered 200 of the garrison. LATER DETAILS OF THE BATTLE. The following telegram appears in the second edition of Thursday's Times:— GUI:RAN, APRIL 3.—The Russians, making a pretext of a change in the position of the Afghan outpost, attacked the Afghans at Penpeb, on March 30, and drove them out. The Afghans fought stubbornly, but the diy was wet, and their muzzle-loaders were ineffective. Two companies de- fended one position till every man was killed. The Afghans retreated in perfect order to Meruchak, and no pursuit was made. The Sarike remained neutral, but plundered the Afghan camp. The Russian loss is said to have been very great. The British officers remained until the Afghans had I effected their retreat, and then joined General Lumsden's c ALIA/MAD, Arm 9, MORNlNG.—Details of the fight between Russians and Afghans on the 30th of March will have reached you through the official sources. Repeated attacks were made on the Afghan outposts by the Russian force on the 29t6, and were only feebly repulsed. It was felt that no serious resistance could be offered by the Afghan troops. It was on the 30th, however, that the main assault took place, and the safety of the British officers present was not in any way respected by the assailants. After the vic- tory of the Russians the force of General Komaroff ocmpied Pen jdeh.—Daily Telegraph. LARGE REINFORCEMENTS FOR INDIA.

The Press Association says ;—Frequent meesages have Passed during Thursday between the War Office and India regarding the military arrangements to be made, and it is believed there will be no delay in despatching to India a large body of men, probably from 8,000 to 12,000, to rein- farce the troops now there. It is also regarded as probable that the First Army Reserve will now be called up. During the sitting of the Cabinet messengers were frequently pass- ing from the Premier's residence to the Foreign and India Offices and back again with despatches. It is imported that Lord Dufforin has had another interview with the Amer in which he conveyed the news of the attaok upon Pendjeh. The Viceroy has been in consultation also with Sir Donald Stewart, and it is believed that the advice of the Indian military authorities is that there should lee no delay in throwing troops into Afghanistan. PANIC ON THE STOCK EXCHANGE. On the London Stock Exchange a state of panic—it might almost be described as one of terror—was caused on the receipt of the news on Thursday. Speculators of all kinds were frantically anxious to sell, but cauld not find buyers, and the result was a general fall. Consols almost immediately fell 2 per cent., and after some fluctuations during the day closed as low as 95. The most tremendous drop was, however, in Russian bonds of 1873, which fell almost 10 per cent., from 91 to 81. Other foreign stocks aclined in sympathy with Consols, and threughout the day the sensation produced by the news affected speculation in a wild degree. Even in English railways there was a seri- ous fall. The pavement in the vicinity of Capel Court was crowded with an excitable mob, while in the " House " itself there was perfect uproar and din. The fact that Russians had declined 10 per cent was considered very indicative of the country's prospects in the money market, and was posted in several London newspaper offices side-by-side with the latest information concerning the col- lision on the Afghan frontier. On the Manches,er Stock Exchange the receipt of the news led to an almost complete stoppage of business, succeeded by panic, during which Rus- sian 4 per cents dropped continuously from 88± to alg. In Liverpool the market Was similarly affected. The Exchange Room was crowded by merchants and shipowners, the fact, as reported, that the Rusaians bad made a serious aggres- sion, being received with the utmost consternation.
