THE SOUDAN CAMPAIGN. OSMAN DIGMA'S SON KILLED. PROGRESS WITH THE RAILWAY. SMARM, SATURDAY, 11-50 A M —Troops began return march from Teselah z3reba at 2-15 p.m. yesterday, and ar- rived at No. 1 zereba at 5-50 pm. General Fremantle re- ports everything most satisfactory. They are now marching back, and will be herd with convoy about noon. &JAKE'S SUNDAY.—Out Of a force of 1,075, only 11 men fell out daring the march. Altogether there were 17 wounded and 33 sick. This expedition to Tamai, and the destruction of that place after Osman Digma's proclamation threatening to drive us into the sea, must have greatly dis- couraged his followers. Stumm, MONDAY, 447 P.m.—A large convoy of over 2,000 camels and 1,500 mules' escorted by four battalions, under Sir John McNeill, marched at 5 a.m. to clear out No. 1 zereba, bringing in the garrison—the 28th Bombay In- fantry—and will arrive about five o'clock. Ths railway has been advanced towards Handbub, protected by the Scots Guards and a troop of cavalry. Sumusr,'Saroupar.—The cavalry returned here yesterday evening from Tamai. The infantry left the zerebi on the road to Tama' at daybreak to-day, and will arrived here at noon. A spy sent out by the British military authorities has returned from Erkowit. He reports that Osman Digma's followers are openly deserting him, and that Osman Digma himself, with 900 followers, is at Shakateb, a strong position between Sinkat and Erkowit. Stumm, MONDAY.—The convoy which left at daybreak reached the zereba on the Tamai road at eleven o'clock, and will return here this evening. The Coldstream Guards and the Australians have arrived at No. 1 statioa, five miles on the road to Handoub, and are now forming a zereba. A few shots were exchaneed on their way thither. They will to-morrow proceed to Handoub, find be replaced at station No. Iby Scots Guards. A week's supplies will be sent to Handoub to-morrow. One of Osman Digtna's sons was shot during the recent fighting. Owing to the hot weather the number of sick is greatly increasing-7-10 p convoy has safely returned here with all stores. The ad- vance on Handoub has been postpened until the 8:h inst. It is believed that the Guards will leave here shortly. Lord Wolseley is expected here soon. SUARIM, SUNDAY.—AIi Kedah, Chief of the Numb tribe, has asked to come in to Suakim with six hundred of his followers. Redab's emissaries confirm the statement made by spies that the enemy are demoralised, and refuse to face our troops again.-Bfandard. SUAKIM, MONDAY.—The present intention at headquarters is to push straight on along the Berber-road, building forti- fied zerebas and block-houses every five miles. The road will go through Wady Otan and Tainbock, on to Es Sibil, 50 miles from Suakim. Es Sibil stands upon a very eleva- ted plateau, end here summer quarters for the troops will be established. Hence it will be easy to occupy Sinkat, as the plateau is open, and rises gradually from Es Sibil to the hill on which Sinkat is situated. The total loss of the tribes- men in the various engagements attained fully four thou- '. sand.—Standard. ; SWARM, TUESDAY.—The Scots Guards this afternoon l escorted a large convoy to No. 1 station, where they will ' for the present remain. i Spies sent out from here returned with confirmation of Osman Digma being deserted by his followers. 1 LORD WOLSELEY.-DEFEAT OF THE MAHDI. • CAIRO, MONDAY.—Lord Wolseley has arrived at Wady Haifa. Haesan Pasha will return to Cairo. DolgGlota, SATURDAY.—RebeI soldiers from Khartoam who have arrived at Merawi, report that a large portion of the Kordofan army has left the Mandi, and cam.nenced to ' return to the country, the men stating that they have served a sufficient time under arms,and that the object of the cam- paign has been attained. The Mandi followed them with a body of troops, and heavy fighting ensued. The Mandi was, however, compelled to retreat, after suffering severely. The Vakeel of the Mudir is performing tha latter's duties during his absence. Downoxe„ TOESDAY.—Further reports have been receiv- ed confirming the news of the rising in Koraofan against the Mandi. Dowaor.e. MONDAY. —lntelligence received here from Abu Gusi states that a brisk slave trade is being carried on from the province of Kordofan. The traders all carefully avoid approaching the stations occupied by the English troops. Further rep3rts have also been received confirm- ing the news of the rising in Keirdefan against the Mandi. DEFEAT OF THE MAHDI IN KOR- DOFAN. DONGOLA, TRURSDAY.—The latest news from Kordofan states that the Mandi sent a large force against Jebel Dair and El Obeid, but suffered a severe defeat at the latter place. His leader, however, escaped. Toe Mandi announ- ces that he will not attack Dongola until after Ransadan, three months hence. Colonel Primrose died yesterday of enteric fever at Aba el Fatmeh. The health of General Dormer's camp is good. The sick have much improved since leaving Korti. The camp is strongly guarded, a line of pickets being established on the hill on both flanks, with supports ready to move out when necessary. The Hassanyeh tribe round Birti are still hostile. The innrgents in Kordofan are stated to include some of the Mandi's best men.

THE RAWUL FIND! CONFERENCE. Sr. PrrEitsstrao, MONDAY.— Though in Government circles and in the press a pacific tone has prevailed during the last few days, the war preparations of Russia are still being actively continued. Considerable forces of infantry and cavalry are now escheloned near Askabad. Twenty versts of the railway from that place have been construc- ted—Daily Ne W 3. RAWIM Pirrnr, 81:N0117.—R rained pitilessly yesterday. The Viceroy held a Durbar of the Punjartb Durbaries to enable them to return to their homes, as it is uncertain on account of the weather, when the durbar in honour of the Ameer can take place. This afternoon the Viceroy inspec- ted the Ameer's troops. Opinion here will be inclined to adopt the view that it will be quite feasible for the Afghan boundary line to be drawn from rulikhatan to the junction of the Kuskh and Murgham rivers. In that case Palikhatan
- would go to Russia, and Penicleh would remain as part of Afghan territory. Universal satisfaction is felt here on all sides that our warlike preparations are not in any way to
be slackened.

Ream. PINDI, MONDLY.—Orders have been received for the immediate completion of the railway to Quetta. The Maharajah of Nepaul has made a definite offer of 15,000 picked Goorkhas, who were ready to march across the fron- tier on the receipt of a telegram from the Viceroy, the troops to be commanded by British officers. A grand review was held here this morning of all the trove-20,000 strong —and native contingents in the presence of the Viceroy, the Ameer, the Duke of Connaught, a glittering staff, and all the native _chiefs. It was one of the 'finest spectacles ever seen
lii India.

Liverpool steamers fitted out. Mr-Jimes Dunn, -chief-con- tractor, and other gentlemen were on beard the America on Saturday, making arrangements for the alterations to be made before the guns are put on board. She is to be armed with ten guns—six 64-pounders to be placed am;dships, and four 5-inch Vavaseur guns to be worked on racers, and placed two on the forecastle and two on the poop. SPEECH OF THE AMEER.

RAWUL PINDI, WEDNESDAY, 1-45 v sr.—The Grand Dur- bar in honour of the Ameer's visit was held this morning, and passed off admirably. The scene was a brilliant and impressive one. The Ameer sat on the right of the Viceroy on a dais, the Duke of Connaught occupying a seat on his Excellency's left. After the offering of presents the Ameer made a speech in which he said that he was obliged for the favours bestowed upon him by the Queen and the Viceroy, and in return he would render every peaceable service as regarded his army or his people. "As the British," con- tinued the Ameer, " have declared that they will help Al. ghanistan in beating off external enemies, the Afghan na- tion will join in the firmest manner, and will stand side by side with the British." At the conclusion of Abdurrahrnan s ' speech the Viceroy presented his Highness with a sword of honotir. The Ameer, in acknowledging the gift, said he hoped to strike with it any enemy of the British. His Highness appeared to be well satisfied with the whole pro- ceedings. GREAT BATTLE NEAR PENJ-DEH. - AFGHANS DEFEATED: po KILLED. CAMP, STORES, AND ARTILLERY CAPTURED. .

ST. PE-maw:Tito, Twausakv.—General Komaroff attacked the fortified positions of the Afghans on both banks of the Kushk River on March 30th. An engagement ensued, and the Afghans, whose force consisted of 4,000 men with eight guns, were defeated and dispersed with the loss of about 500 killed, the whole of their artillery, two standards, the entire camp, with the park of artillery and provisions. The Russians lost one Turcoman officer killed, Colonel Nikschitsot, and three subaltern officers were wounded. Of the Cossacks and Turcoman soldiers 10 were killed, and 29 wounded. The Press Association says confirmation has been received of the cypher telegram published by the Standard. It now appears that the engagement took place near the junction of the Murghab and the Knabk River situated about six or seven miles from Penjdeh. The news is regarded in politi- cal circles as of the gravest character, and important ques- tions are expected to be asked of Ministers this afternoon. Great secrecy has been observed among officials both in London and St. Petersburg respecting this intelligence. The Cabinet meets this afternoon previous to the reassembling of the House of Commons after Easter recess, the sum- monses having been issued yesterday, and the fuller infor- mation which Ministers may be Male to sapply is awaited with much anxiety. RUSSIAN ACCOUNT OF THE BATTLE

- ST. PETERSBURG, TitonsnAv.—The °frier/ Messenger' this morning publishes the following account of the fight- ing on the Kushk River. General Komaroff reports that in consequence of the provocative and manifestly hostile proceedings of the Afghans he was compelled on March 30th to attack their fortified positions on both bmks of the Kushk River. The Afghan detachment, numbering 4,000 men with eight guns, was defeated and dispersed with the loss of 500 killed, two standards, their whole camp, and all I their artillery and provisions. The Russians had one Tur- coman officer killed, and Colonel Nakhitch slightly wounded. Three subaltern officers were wounded. Of the Cossacks and Turcoman soldiers ten were killed and 29 wounded. When the fighting was over General Komaroff returned across the Kushk river to his former position. When some British officers, who were eye-witnesses of the engagement but had not taken part in it, saw that the Afghans were he tten, they asked the Russians for protection; but, unfortunately, a convoy which was immediately des- patched by General Komaroff was unable to overtake the Afghan cavalry, who in their flight carried off the British officers with them. not yet overtaken them, and the extraordinary progress that we have made is due mainly to the adoption of the sound and business-like principle of " payment by results." The large freedom which is spoken of as so ad- mirable is the characteristic, it may be pointed out, of private as distinguished from national schools; but, taking the relative differences of cost into account, who .will ven- ture to say that private schools hold their own as against national schools ? It is a com- mon cry amongst parents of the middle class that, although in many cases they pay three or four times as much for the tuition of their children, they do not "get along" as well as children who are attending national elemen- tary schools. Mr. WILD advocates the "large freedom" of the continental system, and yet, curiously enough, he admits that so far as " results " are concerned, they do not " order things better in France" or elsewhere on the Continent. He says :—" If there could be established any competition between them and us in such results as we professed to gain, he did not for one moment believe they would be in any way equal to ours." This is an ex • traordinary admission, and, in face of it, it seems idle to talk of "fundamental error" in the English system of education. But, perhaps, Mr. WILD means more than meets the eye when he refers to "such results as we profess to gain." He is, possibly, " kinder sarcastic," and would convey the impression that there is a wide margin between what is professed and what is performed. If he does mean this, it would be better to say it than to hint at it; and it would be better still to ac- company his assertion with authenticated facts. Let us by all means improve, where we can, upon the past; but we must be careful as to making fundamental changes in a system which has worked so well, and is still working well. Bad as "payment by results" may be, in some respects, it seems to us to be much better than the system of "large freedom" which is advocated by the President of the National Union of Elementary Teachers.

div.head: LOCAL NEWS.
div.p: LOCAL NEWS.

ACCIDENT AT FIDLER'S FBI/RT.—On Saturday afternoon a serious accident happened to Mrs Johnson, the wife of Mr John Johnson, of the Fidler's Ferry Hotel. It seems Mrs Johnson was sitting on the wall which surrounds the bowl- ing green watching the boat race, when she overbalanced ' herself and fell on some stone steps which lead up to the bowling green. When picked up she was bleeding very freely from cuts in her head. Medical aid was sent for, ' and Dr Smith was get there as soon as possible. Mrs John- son is now progressing very favourably. I PENNETH LIBERAL Assoceerrox.—The annual meeting of the officers and members of this association was held at the clubroom on Tuesday evening, when Mr John Peers occupied the chair. The secretary, Mr Mainley, read his report which showed that the organisation was in a satisfac- tory corulition. The treasurer's report showed that the re- ceipts for the year amounted to £45 1083 d, and paymentelo £45 4s 4d. Mr C E Parker was elected presidente'and the following gentlemen as vide-presidettst—Measra J Peers, H Hughes, J Turner, Joseph Wright, J Watson, G le Bolton, JDO Guest •, committee: Messrs W Longshaw, F Hughes, G Randall, TJohnston,F Baxter, 1 Seed, M Moore, H Dale, Jno Jackson, W Walters, W Gandy ; treasurer, Mr A J White ; secretary, Mr John Mainley (re-elected for the third time). PENICETH WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL.—OB Good Friday the committee and teachers of the above Sunday school held their annual tea party, when there was a large at- tendance. The ladies who prepared the tea were Miss Gar- nett, Miss Wynn Mies Moses, Mies Briscoe, Ac„ assisted by the various teachers and elder scholars. The object of the teachers in providing a tea meeting on the above day is to keep the Sunday scholars from going down to Fidler's Ferry, and the meeting was quite a success. After tea Mr J Watson, superintendent, occupied the chair. A good pro- gramme was gone through, consisting of reading, sacred solos by Misses Garnett, Fildes, Stretford, andMr P John- ston. Mr Raper, temperance lecturer, was also present, and gave a most interesting address to the children, which was loudly applauded. At the close of the meeting prizes were given to the scholars for good attendances. Mr Colin Cook, secretary, read the report, and Mr John Jackson, read a re- port of the financial position of the school. At the close, on the proposition of Mr Mainlerf, a hearty vote of thanks was accorded the chairman and all friends who took part in making the meeting a success. PENKETH Myrcret IMPROVEMENT ASSOCIATION: PRE- SENTATION. On Wednesday evening a largely-attended meeting of the members of the above association was held in the Wesleyan schoolroom, Penketh. A statement of accounts was submitted by the secreeezy, Mr Charles Par- ker, who showed that there was a balance in hand of £1 2s 41. The following officers for the ensuing year were appointed, viz : President, Mr C Parker ; secretary. Me Wilson • treasurer, Mr F Hughes, and several vice-presi- dents. This business having been transacted, the chair was occupied by the newly-elected president, Mr Parker, and a presentation was made to the late president, Mr Jas Dodds, and Mrs Dodds, who now reside at Lymm. The present con- sisted of a very valuable and handsome album, strongly and elegantly bound in Russia leather, and containing fifty original etchings by Alfred Slocombe. It contained the following inscription, Presented to Mr and Mrs James Dodds on leaving the neighbourhood, by the members of the Penkerh Mutual Improvement Association, as a token of the affectionate regard in which they are held, and in grateful recognition of their labours in promoting the social, intellectual, and moral well-being of their fellow-associates " Several members or the associa- tion, including the Chairman, Mr Watson, Mr Hobson, Mr R Garnett, Mr A White, and Mr C Cook, made short and suitable addiesses, in which they referred in very compli- mentary terms to the services of Mr and Mrs Dodds in rela- tion to the association, and to their connection with Penketh. In an appropriate acknowledgment of the gift, Mr Dodds said nothing was needed to remind him and his wife of their connection with Penketh or the members of the association, because, owing to the pleasant feelings which had grown up between them be should never forget the association and its members, or the place. He regretted haying had to leave Penketh, and he had not done so with- out giving the matter much consideration ; but, as it was, Lynam was not far away, and he intanded to still turn up sometimes amongst them. (Applauee.) He concluded be expreesine his pleasure at the success of the association, .end the hope that it would be even more successful in the future.

div.head: EXAMINER. SATURDAY, APRIL 11-,4
div.p: THE EXAMINER. SATURDAY, APRIL 11-,4

Ore MONDAY evening next a concert in aid of the Railway Servants' Society's Orphan Fund will be given in Lacey- street School, Widnes. An attractive programme has been drawn up and an enjoyable evening may be anticipated. A NEW Pooa RATE FOR RUNCORN.—On the application of Mr W Sutton, assistant overseer, Captain C W Hazle- burst and Mr G L Davies, magistrates, have consented to the laying of a new poor rate for the township of Runcorn of leki in the Z, to realise £2,128. • ACCIDENT AT WIDNES.—OR Saturday last a boy named John Battersby, who lives in Oakland-street, was passing the swings on the promenade, when one of the boats struck him on the head and knocked him to the ground. One of his arms Was broken, and he was otherwise seriously in- jured, but under the care of Dr McDonnell he is now re. covering. WESTON POINT WESLEYAN CHAVTL.—A. tea party was held in the schoolroom on Good Friday, and there was a good number of persons present. Afterwards a meeting was held, Mr F 0 Mostyn presiding. The Rev Thomas Hackett, Messrs James Wright, and Spearing, delivered ad- dresses. The choir ably rendered selections of music. The proceeds will be devoted to the fund for the choir treat. MAD DOG AT RUNCORN.—A woman and her daughter on Thursday evening complained to the police authorities that they had been bitten by a mad dog in High-street. P.C. Breeze went in search of the animal, which he found to boa fox terrier showing every symptom of rabies, and having ascertained that several persons had been attacked and bitten by the dog, be qaickly despatched it. The owner weld not be found. ZION CHAPEL, WIDNES,—On Monday night a public tea meeting was held to celebrate the first session of the Mutual Improvement Seciety, and a goodly number of friends gathered round. Mesdames Atherton, Lock, Perrin and Jones; Mdlles. Rimmer, Betney, and Harrison presided at the tables. After tea a most enjoyable entertainment was held, over which Mr Bray presided. The SUMS of the first session of the class augurs well for the future. BALL AT WIDNES.—On Monday evening a hall, promoted by the members of the Irish National Brass Band, took place in the Volunteer Hall. The interior of the building was decorated with bannerettes of varied hue, and the handsome banner of the Irish Foresters' Society occupied a prominent position. Mr Doogan ably officiated as M.C. Dancing was kept up till a late hour next morning to the strains of Mr Powell's brass band. THE EDDISBURY DIVISION OF CHESHIRE.—Mr Thomas Rigby, of Frodshatn, secretary of the Royal Manchester and Liverpool Agricultural Society, and of the Cheshire Chamber of Agriculture, has been invited by the Liberal Association of the Eddisbury Division of Cheshire to con- test the seat for some time. Mr Rigby has been seriously ill, and as he is now convalescent expectations are enter- tained that he will soon find himself in a position to reely favourably to the invitation. A NEW RATE FOR WIDNES.—At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, Mr Goff, the asssistant overseer, applied for the magistrates to sign a new poor rate for Widnes of 29 in the Z. The arrears upon the old rate amounted to £655 163 4d due on two accotents, one of the L. and N.W. Railway Company's of £350, now under appeal, and the other of a bankrupt. These amounts were recoverable. The ratealle value of the township was £l4O 760 10a and the present rate was estimated to produce £14,731 17s 4d.—The Chair- man (Mr E K Muspratt) asked why a bankrupt was allowed to get into arrears,—Mr (Jeff said they were not arrears. The gentleman became bankrupt becore the rate could be collected.—The magistrates signed the rate. Iir.,CORN Bomar. BOARD.—The monthly meeting was held on Wednesday. Present—Messrs Jam's Handley, J.P. (chairman), Rogerson, Moss, Whittaker, Littler, T Norman. and Salkeld (secretary). The Secretary reported that dur- ing the 12 months ending the 25th March there were 381 interments; last year, 324 ; increase, 57. The fees received daring the same period was £394 51 ; last year, £367 03 61 The total number of interments since the opening of the cemetery, Mach, 1860, was 6,780; viz, Church por- tion 2,735, Dissenters 3,495, Roman Catholics 550 The minutes of the Finance Committee, adoptel on the motion of Mr Moss, showed the fees received during the month amounted to £32 19e, and after paying the accounts there was a balance of £l.B 24 to be paid into bank. THE ATTACK ON MR. BUCKLEY AT RUNCORN.—In conse- quence of the charges made against him at the Holy 'Trinity vestry meeting on Monday evening, Mr Brickley has decline.), to accept the office of churchwarden. The fol- lowing requisition, signed by a large number of the mem- bers of the congregation' has been presented to him by a deputation treaded by Mr W Fisher :—" To Mr John Buck- ley.—Dear sir,—We, the undersigned, desire to express our sympathy with you in what we consider a most unjustifi- able attack upon you by Mr Rogerson at the late vestry meeting. In public estimation it has not injured you in the least degree. Hearing that you decline the werdenship, we beg you will recall your decidon, and accept it, for We eeneider not alone that you are fully qualified by a long am-t uprlgOe career as warden, but also that there is not a more honaurable conscientious gentleman to whom it a;:;) can be offered," Me eloelelee; has declined detinitelv to accede to the request of the ramisitionista. DEATH OF A PRIMITIVE METHODIST TAM PREACItEiI. —On Monday morning about 6 am., Mr Joseph Taylor, of Preston Brook, suddenly expired as he sat in his cheir, The deceareel was well-known and highly respected as hborious lay A preacher. He often walked :rem 10 to 20 miles on a Sunday to preace 01. • _ gospel, ant was well-known and WO' i".7v Arrington, Lymm, N ntirivich, Moul- toe, &c, besides the places on the Preston Brook circuit. HQ been a preacher over 30 years, which must have ilecessitated his walking some thousands of mi'ee. On Thursday afternoon when his remains were being interred at Daresbury Church, there was a large assembly of people. Amongst those who met at the residence of the deceased to accompany the body to the grave were the following : Rey J Pickwell, Runcorn' Rev L Miles, Frodsham, Messrs J Spruce, Preston Brook, T Stringfellow, Runcoru, J Whit- ley, Stockton Heath, S Davies, Manchester W Booth, Frod• ahem, R Peacock, Runcorn, L Douglas, Runcorn, besides is number of officials and members of the Preston Brook So- ciety. The funeral service, which was very impressive Was conducted by the minister of Daresbury Church, The coffin plate bore the following inscription 4eseph Tay- lor, died April 6th, 1885, aged 59 years." ' PENKETH SCHOOL —The annual general meeting of Pen- keth School was held on Friday lest week. From most parts of Lancashire and Cheshire appointed representatives were sent by various districts (it being a county school be- longing to the Society of Friends) to examine the state of the school, the various claeses, the finaccial and general matters, and report accordingly. For one day at least daily toil was thrown aside, old and youtg met together, parents and children joyfully united once more and after the busi- ness of the day was over, came tea, and cricket, football, and other games in the school. field, which wound up the day one that is long anticipated by all con- cerned and remembered for a lifetime even by old scholars now at the Antipodes. The school appears to fiourish, except that there are not so many girls as heretofore—a fact that caused some discus- sion—but it was stated that as this was the case at all the society's public schools everywhere lately, it probably pointed to depression of trade as the cause, the scholars being mostly drawn from the classes that are feeling it most There are 77 scholars, viz, 53 boys and 24 girls. This in- stitution has done an excellent work amongst the people for ever 50 years, and great thoughtfulness and tare is constantly exhibited by its friends as to it; efficiency in the great educational race of the future. It has had also the satisfactory character for many years back of paying its way and showing a good balance sheet at each annual meet- ing, notwithstanding the many improvements from time to time carried out. The wonderful degree cf health and almost entire immunity from epidemics, &c., diving those 50 years is the thankful surprise of everyone, as recorded in the an- nual reports from year to year. RUNCORN AND DISTRICT INISUSTRIA-2 INO SO- CIETY.—This society which has been recently formed, with Mr John Brundrit, J.P., as president, held an inaugural meeting on Thursday evening, in the National schools. The Rev W Preston, M.A., presided, and there was a good attendance, Mr.J E Meredith (secretsr:o), and Mr 0 Leak (solicitor) occupying seats on the platform. Mr Arthur Connor, of London, delivered a speech upon the principles and advantages of the society. He decl aree that this so- ciety was not formed for the purpose of creating opposition to the existing societies in the town, which might or may not mist the wants of the public. Although the Industrial had the kind patronage of several well-known churchmen, yet the society would not be sectarian in any sense of the term, and persons of all denominations would be heartily welcome. The primary object of the society was to enable persons to become tbeir own landlords. The entrance fee would be is for £lOO share, and the weekly subscription 63, and shares would be appropriated by ballot and by sale. It was proposed to make a ballot after the society hart been in existence twelve weeks. The ballot balls would be placed in a box, and each person present would have an opportunity of shaking them up, and the ball worrld be drawn under the supers ision of two scrutineers appointed by the meeting. The subscription books would also be passed round to show that the success- ful member was clear on the books. In many societies they made the declaration whether the member was clear upon the books or uot from the ledger, which he had himself posted up. It hoe been stated that a society upon sale and ballot principles was enfair to the working claeses. Of course they might have a gum?* er a bad ballot and sale so- ciety, but if they had a good one, ire contended there was not a society' in existence that would meet the wants of the working classes, or of the better classes so well. If a mem- ber bid £33 Os 8d for £lOO he would have to pay £lOO for £3OO, but he would simply repay to the society at the rate of £2 per month, or £24 per year until he had paid the so- ciety £3OO. the sum lent, and then be would pay off the amount he had bid for the money at the same rate, which would take him about four years longer. Of course when £3OO was lent upon a house, the surveyor and directors de- cided.whether it would realise that amount if they had to re-sell. Other advantages of the society were mentioned ; and Mr Connor answered a number of questions satisfac- torily. Mr Jordan moved a cordial vote of thanks to Mr Connor, and it IV:lo seconded by Mr E liaison and carried. A similar compliment was passed to the chairman on the motion of Mr Leak.

JosEnn MAZZINI, a memoir by E. A. V., with two essays by Mazzini : (1) "Thoughts on Democracy ;" (2) "The duties of man." No pecuniary profit is desired from this publication ; but it is hoped that this eloquent memorial of a noble patriot and a good man may awaken a true patriotic enthusiasm in the hearts of many young English readers ; mai that the principles set forth may help to the formation of wise and just political opinions. People's edition with portrait, price 61. To be obtained from Jolts S. edition, Bookseller, dx.,34,l3ridge-street, Warrington.—.Advf.

LECTURE ON GENERAL GoaDoN.—At Widn—es, before the members of the Widnes C.E.T.S. oa Thursday evening, the Rev J Wright Williams delivered * "gossiping" lecture on General Gordon in the Waterloo-road Schools. There was a good attendance. THE TaxFr BY A Samoa AT Rusconer.—James Duffey, a seaman, was brought before the Runcorn magistrates on Saturday, on a charge of stealing two pairs of trousere, the property of Thomas Nether, under circumstances already reported.—He was sentenced to 21 days' hard labour. LIGHT WEIGHTS AT WIDNES.—Elijah Withi n gton, manager of the Co-operative Stores, Albert-road, Widnes, Was summoned to Widnes Petty Sessions OD Wednesday charged with having unjust weights in his possession. Super- intendent Barker proved that in the shop, on the occasion of his visit on Monday, there were two weights not up to the required standard. The defendant contended that the weights had not been adjusted when the weights were last tested by mistake, and without his knowledge. He Was fined lOs and costs. SAVAGE ASSAULT ON A WIFE AT RUNCORN.-AI Run- corn Police Court on Thursday, before Mr James Handley and Mr J L Davies, John Stevens, a boatman, WAS charged under a warrant with assaulting his wife. It was alleged that on Saturday at noon the prisoner west borne under the influence of drink, and beat his wife with his fist, and also kicked her about the legs and body. He then seized a fender and inflicted a wound on her head and right eye- brow. Her eyes were blacked, and her body was much bruised. The Bench fined the prisoner £1 and costs, lei 10d, or fourteen days' hard labour. The money was paid. THE JEWELLERY ROBBERY AT RUNCORN.—At Knuts- ford Quarter Sessions on Wednesday, Annie Price (24), alias Needham, Margaret Bramble (27), alias Brambury, alias Bcamby, alias Basnett, sad Eliza Nash (30), were indicted for having on the 17th February stolen one jewel. lery case, 30 silver rings, one glove stud, and one set of shirt studs, the property of James Sutton, watchmaker and jeweller, Church-etreer, Runcorn. Mr Bankes prosecuted, and Mr Lloyd defended Price. The other prisoners were undefended. Toe fury returned a verdtet of not guilty. The Chairman, in discharging the prisoners, said he thought the jury had done right. If Price bad been convicted, she would have undoubtedly bees sent to penal servitude for five years, because she had been before the court five times previously on charges of felony. He also warned the other prisoners. IF You Warn GOOD Cases of any description, or tubs, or timber, apply to Mr. Joseph Anderson's Cooperage, Apple- ton-street, Widnes. Cheapest terms in the town.—Advt. PRESTON BROOK WESLEYAN CHAPEL.—In connection with this chapel a tea meeting was held in the school-room on Good Friday. There was a very large attendance, and I the wants of the guests were attended to by Mrs Clare' Mrs Grounds, Mrs Cragg, Miss Jones, Miss E Jones, and Miss A Ryder. Subsequently a public meeting was held under the presidency of Mr T Norman, of Runcorn, who delivered an appropriate speech. Addresses were also given by Messrs J Johnson, W Jones, and S Massey. The choir, under the leadership of Mr T Johnson, sang serveral anthems in capi- tal style, the aedience testifying their hearty appreciation. The children also sang several piec s of music in a highly pleasing manner. The solo "Happy are we," by Misses Grounds, of right and six years respectively, were much en- joyed. Mr Frodshatn presided at the harmonium with his customary efficiency. The usual votes of thanks concluded the proceedings. 'TelleFr OF A WATCH.—At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, before Mr E K Muspratt, Mary Eyres and Mary Morley were elarged with having, on the 3rd instant, stolen from a dwelling-house in Oakland-street, a silver watch and chain, value £5 Sc, the property of Jas Heath, a labourer. On the afternoon of the day in question the articles were safe on the parlour table. Mrs Eyres was in the house during the day. Subsquently the watch and chain were missed, and it was discovered that the Drisnner Morley had taken the watch ts Mr Syred's pawnshop in Waterloo-road. She stated that it belonged to her husband, and the assist- ant, Joseph Reading, advanced her 303 upon it. On the 6th inst Robinson apprehended the prisoners. In answer to the charge Eyres admitted having committed the theft,_adding that Morley knew she had done so, and had hidden the guard in the chimney of her house. The officer afterwards found the guard c)ncealed in the chimney.— The prisoners were committed for trial to the next Quarter Sessions.

LOCAL CASES AT CHESTER SESSIONS.—The adjourned quarter sessions for the county of Cheater were held at Chester Caetle on Thursday, the deputy chairman (his Hon- our Judge Horatio Lloyd) presiding. The following local cases were dealt with: Alleged Theft at Frodsham: Samuel Burkhill surrendered to bail charged with stealing a jar and three gallons of sherry, the property of James Rigby, at Frodsham Lordship. The jury considered the evidence insufficient to convict upon, and acquitted the pri- soner.—Disgraceful Conduct of Boys'at BUILCOM : James Garnett, 15; John Pilling, 18; Samuel Hignett, 15 ; Richard Thomas Reese, 16; and George Alfred Turner; 15, were charged with having improperly assaulted, with in- tent, Beliefs Hayes; I.Q ;sere of age, (laugh*, of Thomas Hayes, Canal-street. Rendorn, in We Cemetery Idris, Run-. .6otn,tingunclay last. The case against Turner fell through. Garnett and Pilling were sentenced to six weeks' imprison- ment, end I:tie;4l and Hianett to one 31onth's imprisonment, with. tiei httoui. • . , WIDNES SCHOOL 130111 b flpeeiat Meeting of Whines School Board was held on Thursday afternoon, Mr T S Timmis in the chair. Present: Dr. O'Keeffe, Messrs Bradshaw, Deacon, Glover, and the clerk. Dr O'Keeffe moved the adoption of a financial statement for the half- year ended the 25th Merch. It showed that the total receipts for that period amounted to £2,891 054 d, including grants from the Council of Education to the amount of £1,967 4 ; and school fees £734 9s 10s. The expenditure was £2,722 Ts' including the following items :—Salaries of officere of the Boyd. £262 1881 ; legal and other expenses of administration £65 9s 101 salaries of teachers, £1,519 4s; !mks, apparatus, and stationary, £135 5s I.dh oontribations toWards industrial schools, £57 8s lel , filmy; Ment of principal AO interest of loans, £542 lOs Ski There was a balance in hand of £l6B 13s 4d. .The outstanding liabilities of the Board were : Loans from Public Works Commissioners, £31,738 193 81 • and other liabilities includ- ing balance overdrawn, £637 8s '2L—The motion for the ad- option of the.statement was Seennded_by the Chairman. and ROBBERY FROM A 131tIGANTINE AT RTINCORIT.—At Run- corn Petty Session, on Tuesday, Wm. Winder and Joseph Debina, young men, were charged with having, on the 3rd April, felonteaely stolen one block, value 30s, the property of John Ace.—The prosecutor is the master of the brigan- tine Constance Ellen, now lying in Duke's Dock. On Fri- day night whilst in the cabin he heard two men walking along the Quay side, and shortly afterwards noticed that one had stepped on beard. He went upon deck and found that one of the men had the block produced in his posses- sion, and woe about to hand it over to his companion, but the captain prevented him. The man who had the block was the prisoner Debina, but the prosecutor could not identify Winder. On Sunday night P.C. Dale apprehended the prisoners at the docks. In answer to the charge they replied, "It wasn't us. We were at Gareton at the time." He recognised the prisoners from tqe description of the prosecutor. They had been knocking, about the docks for the past live weeks.—The Bench were of opinion that there was not sufficient eeidence to convict Winder, who woe dis- charged. Debina was sentenced to seven days' hard labour. GAMBLING Al' FIDDLER'S FEE.—At an Occasional Court held on Saturday at the offices of Mr Bucktoo, Horse- market-street, Michael Hennessy, Cropper's Brow, a young fellow well-known to the borough Police, was charged with gambling with cards at Penketh on Good Friday.—P.S. . Carey, P.S. Barnes, and P.C. Slingsby saw prisoner playing a game of chance at Fiddler's Ferry.—ln defence prisoner said that he saw the game played at Liverpool races; and had he thought that it was illegal he would not " have had the audacity to play it in the presence of the police officers who were near. When he was brought to Arpley in custody he was, he said, harshly treated. The officer in charge of him exposed him through Bridge-street and Buttermarket- street, and refused to take him to the police station by way of Mersey-street. What money be had he would gladly hand over to be given to the Warrington Infirmary or some other charitable institution. (Laughter.) lie hoped that he should be leniently dealt with, as it was not what he had been in the past, but what he should be in the future. He admitted that there was a !mg list attainst him but was sorry for it.—He was fined 103 and costs, or an alternative of 14 days in jell. DARESBERY HIGHWAY BOARD.—An ordinary meeting of the meml-ers of this Board was held at the Board-room, Daresbury, on Thursday afternoon, when there were pre- sent—Mr E Greenall, chairman ; Mr J Cliffe. vice-chair- man ; Rev A Kenworthy, Messrs W Long, James Knowles, Peter Percival, J W Haddock, James Parr, Thomas Bennett, Henry Hayee, Philip Derbyshire, Henry Houghton, Peter Ticks, R L Fryer, CT Whitley, Thomas S Burgess. James Barber, Linaker (clerk), J Darbyshire (surveyor), &c.—ln accordance with notice given at the last meeting, the Chairman moved that £2O be allowed to Mr James Darbyehire for his services for three months, during which time be had taken his brother's place, as the latter had been ill—Title proposition having been seconded, Mr Bennett moved as an amendment that only £lO be allowed.—Mr Barber seconded. —On being put to the meeting, eight voted for the amendment, and eight for the original motion. The chairman gave his casting vete in favour of the proposition, which was carried.— The Surveyor reported that in consequence of damage done to the road in Latchford by leakage from the canal, he had had to put down eight tons of Broken stone, at a cost. of .£4 lie 41—On tbe proposition of the Chairman it was decided to apply to the Bridgewater Navigation Canal Com- pany for re-payment of the £4 Ile 41.—The Clerk read the following estimates for the coming year :—h Surveyor's estimates, prepared by Mr Darbyshire, to be spent on main roads, £2,550 104; salaries and other charges (say) £250; total estimated expenditure for year, £2,800 lOs ; estimated reserve fund in hands Of • Treasurer, March 25tb, 1886, 605 8a fed ; total. £3,405 18e •, balance in Treasurer's bands. HIGHWAY MEETING.—The ratepayers of Cadishead held their annual meeting on Monday evening in the Wesleyan Day School, Mr John A Holmes presided. The secretary, Mr S Barnett, read the statement of accounts, showing an outlay for the year ending March 25th of £345 5s Sld, and leaving a balance of £3. Mr John Howarth, who has been waywarden for two years, was re-elected, and received great praise for the judicious manner in which he had spent the rate. Some lively discussion took place on minor points, but the meeting altogether passed off very pleasantly. A new rate of 6d in the £ was adopted to meet next year's ex- penses ; and a vote of thanks was given to Mr Howarth for his services for the past year, which be responded to. A vote of thanks to the Chairman closed the meeting.
CHARGE AGAINST A WIDNES ASSURANCE
AGENT.

At Widnes Petty Sessions on Wednesday, before Mr E K Muspratt and Mr H Gasket], lan, James Gaghan, a she- maker, living at 4, Margaret-street, Widnes, was charged with having unlawfully withheld certain monies belonging to the United Assurance Society, Liverpool, amounting to £2B 8s id—Mr W H Quilliam appeared for the society, and Mr W T Husband for the defence.—Mr Quilliatn said the case was brought under the provisions of the Friendly Societies Acts. The United Assurance Society was one of the oldest friendly societies in the country, having been es- tablished in 1832. The defendant had been employed for many years as one of their collectors, and under the certi- fied rules each agent undertook to visit the central office or the district manager on the Thursday in each week to pre- sent a statement of accounts, and pay whatever money he had received during the week after deducting commission. Ths defendant did not submit his statement for the week ending July 3rd until the 22nd of November, and then paid Gs short, and no return whatever was submitted nor money received for the weeks between the 31st July to the 31st December. During the period the defendant's collecting. book showed that he had received upwards of £3O. For the first week in January the defendant sent in a proper ac- count, but ignored altogether the live months mentioned, and Mr Quilliam contended had thus acted with a consider- able degree of craft, and had nacre sly escaped beini4 prosccu• ted for embnzlemen‘.—Mr Husband said there was no I doubt the defendant eras in arrears, but the rocie•ty had I seized his books, and he could not sty to what extent. The defendant held policies of the; society amounting to £7O and had paid upwards of £2l. in premiums, and Mr Husband contended that this metier ought to be settled in a civil way, or by arbitration as provided in the rules. He pointed out that for some time past the society had been receiving payments on account of arrears, and under these circum- stances he failed to see how the charge could be mtintained. —Mr Quilliam salt the secretary of the society died some time ago, and he could not say what arrangement the de- fendant had made with him.—Michael Francis Cavanagh, inspector of agents for the society, was called, but he failed to prove the first item against the 'defendant, and one of the vouchers out in bore upon it an item paid on ac- count —The Chairman said the society had been such a long time in bringing the matter forward and had been receiving money on account, that the Bench did not see hew this charge could be supported. He suggestel that the case should be adjourned in order that the solicitors could de- cide as to the amoult due, and settle the matter.—Mr Hue- band said he would advise his client to pay whatever was due.—Mr Wiliam said the society would not object to a reasonable agreement.---The case was adpurned for a wok,

WIDNES LOCAL BOARD ELECTION. The annual contest has excited comparatively little in- terest on the preeent occasion. The mural lieeitaiure haf been scanty, the uenal sepaibe • hatee been entirely absent, and there has been nO adVOcricy.of the claims of the candi- dates by word of mouth. Even an indepentlent caadidate failed 10 enliven the proceedings, and the battle lay simply between tbe Owners and Occupiers' AssoolatiOn :and the Property Owners' Association. The voting papers were distributed on Thursday week and collected on Tuesday, whilst the work of counting the votes was commenced on I Wedneadarmornings. H Geesage, the chairman of I the Boardeofficiated as relurnieg officer. He wae attendee, by Mr C H Lewin as lege.: adviser, and Kr (4.eii, the asais- taut overseer. The. ..a ese .ngernente for essertainiag the vet- diet of the. ratepayers were Sallied out by Mr J T Allen, to a voy satisfactoty manner, a large stiff of clerks being employed. Bleb Candidate had a representative present to watch over his interests, and Mr J W Wareing was present on behe.lf of the owners and occupiers and Mr S Sadler represented the Ratepayers' Association. A state of the poll was issued at 12 o'clock and at four o'clock. At the former tour Mr J W Hargreaves occupied the fourth position with 457 votes, he being the only Ratepayers' Assoseation nominee in the first five. At four o'clock the Owners and Occupiers were altogether in the ascendant, Mr Midwoon being only 14 votes' however, behind the fifth man. The final result, which may perhaps be sub- jected to a slight alteration, WAS declared as follows at 5-30 : J lavior B Brown F Reyes 1,518 W Bader D Wright 1514R Webster 1,017 W T Husband It will thus be seen that the Owners and Occupiers' As- sociation have completely wiped out their defeat of three years ago, when the Ratepayers' Association returned all their nominees by triumphant majorities. Much regret is expressed that Mr Midwood has not secured a seat upon the Board, to which his energetic and able labours of the past three years frilly entitled him. He was strongly pressed to allow his name to be brought forward by the owners and occupiers, but he declined to desert the Association which be had much to do with forming and carrying on. It may be stated that the highest number of votes recorded last year WAS 2,227 (for Mr Gossage) 499 more than given for the bead candi- date on the present occasion. Last year Mr W Sadler polled 1,131 votes and Mr I W Hargreaves only 425. So that although thee- have improved their position they are still unsuccessful. Mr D Wright was the only retiring member re-elected. Toe other retiring members were Messrs Mid- woad, Webster, and Martley. After the declaration of the poll Mr Taylor,. proposed a vote of thanks to the returning officer.—lt was seconded by Mr B Brown, and supported by Mr .1 W Wareing and Mr. S Sadler. Each gentleman spoke of the impartial and effi- cient manner in which the contest had been conducted, and the motion was carried by acclamation.—ln replying, Mr Gossage thanked everybody connected with the election for the kind support they had given to hitn.—Mr Taylor moved a vote of thanks-to Mr Allen and the officers of the Board in eulogistic terms.—Mr Heys seconded the motion. He was sure that the officers of the Board were not surpassed by any officials in the country for their courtesy and ability. —Mr Gossage said he must add his testimony to this mo- tion. Daring the two or three years he had been chairman of the Bard he had found Mr Allen and all the other officers under him most efficient, and as courteous and obliging as officers possibly could. He thought every mem- ber of the Board would hear him out in that statement. (Applause.)—The motion was carried by acclamation.—Mr Allen ackeowledged the vote. The really hard work he said had fallen upon Messrs Hoyle, Wilson, Whitfield, and Hughes. and everybody must bear testimony to the excel- lent manner in which they had performed it. The official declaration of the poll has been issued. Mr Midwood's votes have been incressed by three, and Mr Sadlet's by ten, but the result of the election is unchanged. There were 922 voting papers not delivered. 139 papers were not counted in consequence of the voters not having paid their rates, and there were 808 spoiled papers.

MR GLADSTONE AND ARBITRATION WITH RIISSIA.—Mr Gladstone, having been requested by a number of members of Parliament to refer the matters in dispute with Russia to arbitration in case diplomacy should fail, has replied that he "sees no reason to abandon the anticipation that a satis- factory settlement may be arrived at by ordinary diplematic methods." BOILED TO DE&TH IN A VAT.—A shocking discovery was made at Preston's Distillery, Liverpool, on Thursday. When work was resumed the body of a man unknown, and evidently a labourer, was found in a vit of boiling liquor. He had evidently climbed a wall of considerable height, and in getting into the premises had stumbled Into a vat and been scalded to death. No noise was heard by the watch- man during the night. A FEMALE BURGLAR.—Mary Ann Giles WO charged at Leicester Quarter Sessions on Thursday with burglary. The prisoner, while in prison, made a desperate attempt to com- mit suicide by setting herself on fire, when she was so terri- bly injured that her trial had to be postponed and her life was at one time despaired of. She was found play, and having had a long criminal career, was sentenced to seven years' penal servitude. A LONDON RAILWAY STATION BURNT DOWN.—An alarm- ing fire occurred on Thursday morning, at Shepherd's Bush, Metropolitan station. About two o'clock flames Issued from one of the wooden arches, supporting the station, which was recently opened as a sweet shop. The whole station was soon wrapped in flames. Little remains of it but the signal box and one waiting-room. Half of each platform was destroyed. The cause of the fire is nknown.

LONDON, TErfasnear. The peacefal prospects of last week have suddenly be- come clouded over. Lord Hartingtoa's statement in the House of Commons to the effect that the anewer then oa. its way from St. Petersburg was of a kind that promised peace was accepted to its fullest extent. Lord Ilartington is not the kind of man to jump at cocci usions, or to rashly indulge in sanguine expectations. But it has sinceinbetheme made known that, traced to its source, the basis of the con- clusion of the Cabinet had come to rest wholly up verbal representations of the Foreign Minister at St. Peters- burg. He had told Sir E. Thornton that the rely nee of a most conciliatory nature, and Sir Edward Thornton had telegraphed this to London. The general tone of the answer bears out this description. It is decidedly concilia- tory. But the immediate effect, were it accepted, would b 0 to delay the eettlement of the queetien at issue. 'lbis is a point upon which tke Ministry stand firm. Delay, it is shrewdly suspected, may simply mean epportunity to Rus.eia of better equipping herself for war. This is a trap into which the Government will not fall, and Russie's reply has been 'net by a firm reiteration of the former demand. This is not much, amounting to a request that the vexed question of the Afghan Frontier shall forthwith be settled ha accordance with arrangements approved by Russia less than a year ago. The Delimitation Commission has actu- ally been nominated. Sir Peter Lumsden has, fortunately as it turns out, been on the spot all through the winter. What is wanted is that the Russian Representative should present himself and get to work. The very moderation of tkis demand justifies the suspicion with which refusal to com- ply with it arouses. War with Russia would be a terrible thing. But even those whose principles scf rereesmolPuLtesityi"lly opposed to war recognise the necessity o con- fronting Russia at the prest nt crisis. This attitude is the more generally maintained because of the confidence that the present Ministry, whose jealous and watchful of the interests and the honour of the country, will not recklessly invite war. If England within the next few weeks declares war against Russia it will be because that was the last resource. It is pretty certain that had the present crisis arrived du- lug the late administration we should even now be plunged in the full horrors of war. We were pretty near it in IS7B. There is a story about Lord Beaconefield diniug out ens evening daring the height of the war fever, which illustrates the situation. He had for companion a well-known lady , whose syrnp ithies ran with those of society irr favour of the , Turks. " Why don't you," she said with the courage of ' her sex, " seize this opportunity which may never recur and declare war against Russia ?" Lord Beaconsfield seem- ing to be in deep thought made no answer. " What are you wailing for," cried the lady impatiently. "I am wait- ing for some roast mutton and potatoes "said the Premier. The kind of influence then at work to plunge two nations into war still exists in Leaden, but happily holds a subor- dinate position. Ft:mons DRIV/NG.—The driver of a tram engine running between Manchester and Bury was on Thursday fined £5, with the alternative of two months' imprisonment, for driving his engine at a speed of 19 miles an hour along the highway. The engine drivers are prohibited from exceed- ing a rate of eight miles per hour. GREAT FIRES AND LOSS OF L/FE.—Late on Saturday night a fire occurred at a cottage in Lambeth, London. The first room on the first floor was occupied by Mr W Vise, 79 years of age. The heat thrown out bv the are. as well as the suffocating smoke, prevented the fire brigade for some time entering the room. In the course of half an hour the outbreak was completely subdued. As soon as the prernioe3 had sufficiently cooled the room WO entered, and the re- mains of the unfortunate occupier found amongst the debris. —On Monday morning a fire broke out in an extensive block of buildings at °forestry, belonging to Mr T Parry, skin- ner and tanner, and was not extinguished till it had done damage to the amount of upwards of £40,000. Only a small portion of the loss is covered by insurance. About 120 workpeople are thrown out of employment. '

Let me add that the Royalty opened with the Easter holidays Miss Santley back in her old tteatrO. "Francois the Radical" is a comic Opera of the. Madame Angot type both in plot and music. The latter is by a poor French cemposer, who had never gratlyaig- nalised himself, and died before his very succeseful piece was produced in Paris. The music is most tuneful, and fresh, and varied; bat the English libretto is not Vey good.

The court. was crowded, hundreds being unable to obtain admission,. and the liveliest interest was manifested in the prcerdlngs. Mr Hodgson prosecuted for the police, 'and Mr Salith de- fended Knnck3r. The prisoners pleaded not guilt:, and re- served their defence. They ware committed for trial at the Manchester Assizes.

WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT: Serunnat.—Before Alderman Chandley. " CHARGE OF DESERTION.—JOIOI Samuel Harper IVES -ohttrged- on remand with being a deserter from H.M.S. 'Superb, stationed at Malta, on or about the 27th of January jest. He was apprehen4ed by Iffitpector Sinks, and was at the time wearinv a light overcoat over his uniform. He told the Inspector that he bad been discharged for refusing • 10 do duty, but that he had lost his discharge. Chief Con- *able Hunt said tbat he had written to the Amiraltq Office ,in London for corroboration of prisoner's story, but had received no reply. Having become a member of the League of the Creme, she was allowed her libertv.—Mary Gagban, charged on a war- rant with committing a breach of the peace by fighting in Winwick.street on the 26th December, was bound over to keep the peace for six months. TIIESDAY.—B:fore Councillor Broadbent and Alderman Holmes. The business is reported elsewhere., WEDNESDAL—Before Aderman Pickmere and Mr John Fairclough. DRUNKENNESS —Thomas Dasey was fined 103 and costs, Or 14 days in prison, for being drunk and disorderly in Bewsey-street, the previoes evening, and assaulting his aister-in-law. Teiresreeee—Before Major Litton and Alderman Webster. A LAN' VAORANT.—John Styles was charged with neg- _lecting to perform his work whilst a casual inmate at the vagrant ward at the Union, and doing damage to hie cell to the amount of N.—Prisoner said that it was the first time he had been in a vagrant ward, and he had not done wrong wilfully. The bricks in his cell were loose.—He was dis- missed with a caution. DRUNKENNESS AND VIOLENCE.—MichaeI Riley was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Wilderspool- road on the previous evening, and with assaulting P.C. Taylor in St. James-street, Latchford.—He struck the officer two violent blows in the face, and was taken into custody with the assistance of another cone able.—Fined lOs and costs, or 14 days' imprisonment.--Annie Maher was sent to prison for a month for being drunk and disorderly on the previous evening. Feenes.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Harrison) and Mr John White. MISCELLANEOrS.—John Cook was charged with using threats to Robert Hind, cabinet maker, on the 7th inst. Complainant, who was in the employ of the defendant, said that the latter threatened to dash his brains out with a piece of wood, and said, "I will kill you." Defendant gave an emphatic denial to that statement. Defendant was ordered to be bound over to keep the peace for six months, himself in £lO, and one surety of LIO, or to go to prison for 14 days.—Simeon Monks was charged with sleeping out. The case was not pressed, and he was dismissed.—Albert Allen, John Southall, Thomas Lloyd, and Thomas Roberts, boys, were ordered to receive six strokes each with the birch rod for damaging a house in Catherine-street, OD the 27th ult. of the past curates of this neglected parish have received. We would also respectfully urge the necessity of both gen- tlemen being licensed to, and only removable by your Lord- ship, and further that it is very desirable they should have separate and distinct abodes. The small house in which pre- vious curates have been compelled to live, with one servant provided by the Rector, has been a constant source of trouble. Humbly praying that our petition may be deemed worthy of your Lordship's serious consideration, we remain your Lordship's humble servants.—(Signed) John Edward Wright, R W Prencomb, churchwardens; Thomas Cawley, William Gill, James Morris, Thomas Moores, sidesmen.— P.S.—We have purposely refrained from asking other than the officers of the church to sign the above." The Rector: I think you should hear from me my side of the question. I will begin with Mr Montgomery, who was recommended to me by the Lord Bishop of Liverpool as a curate. Mr White: I would not go into that matter, but speak generally. The Rector: I was only going to mention one particular thing, but I will speak generally. I think there is one part in the document that says" Mr Montgomery was ditmissed, as you know, at a moment's notice, for what reason no one here knows." Mr Montgomery came to my house in a very insulting way to my wife, and the result was that I was obliged to write to the Bishop, who deter- mined to go into the whole case, and he employed his arch- deacon to investigate the matter. The archdeacon came to me and made every inquiry, and he likewise saw Mr Mont- gomery and Mr Weller, and they all agreed that the state- ment that was sent to the bishop was satisfactory and true. The archdeacon then reported to the bishop the whole statement. I must tell you that I bad given Mr Mont- gomery, according to an agreement, if at any time we wished to separate, three months' notice. I gave him three months' notice on the sth February last, and the result was that the bishop writes me this letter. —"Feb. 18, 1585. Dear Mr Quekett,—l have received Archdeacon Bardeley's report about the matter between you and Mr Montgomery. After carefully considering it, I have advised Mr Montgomery to accept three months' stipend and to leave Warrington at once. I trust this will have cut the knot of all difficulties." The bishop wrote at the same time to Mr Montgomery. I agreed to the bishop's terms and paid Mr Montgomery LIO for three months' salary up Ito the sth May next, and Mr White, in whose hands the I money went, got a receipt for it. Mr W H Harrison : May I ask what the offence was F We have not got that information yet. The Rector: I shall not enter into it. (Laughter.) Mr Francomb: It is unfair to make a one-sided statement

WARRINGTON PARISII CHURCH. THE RECTOR AND HIS CURATES. STORMY PROCEEDINGS. At noon on Tuesday the annual vestry meeting in connec- tion with Warrington Parish Church was held in the vestry, under the presidency of the Rector, the Rev W Quekett. Amongst those also present were the Revs J A Drummond (curate), W Wilson (Bartonwood), the Mayor (Alderman Harrison), Alderman Burgess, Messrs J E Wright and R W Francomb (wardens), H B White (vestry clerk), A Browne, Nicholson, T Moores, S Davies, J Clarke, N B Percival, J Dewharst, R Isherwood, W H Harrison, T Eaude, C White, Scotson, J W Whittle, F Taylor, J P Leigh, J C Craik, Fairclough, Littlewood, W H Howard, and A Reid (parish clerk). The duty of auditing the annual accounts was entrusted to the Mayor (Alderman Harrison) and Alderman Burgess. That having been done, the rector's warden, Mr Wright, said, that the total receipts for church expenses amounted to £294 12s sd, and the expenditure to £3OO Be 2d, leaving a balance due to the wardens of £5 15s 9d. Although this account, Mr Wright said, showed £5 15s 91 due to the war- dens, there were also liabilities amounting to £97 6s 9J, the bulk of which was due to Messrs Gibson and Son. The sum of £6O was owing for work done to the structure of the fabric. He was very anxious when he took office that at any rate they should leave the fabric of the church in good order—(hear,hear,)—and he ventured to say that it was in batter order row than it had been since the day when it was completed. It had been thoroughly gone over and reno- vated, and everything was left in perfect order. They had had several calamities during the past two years—one in which several pinnacles and other things were blown down —which involved a cost of about £3OO. That sum the congregation generously subscribed towards, and it was nearly all paid over before last Easter. There was only left a balance of about £l6, which had been paid out of this year's receipts. The only items of ordinary expenditure that were owing were ene to his colleague Mr Francomb, of £1.2 19s Bd, one of £ll 2s 5d for heating apparatus, and one for organ tuning of £l2 12s. The ordinary expenditure owing in connection witn the churchwardens' expenses was something like £35 or £3O. When the tower and nave were struck by lightning, it was thought that no great amount of damage had been done, and he must say that the Manchester Fire Insurance Company met them genesously, and paid all that was claimed, though, he believed, they were not bound legally to do so. The amount claimed was £37 10s. However, on

going more carefully over the building I found that the gutters of the main roof, and other things, were very defective, and there was one gutter that had never been fixed at all. In addition to what was caused by the actual damage this extra work incurred an outlay of £37 lie. There was also the sum of £23 Os 11d, balance due to Mr Gibson for re-hanging the old bells—which he had no doubt would now last for a century to come. The fittings and wood work had been found very defective. Mr Browns: I should like to ask how do the offertories for this year compare with those for last year ? Mr Wright : They are somewhat less, and that has also been a drawback to us. We have had less offertories, and have had two Hospital Sundays out of our financial year, which makes a difference of from £l4 to £l5 at least. The offertories for last year for actual church expenses were £209 5s 11d, and this year they are £195 Sc 6d. There is not a very great difference, but still it is a material item. The Rector: That. I suppose, was fer the Infirmary. I thought the offertery this year was more than last year. Mr Taylor: Was there not a special collection in connec- tion with the damage done by the lightning to the church ? Yes, there was one of £l6 Is 7d.—Was that in connection with the item paid by the Insurance Company ? No. It was for the extra work. Mr Taylor : Afttr the church was struck by lightning, there was an announcement made that there would be a special collection, and on that Sunday I gave to it, and I find that between the Sunday when the announcement was made and the day of the collection it bad been made known to some one in connection with the church that the Insnr- ance Company would pay the amount. If that was so I think it was hardly fair it was not announced. I was not the only one, by many, who gave to it, and I have not for- gotten it. Mr Isherwood : I wish to ask a question about the money handed over for charitable purposes. When can we discuss that matter—whether or not it has been properly distri- buted? The Rector : This vestry has nothing whatever to do with the charitable money that is given in the hands of the Rector. Mr White : It is clearly a voluntary act on the part of the Rector if he renders an account of that money. The Rector : I render an account every year, which is put into everyone's pews, but I cannot do that until I get the whole of the accounts due. Mr Isherwood : So we have no chance of examining them. Mr White : It is a voluntary offering, and the money is to be distributed as the churchwardens and the rector may think ht. Mr Isherwood : May I ask what offertories are due to the rector for this ? The first Sunday in every month and festival days. Mr Isherwood : I may tell you that In my rounds in the parish I find that our own congregation are really neglected in charitable matters, while people not connected with us at all can have all they require and ask for here. Ido not think it fair that our own congregation and scholars should lie near the parish churchyard, not 200 yards away, sick in bad-- Mr White : I rise te order. This is not a discussion that should take place in the vestry. Any information you want from the rector you can get privately from him. The Rector : All I can say is that everyone that comes for relief is relieved. Anyone who wants information must come to me.

CONSERVATIvII CLIM BILLIARD FIAN`DiCAP.—The Con- cluding rounds in the billiard handicap at the Conservative Club, Earle-street, Earlestown, have been played during the present week, and the final tie was witnessed by a consider- able number of members on Wednesday evening. Out of the last four competitors, F Jackson (10 points start) beat W Slit= (45 start) by 14 points, and S Spurr (15 behind scratch) defeated H Williams (40 start) by 21. The final between Spurr and Jackson resulted in a victory for Jack- son by 36 points. The first prize was a splendid cue and case, with Ll ; second, 15s; thild and fourth, 5s each; and four other prizes,. 2s 6,1 each. Mr J W Thorp. who kindly gave £2 as prizes in the handicap, afterwards presented the prizes to tbe winners, and in doing so he observed that if the times had not been so bad as they were at present he would have been glad to make the first prize £5. (41- planes.) GOOD FRIDAY AT RaurresiTowie AND NEWTON.—More beautiful weather could not have been desired than that which was enjoyed at Earlestown and Newton on Good Friday. From an early hour in the forenoon the streets had a holiday appearance, and numerous pedestrians were met with in the country lanes. In the afternoon the charm- ing Newton Lake was the chief attraction to a large propor- tion of pleasure seekers, and here many spent the best hours of the day. There were no pubic festivities of any charac- ter, but the most interestiug feature of the afternoon to the residents of Earlestown and Newton was the opening of a new ground on the Messes, midway between the two places, for the Earleetown Football Club. Some two thousand per- sons assembled to witness the match between the Earles- town Club and a strong eleven representing the Darwen Club. In the evening the annual gathering was held in connection with the Earlestown Primitive Methodist Sunday School.

The Livcrpool Courier, a Tory organ, commenting on the ' meeting save Lively" proceedings such as those at the Easter vestry meeting of the Warrington parishioners are more depressing than cheering to churchpeople, indicating as they de a greater regard for self than for the interests of the church and the cause of religions. We will not pre- sume to decide who is blameworthy for the squabble, and probably in this as in many other quarrels there are faults on both sides. The Rector is an old man—nearly, if not quite, an octogenarian, having taken his B.A. degree at Cambridge so far back as sixty years ago—and he has been Rector of Warrington over thirty years. Thus the Rev William Queckett, M.A., has been in the town and the rec- tory sufficiently long to know and be known by the people, and to have established those relations which should subsist between a clergyman and his parish- ioners. Why, then, have the people felt obliged to appeal to the Bishop? It is noteworthy that the memo- rial to his lordship is signed by the rector's warden as well as the people's. The petition preys the Bishop to prevent the continual change of curates at the Parish Church; tells his lordship that the Rev. Mr. Montgomery was dismissed at a moment's notice, causing much unpleasantness in the parish; and asks him to take a firm stand and appoint two cara'es, protecting them from the unfair treatment every curate of the parish has received. It thus appears that the disagreeable incidents of yesterday were the outcome of a series of other unpleasant incidents arising out of incom- patibility between the curates and the family at the rectory, for Mr. Montgomery was dismissed because he insulted the rector's wife, according to Mr. Quekett's account. But is it certain Out the insult Was not the other way about ? One of the parishioners (Mr. A. Woods) declared he had " some respect for the rector but pone for his wife," a remark indignantly protested against by Mr. S. Davies, while the re- tiring and re-elected people's warden (Mr Francomb) re- marked that though it was improper to mention the lady's name, 0 if she would cease to be rector of Warrington they would have no more trouble." This remark indicates with tolerable distinctness the popular view of the position ; hut, of course, it is one the Rector declines to accept, es it is scarcely complimentary to himself, especially as "good authority " has fortified him in his resolution to have his own way, even if obliaed to obtain the help of the law. The parishioners on the other hand showed no signs of concilia- tion. Against the Reetor's wish they re-elected Mr Fran- comb, and also against his wish they insisted upon elect- ing six sidesmen, as maggested by the Bishop, the meeting ending in uproar through his refusal to entertain the epis- copal advice. Surely Mr Quekett must perceive that the conciliatory spirit would be most likely to restore that peace which has been absent from the parish for many mouths.

OPastrwO oF A Naw FOCTBALL FIELD.—The com- mittee of the Earle.town Football Club having made an arrangement with Mr J E Pardey, agent to Mr W J Leah, M.P., whereby they obtained possession of a portion of the large field known as the Mesnes, opened their enclosed field i on Good Friday. The part allotted to the E trlestown Club is the end nearest Eat lestown, and the club has had it en- closed by the erection of a strong wooden fenee 7 feet high. A' reserved" place with a separate entrance has been pro- vided for the members of the club and its principal sup- porters ; while the ex tct measurements of the field of play are—length ,120 yards; width, 80 yards. The opening game was played with the Darwen Club, winners of the .14anca- shire Cup and the East Lancashire Charity Cup, the result being a draw, each side scoring one goal. There was an exceedingly large attendance of enthusiastic spectatots. On kiattarday the Earlestonians were defeated by one goal to none by a strong " A " team representing Om Blackburn Hovers Club, and on Easter Monday the Darwen Old Wan- derers, after a slow game, defeated Earlestown by six goals to one.

CILoW•LANE CONGREGATIONAL BAND OP HOPE.—A number of the m,mbers of the Crow-lane Congregational ; Band of Hope visited the Good Templars' Lodge-rpom, Bridge-street, Earlestown, on Wednesday evening, and gave an entertainment under the auspices of the Pride of Earles- , town Juvenile Temple. They were cordially welcomed and I introduced by Brother E Newman, superintendent of the Temple. The gathering was of an open character, and there was a good attendance. Mr Jones, of Newton, pre- sided, and gave an appropriate address. Miss Sarah Hol- croft recited " Live for Jesus ;" Miss Florence Randall gave "The Little Circus Boy " and Mr RU Jones sang Merry Dick." A recitation No answer but a kiss " was given by Miss Emily Holgate ; Miss Annie Naylor recited " Same- body's darling," and Mr Blake gave a capital reading, which was followed by a reeitation " I'll never drink again" by Miss E Roberts. Miss Ada Adams recited " Somebody's mother "; Miss Emily Jones gave " The old, old clock," and Mr R H Jones sang "Joe Perkins." Miss Eva Jones next recited " Self pleasing ;" Hr A Jones read " The new Foot- man ;" Miss M Owen recited " Play at public-house," and Mr Jones read " Drinking 16 cows."
