The annual vestry meeting of the parishioners in connec- tion with the church of St. John the Baptist, Earlestown, was held on Easter Monday in the vestry of the church. It had been expected that the proceedings would be of a lively character, and there was a large attendance, the room being crowded. Among those present were Messrs B Corlett, M Birkhead, Nevitt, Foden, Jackson, Burchall, &c. In the absence of the vicar, the Rev T R Matthews, who has been at Southport for some time with the object of recruiting his health, the curate, the Rev J Lovett, occupied the chair. The Chairman read the notice convening the meeting, which was stated to be " to appoint churchwardens and sidesmen, and lay a voluutary rate for the ensuing year ;" and the notice was signed by the Rev T R Matthews, vicar. The Chairman, proceeding, remarked that through the church not having any churchwardens for the past year their names had not been attached to the notice. He thought they would be aware that in the absence of the vicar he, as the licensed curate, took the vicar's place, and was qualified to make appointments for the vicar and sava documents. He explained his legal position in occupying the chair, and ob- served that he was not a young man, as they would see. He had been a good while in the ministry and bad had some experience. Ha mentioned that to show that he was not altogether green in taking the chair. He wished to conduct the meeting in a friendly manner, and he knew nothing but that those present were his friends, willing to work together to do the best they could for the church and for the common good. He could assure them he had no other feelings in any matter, and he was to know nothing more about one side than the other.—Mr Bailey, at the chairman's request, then consented to act as secretary and take the minutes of the meeting. The Chairman thereupon stated that as he oould not lay his hands on the vestry book, which should have been in the safe with the other parish books, be was not able to read the minutes of the last meeting. He did not knowwhere it was, and they had got a new book to enter the minutes in.— Mr Birkhead: Yes, but where is the proper minute book ? The Chairman: I don't know.—Mr Birkhead said he thought they ought to know where it was. It was a church book.—The Chairman said be expected it would have been in.the safe.—Mr Birkhead: Yes, but it is not there. If it is possible it ought to be got.—The Chairman remarked that they had no time to search for it. Whoever had it might have sent it if they had wished; er it might have been for- warded to him as the only clergymen in the parish. But the proper place for all vestry books was in the safe.—Mr Burchall asked if they could get into the safe, to which the Chairman replied in the aflirmative.—Mr Burchall : Have you inquired at the Vicarage 2—The Chairman said he had made iequiriee, but he did not know where it was. He sub- sequently remarked that they had better get to the business of the meeting. They were aware it was his right, acting in the interests of the Vicar, to appoint a churchwarden and sidesmao, and the parishioners would have an opportunity of electing their own wardens and sitlesmen.—Mr Oldham Said he would propose Mr Birkhead as one of the wardens. (Hear, hear.)—The Chairman said he Gould not do that ttntil his (the chairman's) business was done first. He, as ' the chairman, had to appoint his own officers before they appointed theirs.—Mr Birkhead interposed and said it was a very unsatisfactory thing not to have the minute book, which ought to be a record, and not smuggled out of the way—(hear, hear)—in the manner it bad been. He could not call it anything else bat smuggled, and it was a very unsatisfactory state of things.—The Chairman remarked that it was a fact that the minute book had been taken away and never returned. It was not in Mr Matthews' house, and they had not had it in their possession sines the last vestry meeting.—Mr Heaton was under the impression that Mr Blinn (a former warden for the vicar) took the book after the last vestry meeting. The Chairman again remarked that the first business was for him to appoint a minister's warden, whereupon Mr Bur- chall said they disputed that right until he (the Chairman) said whether he would disagree with the selection made by the parishioners or not.—The Chairman urged that he bad to appoint officers first.—Mr Burchall said it was not accord- ing to the canoes, and he disputed the Chairman's right to be present.—The Chairman replied that he was the licensed curate of the parish and was permitted by the law of theland. —Mr Burchall did not question that bathe questioned his right as a non-parishioner—The Chairman stated that be was al- so permitted by the Bishop who signed his licence.—Mr Birkhead said that so far as he was concerned he had no ob- jection whatever to being appointed warden. What they had to do was to manage things in an amicable spirit if they could.—lhe Chairman observed that there might be certain things they desired to say, which might not seem so satis- factory, but they were all good men and true, he hoped, and would study to do to the best of their ability all they eould to aid the common cause. That was the feeling which ought to actuate them and be hoped they would not imagine he had any interest in asking them to do those things; be- cause he had not. He was simply there because they had not another person to take his place. If a person was named as minister's churchwarden—a member of the congregation— who resided oat of the parish he was eligible for being a warden.—Mr Burchall said that was a reading of the law he never understood, because Mr Matthews ordered non- parishioners out of the room at the last meeting.—The Chairmen maintained that what he had stated was the law. —Mr Birkhead asked who was to decide what was the law veten Bishops, their secretaries, and vicars disagreed, and one rendered the law in one , way and another in another way. He thought they had no law for regulating church affairs.—The Chairman said they had a very old law. They were also regulated by cuseaes. as well as by law. After sortie farther conversation, the Chairman said : lap- point as nainilter's warden Mr. Bell, of Cross-lane, and I appoint Mr. Foden as sidesman. I should appoint two sides- men, but I will appoint the other by and by.—Mr. Bur- chat' : The usual course is to read the minutes of the pre- vious meeting and to produce the balance sheet—use Chairman : There is no balance sheet to produce.—Mr. Birkhead : And for a very ostensible reason, too.—Mr. Lnham asked in the event of their appointing a church- warden and no balance sheet being presented, would the churchwarden be liable for any debt there might boon the church 2—The Chairman said he would not be liable for anythiag in the past.--Mr. Latham asked if the wardens would have a voice in the election of an organist.—The Chairman replied that the organist was appointed by the clergyman.—Mr. Birkhead said they had appointed the or- ganist at the first, and they were prepared to test the clues- , tion.—Tr e Chairman remarked that they already had an organist —Mr. Burchall replied that the organist they had I at the present was only temporary.—The Chairman said it I was only where a clergyman resigned kis right that the churchwardens could appoint an organist. div.head: EARLI4,gTOWN.
div.p: EARLI4,gTOWN.

PRIMITIVE METHODIST TEA PARTY.—The Primitive Methodists of Earlestown held their annual tea party in the schoolroom, LOrd.street. on Good Friday afternOon. The proceeds were in aid of the trust funds, but there was not a large attendance. The tea was of a very enjoyable clsarac- ter and Was nicely served by several lady friends. After tea a service of song entitled " Lost Gip " was given by the chapel choir, under the able leadership of Mr W Barton. Mr W Austin presided at the pianoforte. The connective readings were given by the Rev F N Shimmin, resident minister. The evening was pleasantly spent. DANGERS OP SLEEP. WALKING: SERIOUS ACCIDENT,-- A Mrs Kilbey, wife of a grinder, residing at the Vulcan, met with a serious accident on Tuesday morning under cit.. cumstances ef a sad and peculiar character. It is stated that at an early hour on Tuesday morning Mrs Kilbey arose from bed in her sleep and walked towards the stairs, Be- fore the other inmates of the house were apprised of the danger to which she was exposed, she fell headlong down the ivairs. Dr Mouncey, of Haydock-street, Earlestovrn, was immediately sent for, when on his arrival, it was found that in addition to a severe shock to the system she had sustained such serious injuries as have since necessitated daily attendance oaths part of the doctor.

CONBERVATTVE OBOINISATION IN THE NEWTON DIVI- SION.—A meeting of the Executive Committee of the Con- servative Association of South-West Ltncashire was held in the magistrates' room at the Town Hall, Newton, on Thursday evening. The committee is representative of the various districts comprised in the Newton Parliamentary Division, and there was a fairly good attendance. Mr M B Westhead, Newton, presided, and there were also present Councillor T Sutton (Warrington), Mr Wordnorth (Liver- pool), die. The committee considered the steps to be taken in view of the forthcoming Parliamentary election, and the beet means of securing the election of Sir Richard Assheton Cross as the Conservative candidate. The proceedings lasted over two hours.

EARLE-STOWS LIBERALS AND TRH GOVERNEENT.—At a recent meeting of the Liberal Three Hundred far the New- ton Division of South-West Lancashire, a vote of confidence in Her Majesty's Government was enthusiastically passed, and a copy of the resolution was directed to be forwarded to the Prime Minister. That has been done and the following acknowledgment has been received:—" 10, Downing—treet, Whitehall, 4th April, 1885.—Sir,—I am directed by Mr Gladstone to inform you that he has received the commu- nication which you have done him the honour to send him, and to convey to you his thanks for the expression of ap- proval and confidence in Her Majesty's Government which it contains.—l am, sir, your obedient servant, E W HAMIL. TON.—The Stcretary of the Liberal Three Hundred, Newton Division of South-West Lancashire." GOOD TRXELARY.—The annual session of the Grand Lodge of England in connection with the Good Templar Order, which has been held at Manchester during the pre- sent week, was the occasion for a plc-nic of local Good Templars on Easter Monday. A party of 13 members of the Hope of Earlestewn Lodge left Earlestown at nine o'clock in the morning, and spent the forenooa in visiting ' the chief places of interest at Manchester, including Peel Park Museum, Town Hall, Jrc. They afterwards attended the session in connection with the Grand Lodge. The "out" was enjoyed by the whole of the party.—On Tuesday even- ing Bro Joseph James, VV.C.T., presided at the weekly ses- sion of the Hope of Earlestown Lodge of Good Templars. There was a fair attendance. After the transaction of the lodge business the programme " Social Meeting" was pro. ceeded with. Several melodize were sung bythe members. TRH A.NTI-VACCINATORS AND VIE ELECTION FOR NEWTON.—A meeting of the friends of the anti-compulsory vaccination movement was held at t' e Welcome Coffee Palace, Merket.street, Earlestown, on Wednesday evening, when there was a good attendance. Mr B Har iaon presided. It was explained that the meeting bait been celled to con- sider what steps should be taken in view of the forthcoming election of a Parliansentary representative for the Newton Division of South-West Lancashire. The selection of Col. George McCorquodale as the Liberal candidate was briefly discussed, and some dissatisfaction was expressed that only One gentleman had been interviewed. The meeting was ultimately adjeurned without any definite decision having been corns to. It may be stated that the local anti-vacein- atom have lost an energetic worker by the removal from the town of Mr Alexander Forster, who officiated as the secre- tary of the local branch of the anti-compulsory vaccination society. WARGRAYS CHIIRCII : VESTRY MEETING. The parishioners of Wargrave Church held their annual vestry meeting in the vestry of the church on Tuesday afterno n, when the Rev Canon Whitley presided. There were also present Messrs William Thompson (warden), Tootall, It Jones, J Davies, J June*, lac. The accounts, which showed a balance of £39, were passed. Mr William Thompson was re•appointed vicar's warden, and Mr Thomas Hunt was re- elected people's warden. The followieg sidesmen were ap- pointed :—Messrs William 1 hompsnn, jun., Cave, Cetterall, Footall, Starkie, Bate, T Hasehline, and H Bradshaw. As representatives of the parish at the Liverpool Diocesan Conference, Messrs Henry Bradshaw and Toqtall were elected. During the evening the rev. chairmen alluded to the balance in hand, and remarked that it could scarcely be a matter for rejoicing, as it was mainly owing to the fact of the great number of interments that bad taken place dur- ing the year. NEWTON CHURCH VESTRY MEETING.—The annual vestry meeting of the parishioners of St. Peter's Church, Neu ton, was held by adjournment in the Magistrates' Room at the Town Hall, Newton, on Tuesday evening. The chair was occupied by the Rev H Monk, vicar, and among the gentlemen present were the Rev Mr Pugh, curate, Messrs J Devereux, W Haskell, Sankey, Ltptrott, D Ritchie, Henry Houghton, atm, The minutes of the last meeting were read and confirmed. The wardens, in their annual statement of accounts, stated that they were some £8 in debt at the end of last year, but that had been cleared off, and they had now about £4 of a balance in hand. The debt on the burial ground had been paid off, and consequently no rate would be needed in future. The accounts were peesed as reed. The accounts in connection with St. Peter's Poor Clothing Stock Charity, which had been audited by Messrs William Haskell and Sankey, were next submitted and adopted. A cordial vote of thanks was accorded to the retiring officers for their services during the past year, after which the elec- tion of officers for the ensuing year was proceeded with. Dr Watkins was reappointed vicar's warden and Mr .1 Devereux was re-elected people's warden. Mr Peter Percival was re- appointed vicar's sidesman and Mr D Ritchie people's sidesman. The report of a Special Repairs Committee was then presented, and after consideration it was decided t carry out certain recommendations in connection with the repair of the church. The plieter will be taken from the roof of the church and replaced with pitch pine. Eetimates for the work were submitted, but it was drclded to leave the matter in the hands of the committee. The question of better ventilet on was next brought forward, and the vicar and wardens were reqaeited to consider the matter, with the view of seeing what improvements could be effected. The meeting closed with a vets of thanks to the chairman.

CHEESE FARMING IN COLORADO.- Br AN OCCASIONAL Commie:mina. DENVER, COLORADO, MARCH 18r, 1885. Occasionally Lancashire papers reach Inc in this far away spot underneath the shadow of the Rocky Moun- tains, and I have read with feelings of deep interest the agitation which has recently taken place among the farmers in regard to high rents, tithes, and other out- goings, and the low prices of farm produce. Knowing the extent to which your paper circulates among the agriculturists of Lancashire, a brief description of a cheese farm in Colorado, showing the position of compa- rative comfort within the reach of an enterprising and industrious British emigrant may be interesting to your readers. Several months ago, when the beautiful "Indian summer" (or, as we should call it in England, "early autumn") was decorating all foliage with the most lovely tints imaginable, to an extent not conceived in England, I and my wife left Denver via the Denver and Rio Grande Railroad for Monument, a small station fifty-six miles south. The route for miles lay along the right bank of a river known as Plum Creek, its course marked by comparatively luxuriant vegetation for this arid rain- less climate, consisting of pine, aspen, scrub oak, and dwarf shrubs. Be it remembered that Denver is 5,192 feet above the sea level, or about one mile high, and our road gradually ascended for 52 miles until we reached an elevation of 7,186 feet above the sea level. This alti- tude will account for the presence of the pine trees, which with their rich deep green foliage were in marked contrast to the aspens, whose millions of little round leaves quivered with every passing zephyr like brilliant golden guineas in the bright sunlight, while the rich browns of the scrub oaks mingled with the crimsons and sca,rlets of the dwarf shrubs presented a charming corn- bination of colours not to be found in the Old Country autumn for brilliancy of tint. The country between Denver and Monument presents a most delightful variety of scenery; ON 'either side are rolling plains dotted with numerous herds of sheep and cattle, and agricultural settlements with cultivated ranches, giving evidence of enterprise and thrift. Now and then we catch a glimpse of the river threading its way amid the valleys and glens, while stretching away in the distance the cliffs and towering peaks in their dazzling whiteness appear like fleecy clouds upon the horizon and form a striking contrast with the blue-tinted foot hills, which as we near them appear covered with oak shrubbery, bright flowers, castled rocks, scattered pines, and quaking as- pen glimmering in the sunshine. Gradually ascending the mountain pathway, we reached the sum mit(2,ooof t. higher than Denver), and entering a gap in the mountains, before us lies Palmer Lake. Nestled here in this moun- tain scenery, sparkling like a diamond in its emerald setting, this lake is a delightful surprise. Along the shore is a substantial stone embankment, and in front of the station a neat boathouse has been erected, well stocked with boats bearing names from Sir Walter Scott's novels, such as "Meg Merrilees." In the centre of the lake is a fountain which throws its water 80 feet high. This is naturally a favourite resort for Denver picnics, and one day last summer 1,200 English, Scotch, and Welsh assembled here,- and had "a good time." From this place, which is often known as Divide, from its position on the crest of a dividing ridge, the road descends into the valley of Monument Creek, and a few miles brought us to the small town and station of Monument, where Mr. Gwillim, the gentleman we were visiting, met us with a waggon. Enough has been said above about the scenery of this part of the country, or much more could be written as to the vicinity of Monu- ment, and the extraordinary natural upright monoliths which have given rise to the name. A beautiful drive of about five miles over a rolling ridge, through what had once been a fine forest, now devastated and wasted by saw mills, Brought us to Gwillimville, the home of our friend, a handsome house situated about the centre sohfeiatering wide, shallow, saucer-like valley, surrounded ';;;Linentiy adapted for agriculture. Owillim Was formerly a small farmer in the Old Country, but not being able to submit patiently to the rabbits, &C.., of a game preserving landlord, he left Eng- land in 1869, and, after spending six months in Illinois, made his way to New Mexico where he stayed a couple of months. Not being satisfied with that locality, and having become "hard-up," he moved to Colorado in April, 1870, and located his present farm five miles from Monument, and on the head waters of Cherry Creek, in June, 1870. He commenced by pre-empting 160 acres of land, paying the Government ss. an acre for them, and then, under the Homestead Act, he acquired another 160 acres, at a cost in fees of 16 dollars, or a little over £3, thus obtaining a farm of 320 acres. Since then he has bought additional adjoining land, until now he has 500 acres in a ring fence, and no acres in another lot. The first 160 acres he got is used mostly as hay land. In 1870 he built a log cabin, and got his wife and little boys from Illinois before it was roofed. In 1873 he built his present house, at a cost of £5OO, the proceeds of his crop for that year. In those three first years he grew oats, barley, and potatoes, and kept some dairy stock, but no fat stock. • A physician at Denver, Col., has recently been con- ducting some curious experiments in the transfusion of blood from living to dead animals. The. Denver Daily New gives the following account of them :--" The sub- ject operated upon was a medium-sized terrier dog. It was securely tied, and an incision made in an artery.in his neck, by which the animal was bled to death. He Certainly passed through all the symptoms of dying, and soon after the last blood issued from the wound his frame became fixed and rigid, and his eyes showed the senseless glare of death. The room was kept at a temperature of 70 degrees Fah., while the dog lay for three hours dead. By this time he had become very stiff and cold. He was now placed in a warm water bath that was constantly maintained at a temperature of 105 degrees and was continually and thoroughly rubbed, and as he became pliant his limbs were gently worked shout and his whole body rendered supple. A half-pint of hot water' was now passed into his, stomach through a hard rubber tube that was forced down his cesophagus. When this was accomplished, the meuth of a rubber tube, attached to a bellows, was introduced into his windpipe, and as the bellows were provided with a double valve, by which the air could be withdrawn as well as inhaled, the dog's nose was securely f as- tened up. A large and powerful Newfoundland dog that had been obtained for the purpose had been tied near by, and now bled, while the attending surgeon pro- ceeded to adjust the transfusing apparatus, and began to slowly inject the live dog's blood into the dead one. Simultaneously, Mr. Annitage began slowly working the respiratory bellows, i while I kept rub- bing the animal and bending his limbs and body to facilitate circul.ationla We could not have been more anxious about the issue of our efforts if they had been made on a human being instead of a dumb brute. When a pint of fresh blood had been injected I could see some change about the eyes of the dog. But no one spoke. One thought was common to all—would life come back? In a few moments more there was cer- tainly a convulsive tremour noticeable in the body. Mr.' Armitage, in undisguised excitement, said to the sur- geon, Press the blood.' In a minute or two the dog gasps, and soon attempts to eject the respiratory tube, which was accordingly withdrawn. This was followed by gasps and a catching of the breath, while the eyes grew brighter and more natural. The rubbing and blood- injecting were yet applied, and the dog was struggling as if in a fit. But his efforts soon become less violent, and he begins a low whine. A compress was now placed on the artery, and in 22 minutes after the first blood is injected he sits up, after having been dead three hours and twenty minutes. The dog then drank a broth that had been prepared for him in case of his revival, and soon got up and walked about. He was 'furnished with a comfortable bed near the stove, and from this time forward his recovery was so rapid that in two days he was turned out to run the streets. He is now a rugged character in good health, with seemingly no bad remembrance of his resurrection. The second case was tested on the second day of December. The sub- ject selected was a calf six weeks old. The details of treatment were similar to the foregoing, except, for greater convenience, a hot vapour bath was substituted for the warm water immersion. The calf, after being bled to death, was left for twelve hours before its resus- citation was undertaken, as it was desirable to see if a longer death interval could be successfully passed over. The fresh blood injected into its circulatory system was drawn from a yearling steer. It required thirty-five minutes to restore the calf to life after the trans- fusion of the first blood. The calf then drank some warm milk, and has since grown and thriven, without perceptible interruption or ailment. The next experiment was of a different character, and was made with a view to see if a drowned animal could be restored to life. A small dog was forced under water and drowned. He was then takeu out and laid with his head inclined downward to drain his hangs of water, and left for four hdurs in a warm room. It will be noticed that this was quite a different and more hopeless case than the preceding, as- the dog had all his own blood yet in his veins. After an hour in the warm bath and constant rubbing and working, his veins were opened at three different points to admit of the escape of any blood that might issue from them, and the injecting apparatus was vigorously applied to the arterial system. After 50 minutes of anxious labour, signs of revivication were observable. The poor beast whined piteously as life was being once more enthroned within him. Notwithstanding great care was taken of him, he remained weak for several days, but seems now to be in good condition. A fourth case re- cently tried, in which the subject was a dog that Was strangled, and afterwards frozen—as he. could not be frozen without strangling—was unsuccessful. After hours of labour, no signs of returning life were notice- able. It is believed, however, that this experiment may yet succeed, and the life of a frozen animal restored." In 1873 he commenced experiments in cheesemaking, the climate, altitude and dryness altering all the circum- stances and rendering new methods necessary. In 1876 he built a cheese factory, purchasing the plant In Ohio and employing an experienced cheesemaker from that State. Al the time of commencing he had 30 mulch cows and purchased the milk of about 200 cows from adjoin- ing ranchemen all milk being bought by weight at one cent. per pound. The following is a brief description of his snider operandi:—On arriving at the factory the

milk is emptied into a very large can, which swings on a teagle, and after being weighed is "emptied into a vat, sixteen feet long, four feet wide, and two and a half feet deep, capable of holding 600 gallons, lined with tin polished like a mirror. Ile has two such vats. The tin vat is inside a wooden vat, with an interval between the two, filled with water, which is boiled by steam. The rennet is put in the milk at a certain heat and the entire mass curded. It is then broken and cut by a horizontal and a perpendicular curd knife, until it is in small blocks or dice about a quarter of an inch square, after which it is allowed to settle for a while. It is then stirred up again, and the steam is got up to cook it to a certain temperature, the whey being then removed by means of a syphon to a large vat outside, each farmer supplying milk being entitled to a proportionate amount of the Whey. The curd left is lifted from the vat to the curd "sink,' the remaining whey strained off, the curd kept handled to keep from packing, then salted at the rate of two and a half pounds of salt to 100 pounds of curd, then put in the press, allowed to stay there for about an hour or two;then taken out and bandaged. Next morn- ing the hoops are removed and it is placed in the curing room, where finally, after being tatted and found to be perfect in flavour, it is marked " Gwillini's Cream Cheese," and can be warranted first-class. No imperfect cheese is ever so marked, but is at once put aside, and the presence of the mark is therefore a guarantee of quality, and has done very, much to build up the large bu,siness connection which Mr. Gwillim deservedly en-. joys. In the factory there are 17 screw presses, and the capacity of the establishment is I,ooolbs. a day. The cheeses are of various sizes, from 30 to 601bs. each, but a small kind is also made for family use of Sibs. each, selling at one dollar each, or 10d. per lb. In 1878 Mr. Gwillim made no less than 70 tons of cheese, but unfortunately that year was succeeded by an un- usually severe 'winter, during which some stock perished, generally owing to the very primitive protection the farmers then afforded their. cattle. About that time, too, the discoveries of the immense mineral deposits of Leadville took place, which was followed by a stampede in that direction of a large population, and some of the ranchemen moved into the mountains with their cattle to supply the miners with milk. These causes limited the supply of milk for cheese-making, but there is no reason why the stock of dairy cattle should not now be increased. In 1878 Mr. Gwillim built a cheese factory in the village of Monument with a capacity of from 5001bs. to 6001bs. a day, which he now leases to a tenant He also built a shop and a dwelling-house there. At Gwillimville, besides his house, there is a shop and post- office, the cheese factory, farm buildings, three dwelling- houses, and a blacksmith's shop. Mr. Gwillim's house is roomy and handsome, being two storeys, painted white, with green shutters or blinds. In 1883 he raised 140,0001b5. of potatoes and 3,230 bushels of oats, but in 1884 his crop was rather short, viz., 2,125 bushels of oats and a slight falling-off in potatoes. Owing to his loca- tion near the summit of a dividing ridge and the conse- quent greater rainfall, he manages to farm without arti- ficial irrigation, which is the exception in Colorado. He also cuts every year from 50 to 100 tons of natural hay. His neighbours are relatives and friends from the old country who followed him out here on learning how well he had succeeded. In the neighbourhood of this farm there is a fair amount of game such as jack rab- bits (a species of hare), prairie chiaeus (a species of partridge), and deer, and Mr. Gwillim keeps a couple of greyhounds, two collies, and a Newfoundland and many, a tasty dinner is the result, as there is no gamekeeper here or even game laws, except to establish a close sea- son. When it is stated, as is the -fact, that Colorado during 1884 imported from adjoining States butter to the amount of £200,000, cheese £14,000, eggs £50,000, poultry nearly £60,000, and other farm produce in pro- portion, it will be seen that there is still in this State ample room for the development of agriculture. To show Mr. Gwillim's indomitable enterprise, I may mention that at the time of our visit he had a contract with the United States Government for the furnishing of potatoes{ W the igiu §ricl garrisons in Colorado, New Mexico, Arliettil, and ItanSaii, gupit'?-1: in 1841 111)Q0 350,000th5. Such is a brief sketch of an instance taken at random from among the many Britishers, who by dint of indus- try, steadiness, shrewdness, and taking advantage of the opportunities presented here, have attained positions of worldly comfort they could never have hoped for at home. I left Lancashire for Denver in August, 1883, settling in Colorado about two months later after a tour through the North-Western States and Territories, since which time in my journeyings through various parts of this State I have frequently met Britishers, who regard.' their emigration as the turning point in their fortunes. In Colorado alone, according to the official census' there are over 10,000 citizens of English, Scotch, qrWelsh birth, who are engaged in mining, farming, dairying, stock-growing, fruit-growing, tsc., many of whom have prospered beyond their expectations, and have no wish to revisit the old country, except for the purpose of see- ing once more their reflitives and friends, and then to return to the State where their honest exertions have been so largely rewarded.

REPUBLICANISM. Sir,—l don't know why Councillor Mackie should have gone out of his way to abase the Republicans. If he has more money than he knows what to do with, he had better !spend it its clearing away the bleak wall opposite his print- ing shop. If he would be at the expense of clearing out a frocoage to the Town Hall, I fancy the Tory brewer he so mach admires wouldn't mind being a trifle towards a Mackie monument to "grace" the space; a lot more sense in this than shipping off the Itepublicans. I see from my Rey- nolds " a few very ugly facts are being given just now, of promotions in the army and navy of fellows like him that used to captain the Queen's yacht until he ran down the yacht of a Manchester me. ant. This Prince Leiningen, cot qualified to take care of a woman of boundless wealth, is to be Vice-Admiral and Commander-in-Chief at the Nore. This German paupsr's qualification consists in being the nephew to our gracious Queen. Our Commander-in-Chief, who always takes his " gingham " when he goes to a re- view- is 000 of those whom P mublicans would at once tumble out of his snug births. He is receiving £12,000 a year becsnse the colour of his blood happens to be blue. tie also receives £2,132 re Colonel of Grenadier Fe•it -Guards; as Commander-in-Chief £1,50) is paid to him. Rxppose Councillor Mackie were to transfer some of his sympathy to this Royal Duke, who must be overdone with work, seeing that he is alto colonel of reveral other ,regiments, besides being ranger of reveral public parks, for which hard and exhaustive labour he has the game rights, residences, pasturage, and the sNail weekly wage of £6. Poor fellow! I suggest a public subsc.:ption, to be headed by our local sycophants.—Yours, &C,

LOOKERS? Sir.,—Being out for a stroll the other day, in the course of my peregrinations I rambled as far as the Mesnes," near Earlestown, when I observed that a portion of it was boarded Oil from the public gaze, and en inquiry I found it was be- ing set apart for a football ground. Now I have no objec- tion to the footballers enjoying therncelves to the utmost of thair ability, but on a little further scrutiny I found the plot of ground occupied by the footballers was that which is traversed by people using the footpath leading out of Crow- lane, and it was intended to stop the footpath. With all due deference to the friends of football, I contend their amusement should not interfere with and deprive the public of their long-eatablish ed rights and privileges as in this inst....nre. I feel certain if no action be taken by the autho:ties, that directly the land has been SO enclosed and the footpath stopped a certain length of time, the land-grabbing agent will again come to the front and say the land is wanted for other and more useful purposes. I have always understood the mesnes was Common lands," and I hope the Commissioners or Common Lookers will at once take action, and thus provent the land-grabbing from taking place. That the road in question is public property I consider cannot be doubted, and that it has been so for over 50 years is proved by the fact that at the construction of the rail- way a bridge was erected for the public use of the road in question converges to that point. A good deal more might be said, but I trust the matter will be taken up by some more able pen and the road re- stored to its rightful owners—" the public." Your inser- tion of the foregoing will oblige A RATEPAYER.

NORTHWICEI Sir,—ln view of the important work which will devolve upon the Northwich Liberal '300" on Saturday nest, : the selection of a candidate to contest the new constituency of Northwich at the next general election, I beg to offer a f situa ov remarks on the tion. There is an ominous reti- cence on the part of those to whom we usually look for guidance in political aff iirs. If it is because they do not wish to appear to lend official countenance to one or other of the two candidates before the council, well and good. At the same time those who are not in the swim ought to be better informed on some points, lest they be led to take a lean in the dark. The three hundred delegates, as their name implies.ro- present the rank and file of the Liberal party in the divi- sion. They have accepted a trust on behalf of those Liberals who elected them, and the, cannot do other than act in accordance with the interests of the Liberal party —which for the time are placed in their hands. If they allow considerations of a personal character to weigh with them, they will prove false to their trust and unworthy of the confidence reposed in them bv the Liberal electorG. Now it is known that one Of the gentlemen seeking to be the candidate IS the nominee of the Salt Chamber of Commerce. Will it be in the e interests of the Liberal party to select such a can- didate 1. Certainly not. Having got rid of the Egerton domination in the division, are we to place ourselves under i another ? It s none the less objectionable because it goes under the name of trade. It may be said that to follow oat that policy and ref use the help of the salt trade will be to throw the constituency into the hands of the Tories. So let it be. Better to die lighting than to commit political suicide by placing our neck under the heel of a corporation -which, however useful in other respects, is not in sympathy with the aims of ardent Liberals. But if the delegates do their duty, that is, it they do not lower the Liberal flag,

there will be no fear as to the result,. Ido not doubt the wisdom of the choice the salt proprietors have made; but if they had selected an archangel, the principle of freedom of choice, which we as Liberal workers claim, would be viclated just the same, and we should feel bound to reject him. There are higher aims before the country than seeking by Parliamentary action to find fresh markets for salt, or any- thing so sordid, and I shall be disappointed if, by the action of the delegates on Saturday, the newly-formed Liberal Association of the Northwich Division is reduced to the pitiful position of a sub-committee of the Salt Chamber of Commerce.—Yours, , April Bth, 1885.
LIBERAL.
SUNRAY CLOSING.

Sir,—l suppose this question is still within the realms of diecussion, because at the meeting held in the ?üblic Hall "no hands were held up in favour of opening public-houses on Sunday." I hope it is not argued therefrom that Warring- ton is in favour of closing them. Allow me to say that the English people are not in faveur of being humbugged out of their liberties by such twaddle as that talked by the speakers at this meeting. I must say something even stronger than this, and enter my protest against the dishonest tactics pursued by the total abstinence party. Failing in their efforts to dragoon the people into teetotalism, they are now resorting to the thread-bare plea that "When the great Author of the world had formed it, He was disposed to hallow one day out of the seven for the special good of men's souls." This argument might have done for children 50 years since; to-day it is seen through. I If it is good in principle, let the gentleman who used it and those around him who listened to it, come forward and say they carry it out. Da they on Saturday night dispense with ' the further services of cooks, coachman, and butler until Monday morning? Could each one standing on that plat- form say that no wine appeared on their tables on Sunday? Of course they could not say this. No, but in their grand- fatherly way they must come forward and try to make the one day when workmen are most at liberty a day for draw- ing long and miserable faces, when we should all have to join in the chorus— Let us all be unhappy on Bunchy. .But there is a still more relimarkable feature in the meet- ing to be noticed, and that is the composition of the plat- form resembly. The Rev :S. Wilkinson said it was a grate. tying fact that the object of the meeting bad enlisted men of varied political and theological opinions. He might have gone furteer than this, and have added, " Gentlemen with no temperance principles whatever." Mind you, Mr. Editor, mattes are not manage I at gentlemen's clubs In so secret a fashion as some people think. Truth this week tells us that Sunday dinner parties and lawn tennis parties are now becoming quite the thing amongst those who are so anxious for the welfare of the working-man's soul. Will,about the gentlemen on the platform ; I notice at least half a dozen pledged Tories ; three of these clergy- men of the Church of Enenad, of course. Now, how will these gentlemen vote? Did Mr W Roberts feel comfortable in their company while working for the teinp-rance canes? I trow not. Was it not plain daring Dr Mackie's speech that special pleading for the " one who had perhaps the greatest share in the liquor tride within some miles of War- rington" had to be done'? . Active members of the teetotal party like Mr Itoberts must have winced to hear the Dr. refer to the "traffic" and in eugolistic terms say that he Would "-just as willingly assist those who were publicans to carry on an honest and what was a respeztable trade known in sacred history es innkeepers." The fact is the teetotal party is descending to the use of somewhat ques- tionable measures in order to gain their end. The men I refer to will at the next election vote for the man who has the "greatest share in the liquor trade " in this district, whose riches are gained through employing "2CD wi- ee, and respectable young women." Why, Mr Editor, words fa.; to express my contempt for the incong,uons m--lley of men who met for the purpose of inaugurating a Scottish Saw.. bath" in our midst. Speaking of publicans being compelled to work for many hours on Sunday, the chairman said "he contended that it disabled them. They had not the same energy to carry OR their business on the following day." Now, er, mark the argument: because the publican works on Sunday be is unable to supply drink fast enough on Monday. This is only a sample, sir, of the whole of the speeches. You find no references to the duty of employers towards workmen, of cottage property owners towards tenants. Actual and ameliorative measures were never rg- tarred to.

Having read the speeches I was curious to refer to one delivered by Dr Mackie at Perth in ISTS, in which he utttered these words :—" If you want to cure drunkeniess it is not by locking up s:reet doors, for if you want to ca-ry out tha Maine Law you must put gates upon every street," and yet on a Warrington platform he has the effrontery to urge the locking the doors of a "respectable business." Standing side by side with local nptionists, he yt in Scot. land says that "temperance meetisgs are practieally come to an end," and that he "cannot vote for the Pernisaive Bill."

One would think from the speeches that the world was going altogether wrong ; that in consequences of drunken- ness and a want of attendance at the Sunday school crimin- ality must be on the increase. Reshooting the first, allow me to refer to the report recently forwarded to the " Times " by the Duke of Westminster, in which he says :—"lt ap- pears that while the population of England and Wales has increased from 1869 be 1884 from 21,680.874 to 26 213.629 the prison population has diminished from 11,660 to 9,942." This he ascribes especially to the spread of education. With regard to Sunday school attendance, allow the Rev W Caine, late chaplain of Salford Gaol, to speak. He says : "I made diligent inquiry as to the criminals in the county gaol of Manchester, and found that out of 649 Protestant prisoners 593 had been at Sabbath schools on an average of from six to seven years each. This is a very startling state- ment. But that was not the only sad fact I discovered in the county gaol of Manchester. I found that out of 721 Protestant prisoners 81 had been Sunday school teachers. I found that one in nine of the Protestant prisoners had been a teacher in a Sunday school, and some of them bad been so from 14 to 16 years. From this I gather that more secular education we have and less criminality ; less theology and leas need for prisons." This I give in answer to the cant of the platform orators. There is a way to stop drunkenness, not in one day only but the year round. Let us do as they do in Newcastle Through the winter months, instead of opening the Public Hall for the use of degraded and blasphemous Salvationists, let public lecturers of known ability have the platform. Moncure Conway lecturing on Carlyle and Emerson would elevate the people. The followers of Booth only degrade them. Witness the recent " faith healing" frauds. There can be no doubt that Sunday is destined ere long to be ob- served more as a day of intellectual rest than it has been hitherto, as the following cutting from a religious news- paper proves : " The Illy. H. Hubbard, of St. illichae''s, Folkestone, has started an experiment which will have the sympathy of all whr, car, for the rational observance of Sunday, by opening his church for musical Sunday afternoons.' At the first of the ua Mr. Hubbard, whole an accomp.ished organist, gave an organ recital, which contained such secular numbers as The Lost Chord" and Clowen's 'Better Land.' I think it was the Bishop of Lichfield who, the other day. suggested the tne of chnrehes on Sunday for entertainments of this kind, and the fact that Mr. Hubbard has been able to fill every seat in his church is a conclusive proof of what the ideals worth. 'lf a thing is right on Monday,' said Mr. Hubbard, in one of the utost sensible ad- dresses ever delivered by cler!cal lips, it is right on Sun- day, and if a thing is wrong on Monday, it is wrong on Sun- day.' I rejo'ce at this movement, cuning as it does from the cletgy, for well.do I remember the looks of horror that were cast at me when, at a rural gathering at which I had to speak, I suggested that the village church should. during the week. be cmverted into a village hall where the villagers might meet to Indulge in harmless recreation." April 6th, 1885. PETER PLYMLEY.

div.head: I,YM hl.
div.p: I,YM hl.

VESTRY MEETING —On Tuesday evening the Lymm Parish Church vestry meeting was held, the Rev Mr Guest presiding. VioanaNCY.—At no Police Court on Tuesday a tramp named John Burke was sent to gaol for seven days by Mr J Barton for begging at Lymm, and on Thursday a similar eentence was inflicted upon another tramp named James Seaton, also for begging, by Mr G C Dawhurst. LOCAL BOARD ELECTIONS.—The following is the result of the election of members of this Board :—George Hall, Oak Lea, Statham. 013; John Dalbv Dowlourat, Oughtrington House, 508; David Forster, Reddish-lane, 431; William Brazendale, 318; Matthew D Woodhouse, 277. The three former were declared elected.

THE EARLY CLOSING Mona.'"Err.—A meeting of the Lymna Early Closing Association was held at the Coffee Tavern on Wednesday evening, when the chair was occu- pied by Mr Brown. It was decided to adhere to the plan that was brought into force in November last, regarding the hours of closing, and was further decided to suspend business on Bank Holidaya and to close at six o'clock on Wednesday evenings. THE PROPOSED DIVERSION OF A FOOTPATH—On Tues- day, at the Cheshire Quarter Seliorta, held at Knutsford, Mr Marshall (Instructed by Mr Ridgway, clerk to the Lymm Local Board) applied to the court to sanction the diversion ef a footpath at Lymm' by the substitution of a metalled road 33 feet wide, the lad for which had been given by Mr G C Dawhurst, in addition to the coat of its construction. The necessary farms had been complied with, and the road inspected and approvetl by two justice. Thera was no op- position, and the Court made the necessiry order stnctioning the diversion of the foatpath, and its substitution by a new toad.

THE ATTEMPTED SUICIDE OF THE GIANTESS. At Cheshire Quarter Sessions, at Kautsfor d, on Tuesday. Sarah Whitclegge, known as the Lymm Uiantess, answered to her hail, on an indictment charging her with attempting to com- mit suicide at Lynam on the 17th February last. She pleaded guilty.—The counsel for the prosecution said that the prisoner was the step-daughter of Thomas Holt, a labourer and greengrocer, of Lymtn. She was only 14 years of age. On the 17th February, in the morning, prisoner had some dispute with her mother, who complained that she had received some money and not accounted for it, and threa- tened to whip her. Shortly afterwards a man came into the shop and wanted some money, and the mother followed the girl into the back premises, and found her suffering from a very severe wound in the throat about eight inches in length. The counsel further stated that he believed the prisoner was of very drunken and immoral habits, and that her step-father and mother had been very kind to her.—Mr Higgins defended, and said he did not think there wis any foundation for the statement that the prison-r was of drunken and immoral habits.—The prisoner was discharged on her step-father and herself entering into recogniz tnces of £2O each that she should keep the peace towards herself and all her Majesty's subjects for the apace of six months.
