EASTER VESTRY MEETINGS.

RUNCORN PARISH CHURCH. The annual vestry meeting was held in the chancel on Monday. The Rev Canon Barclay, vicar, presided, and there were present the Rev R Edwards, Messrs J Brundrit, J.P., W Whittaker, George Moss, W Mellor, 3 Johnson, W Farrell, James Littler, C Cooke, E Marwood, George Sum- merfield, F Barker J Tonks, W Hitchmough, T Houghton (apparitor), and iri7 Sutton (olerk).—Mr Moss and Mr Sum- merfield audited the churchwardens' accounts, of which Mr Brundrit submitted an abstract. The total amount col- lected during the year was £l6B 7s 3,1 d, against £l7B' Is 24 in the previous year. The expenditure WAS £ll3l Us Bd, leaving a balance in hand of £4 15s 7P. The seat rates realised £9B lOsemaking the total income £266 as being an increase on the previous year of £l4 15s 3tl.—Mr Brundrit having expressed a wish to retire in consequence of ill-health and press of other duties, the Vicar appointed Mr F A Lake, solicitor, as his warden.—Mr Brundrit said Mr Crosby wished to retire from the position of parishioners' warden, and he proposed that Mr W Whittaker take his place.—Mr Mellor seconded the resolution, which was car- ried unanimonaly.—Mr M Barker was appointed Mr Like's sidesman, and Mr J Moss Mr Whittaker's sideeman. Mr Mellor and Mr Marwood were also appointed sidesmen.—On the proposition of Mr Johnson, seconded by Mt Stemmer- field, Mr Brundrit and Mr Whittaker were appointed lay re- presentatives ta the ruri-decanal and diocesan conferences.— The Vicar said it would be necessary for a motion to be passed to the effect that the two seats in the chrencel and the one on the south side of the nave should be rated at £2 per annum, and the remainder at £1 per annum. It would- be necessary to pass that before the churchwardens could act.—Mr. Moss : I suppose if. that resolution was not carried, the church would be free and open. (Laughter.)— The Chaizman : I suppose so.—Mr. Moss said he had no ' desire for a change at present, and would move the resoln. tion be parsed.—Mr. Brundrit seconded the proposition, and it was carried nem. con.—Mr. Mellor drew attention to the sub-letting of their pews by various seat-holders he the church. He thought it was a great shame that money should be made by the practice. It was like robbing the church. (Laughter.) The Clerk It is robbing the church.—Mr. Cook said be paid within 5e a year the full rent of a pew in the church for two seats. The person who held the pew from the churchwardens had sub-let it to so many persons that very often he found himself unable ta enter the pew. He thought this was a great shame. The owner must be making a considerable profit on the whole seat. —''The Vicar : You must bring moral influence to bear upon him. (Ltughter.)—Mr Brundrit, on referring to the books, said that the owner of the pew paid £2 per year, and not £l.—Mr Cook said he was under the impression that he paid only Ll. He paid 15s per year for the two sittings.— The Vicar: Still he has no right to sub-let to so many.—Mr Summerfield said he had often heard of the same thing be- fore, and he thought it only required a littliinerve of their own to put a stop to it. If they found the owner of a seat had overlet the pew, be suggested that the sub-tenants should go out and it in the free seats and let the holders have the pew to themselves. .It would, he thought, be much better to give the money direct to the church, and not let it pass into the hands of those who desired to mike money out of their pews. He was sure many of them would hive more pleasure in giving the money to the church than to the holders of pews.—Mr Cook said he should be very glad to go into the free seats, but he was afraid he should often find them filled, unless he went at five minutes to six in the evening to secure a place.—The Vicar said he was glad to hear that the attendance at church was so good.—The sub- ject then dropped. RINGERS' SALARY.—On the motion of Mr Marwood, seconded by Mr Conk, the salary of the bell ringers for the ensuing year was fixed at £B, the men having permission to collect gratuities at Christmas as heretofore. Tam CROIR.—Mr Whittaker proposed that the best thanks of the meeting and congregation be given to Mr Johnson, choirmaster, and to the choir, for the very excellent musi- cal services they had rendered during the past year. The service's had been marked by good taste and feeline, and he was sure they all felt deeply obliged to Mr Johnson and to the choir.—Mr Brundrit said as retiring churchwarden he very cordially ikorided the motion. He was very glad to say that in his opinion and in the opinionL of many of the congregation there ha 4 been A i,7;;;at in^r..!fc":l9..t In t.bp singing during the last two or three years. A great deal was due to Mr Johnson for his untiring patience, and be trusted that the choir would remain together and still fur- ther enhance their high reputation.—The motion was unanimously carried.—Mr Johnson, in replying, said he was much obliged to the proposer and seconder for having used such kind expressions.— Mr Moss said he had great pleesure in proposing a vote of thanks to the Vicar for presiding over that meeting.—Mr Snmmerfield seconded the proposition, which motion was carried by acclamation.—The Vicar said he was much obliged to Mr Moss and Mr Summerfleld for their kind ex- pressions. He only hoped that with improved health he would be able to render much more efficient service than he had done hitherto. He was sure if the good will of the parishioners hr anything to do with it he had their sym• path}, and their kind wishes. (Hear, hear.)—The meeting then terminated. HOLY TRINITY, RUNCORN.

LIVELY PROCEEDINGS. The annual meeting was held on Monday night, the Rev W Preston presiding. There were present—Masers W Fisher, R Killcrose, W H Rogerson, W Hankinson, W Cro- ley, and Joseph Pollitt.—The Chairman, in opening the proceedings, referred in terms of praise to the services of Messrs Fisher and Buckley, churchwardens. He observed that the spirit of systematic giving was becoming more general amongst the congregation. Since the last vestry he had secured and pail' for the piece of vacant land by the church, and also paid for the removal of the unsightly soil. lie had done this as mach for the sake of the ap- pearance of the town as of the church. Since he had borne the burden of doing so much, he trusted others would imbibe a little of his spirit, and do the remaining work of raiting in the land. The next matter he would take in hand was the cleaeing of the church, which had not been done for 13 years. He thanked all the officers connected with the church for their services during the past year.— Mr. Fisher thanked the chairman for his kind expressions, and said he had only tea much pleasure in serving as vicar's warden for another year. He had pleasure in mov- ing that Mr. Buckiey be appointed peop'e's warden for the ensuing twelve montles.—Mr. Hinkinson, in seconding the proposition, said in the past Mr. Buckley had proved a good and efficient warden, and he fully endorsed all that had been said with reference to his qualifications for the pose—Mr. Rogerson rose to propose an amendment. He thought that Mr. Buckley had forfeited the confidence of the congrega- tion, and he thought they would agree that that was so when he had finished what he had to say. He believed that Mr. Buckley had been guilty of conduct which had ren- dered him unfit to hold the office which they now proposed to confer upon him. He was sorry Mr. Buckley was not pre- sent, and if he (Mr. Rogerson) had been aware that it was his intention to absent himself, he should have given him notice of what he intended to bring forward that even ing. He had been looking over the books and found that it was the first time Mr Buckley had been absent for several years. He did not believe in saying behind a person's back that which he was not prepared to say before his face, but he was sorry that had not been Mr Buckley's procedure in the past. He was sure they would all give him credit for truthfulness when he said that he believed from the bottom of his heart that he (Mr Rogerson) and others with whom he had been associated had sustained a very great wrong at the hands of Mr Buckley. He felt very deeply on the subject, and he was impelled to perform a duty which he felt he owed te the congregation, to the members of the old choir, and to himself. As a member of the congregati- n he charged Mr Buckley with having at the last Easter Vestry pre- sented a bogus or a false and misleading balance sheet-- The Chairman: I beg yonr pardon. Mr Rogerson can make no such allegation as that, for the simple reason that Mr Buckley presented no such statement. It was Mr I Fisher.—Mr Fisher: Oh, yes ; Mr Buckley presented the statement. I have here a balance of Le 17s 3d, but there may be some outstanding accounts which cannot be included.—Mr Rogerson said the accounts did not come In until OW the meeting. In the first place, there was a debt owing for tuning the organ. That account had bean sent in repeatedly, and it was given to Mr Beckley, but left unpaid. There was also an account owing to Withington, who lighted the fires, which was not paid, and Withington went in the next day to Mr Fisher and asked for the pay- ment of the account. Then there was an account owing to Mr Sharrocks for playing the organ, which was sent in to Mr Buckley before the vestry meeting. Mr Buckley sent the account back to Mr Sharrocks saying that he knew nothing at all about it. They would remember that Mr Sharrocks succeeded Mr Joule as organist. Mr Sharrocks sent the account to Mr Buckley, who returned it, stating that Mr Sharrocks had never been appointed organist, and that if he had wished for the appointment he should have applied to the proper person for it. Now, Mr Buckley knew that Mr Sharrocks had been playing the organ for some months, and that the account had been owing, but he had never said anything about it. Mr Rogerson then alleged that the choir boys, who should have been paid twopence a week, had been left unpaid. He maintained that Mr Buck- ley had an object in withholding the money, because Mr Fisher complained of the number of accounts that were sent in. —Mr Fisher hoped Mr Rogerson would withdraw the charge, because there was nothing ever said in the way of a corn- plaint.—Mr Rogerson held that Mr Buckley's object in withholding the accounts was that he might show a balance, and he remembered at the last vestry meeting there was a great flourish of trumpets because there was a balance of £3 169 61, such a thing, as Mr Preston remarked, as had never been known before. Not a word was said about the out- standing accounts, although it was known there were such. Mr Rogerson then referred to the resignation of the choir some two years and a half ago, and the formation of a new one, at the request of Mr Preston and Mr Buckley, by Mr Annett. He also complained of Mr Buckley not having attended the practices, while since the new choir was formed he had often found it convenient to be present. The old choir never saw Mr Buckley more than once or twice, when he came to pay them, and they only saw Mr Preston about the same number of times.—The Chairman: I think I was there about three times.—Mr Rogerson said it was very un- kind that the choir had not been visited oftener, so that they might have profited by any suggestions which might have been needed. He pointed out the amens were now accompanied by the organ, although the new choir was formed of experienced singers.—The Chairman: Excuse me; the object for which you rose was to propose an amendment to the nomination of Mr Buckley. You are only wasting the time of the reporters. I don't want to stop you, but do keep to the point. These are extraneous

matters.—Mr Rogerson : T beg your pardon, they are not. —The Chairman : I don't know how you can see that the singing of the arnena has anything to do with the appointment of a church warden.— Mr Rogerson said the amens were now merely rnonotoned, while the old choir was placed at a disadvantage in having to sing them unaccompanied.—The Chairman : Who is to blame for that? If lam I will take the blame, so that we may stop that part of the discussion. Mr Buckley had nothing whatever to do with it. I wish you would proceed to something else and let the amens alone.—Mr Rogerson said the choir did not deserve treatment of that kind, and he then eulogized the services rendered by Mr Annett, the eld eloirrcaster to the chinch, as well as the services rendered by Mr Broughton. He also pointed out that they saved the church £4 per annumin not requiring ''le wardens to pay the expenses of a treat.which the choir did. I Mr Buckley had shown unastak interest in the new elicit', I and strongly critic,eed the conduct of some of the members. As they knew, Mr Buckley formed an antipathy to Mr Au- nett in connection with day school matters.—Mr Killcross requested Mr Rogerson not to mention the day school. Give in enemy rope enough, and he would hang himself soon enongh.—Mr Rogerson said Mr Buckley brought a most serious charge against Mr Annett, but Mr Annett was proved to be right and was exonerated from all blame. On th-se grounds he held that Mr Buckley did not deserve their corgi lence.—The Chairman said he did like a bit of a breeze, but be did not think there were raany chairmen who could have kept their tempers better than he had done while Mr Rogerson was speaking. His name had been brought for- ward prominently amongst other extraneous matter which had no more to do with the subject than the man in the moon. The Chairman then went on to say that owing to complaints of several discordant voices in the choir he asked Mr Annett to put his finger upon them and send them downstairs. Mr Annett said that meant sending down the whole of the lads. He (Mr Preston) said "Do not let them sing next Sunday just to see how the singing will go on." Nothing more was said, and he left it in Mr Annett's hands. The next he learned waa that all the choir bad walked downstairs. He for one never sent the boys about their business, because he knew the trouble Mr Annett had bad with them. He thanked Mr Rogerson for all the valuable help he had given Wm in church work, and he endorsed all that he had said on that point and ha hoped he would continue. (Mr Rogemon : No, no.) But he emphatically denied that any lack of sympathy had been shown to the choir. He pointed out that the reason of the more frequent [attention of Mr Buckley and himself at the practices of the.] 'choir at the present time was because the practices now took place alter the Wednesday evening services when they were already at church. Alluding to Mr Buckley, the Chair- man said that there was not a more honourable and more [upright Christian in the congregation, and whatever little [ discrepancy there might have been in the accounts there W 29 nothing but what could be explained to their entire 'satisfaction if Mr Buckley were present. If it had been to show a balance of £3OO imaead of £3, then there might have been something in what Mr Rogerson had said. Alluding to the account of Mr Sharrocks, the Chairman pointed out that Mr Sharrocks was never appointed organist, and Mr Buckley declined to pay the account until he had a definite understanding of his arrangemert wiot his predecessor.— Mr Fisher regretted tha, the discussion had taken place. He had been brought into it rather ir iocently. Ile held that no complaint could be made with regard to the way in which Mr Buckley kept the r co. it, as they could not help a number being outsanding.—Mr Hankinson regret- ted that these "tastily jars" could not have been settled outside the vestry instead of being two- ,ht before the pub- lic.—After some huller remarks, Mr Buckley was appoin- ted ou:er warden.—The following were also appointed sidesmen : Merirs W H Rogerson, J N Lello, James Foulkes, W Hankineon, W Ci °ley, and J H Salkeld. Meows E Timm , , a Yates' and R Kilcrose were elec- ted members of the Church Coancil.-351 Rogerson only allowed his name to be put on the list after much pressure from Mr Fisher.—Messrs Lello and Fisher were appointed to represent the church at the Rarielennal and Diocesan Conference.—A vote of thanks was passed to Miss Imison, on the motion of Mr Hankinson, seconded by Mr Croley, for the gift of the pulpit cloth.—Mr Hilcross moved that the thanks of the meeting be given to the old choir for their services.—Mr Rogerson said he felt rather jealous of the honour of the Qiti Choir, They were the only members of the conception wbo could be found to attempt any- thing, while the Choir they bad now was not formed of mem- bers of the congregation.—Mr liankinson seconded the mo- tion, and spoke very highly of the services rendered both by Mr Rogerson and Mr Annett.—ln putting the motion to the meeting, the Chairman said there had never been any lack of sympathy between himself and the old choir, and be very cordially supported the motion.—The motion was unanimously carried.—Mr Fisher submitted the annual statement of accounts, which showed that the income for the past year amounted to £65 93 Sd. The total expendi- ture was £61;12e 513, leaving a balance in hand of Ed 173 31. The sum of £5l 178 101 had also been received for pew rents.—The accounts were passed. WIDNES PARISH CHURCH.

The annual meeting was held in the schootrolm on Wed- nesday night, thu Vicar presiding. There was a very good attendance and the proceedings were very harmonious.—Mr F Neil (Vicar's warden) submitted the statement of ac- counts. At St Mary's the offertories had amounted to £lOl 5s od, and the expenses to £B5 Is 3!td. At St Paul's the offertories had amounted to £l2O 11-s 9id. and the ex- penses to £153 15s fid. The total income, including the proceeds of the tea party and the ground rents, was £240 3s sd, and the total expenditure was £239 Se op, leaving a balance in hand of 14s 100.—Mr J B Imisen who had audited the accounts, certified that they were correct, and on the motion of Mr Cave. eeconded by Mr Whittle, were pas- eed.—The Chairman referred to the good feeling and bro- therly spirit that had existed amongst the officers, and the church generally dining the year, and on the motion of Mr Deny, junr, seconded by Mr P Hewitt. a cordial vote of thanks was accorded to, the wardens and other officials.—The Chairman then re-elected Mr F Neil as his warden amidst applause. and on the propositioa of Mr H White seconded by Mr Beattie, Mr L Kiieross was re-appointed people's war- den. It was decided that the number of sidesmen, who also form a church council which meets once in each month to discuss the affairs of the parish, should be increased to 24 persons. The following were nominated by the Vicar: Messrs Hughes, Williams, Showan, P'ankhurst, Treacy sear, C Jones, Atherton, Edward Lowe, Beattie, Brocklebank, and Hewitt. The meeting appointed Messrs Lord, Cave, Rich- ards, Farrant, U N Wharton, Chadwick, Dwerryhouse, Whittle, Watson, Matthews, Beech, and Pemberton.—Messrs J B Imison and J White wererappointed lay representatives. —Mr White moved that the best thanks of the parishioners be given to Mr J C Crawford, choirmaster of St Marys and to Mr J B Imison, choirmaster of St Pauls, and to the choirs, whose services are voluntary,, for their efficient ser- vices during the past year.—Mr W Treacy junr, seconded. —The Chairman also expressed his oblkations to the choirs and their leaders, observing that a very fruitful source of misnnderstanding and disturbance at other vestry meetings was the choirs.—The motion was carried by acclamation and responded to by Mr Imisom—A. vote of thanks to the chairman concluded the proceedings. FARN WORTH.

The annual vestry meeting in connection with the St. Luke's Parish Church was held on Easter Monday. The Vicar presided and re-appointed Mr Longton as his church- warden. The following were also elected churchwardens : —Mr Thomas Baker, for Bold ; Mt Wareing, for Cronton ; and Mr M Taylor, for Cuerdley. It was decided to elect Mr John Newton to serve as churchwarden, in case Mr Baker refused the appointrnent.—Mr Newton expressed his will- iegness to serve on that understanding —The church- wardens' accounts were read out and unanimously passed. They showed a balance in band of .10s sit—Messrs Brock and Brunner were unanimously re-appsinted lay representa- tives to the ruti-decanial and diocesan conference.—The Vicar stated that in view of the proposed restoration of the church it would be advisable to have a stronger church council than in past years.—The following were appointed sideernea and to serve on the church council :—Dr Cooper, Dr Thoth, Messrs J Brock, Kilian, T Fletcher, J W Ware- ing, W A Watts, A S Hanele, Joseph Glover, R Kidd, W Pritchard, T Sbuttleworth, J R Lea, T Baker, T Whitefield, J Newton, J H Davies, If Roberts,' H Lea, J Gough, E Bul- lough, D Forster, W Davies, Hargreaves, W Houghton, J B Imison, P Allen, W B Longton, Jas Wright, F Nand, W W Tipping, W Grace S Hoyle. R Whiteside, etc.—The Vicar said Mr Palmer, their clerk and sexton, had never been legally appointed by a vestry meeting.—Mr Palmer was then formally appointed.—The Vicar said the plans of the pro- posed alterations to the church were on the table, and could be inspected. The cost of the restoratijan would be £1,680' —This concluded the business. ST. AMBROSE, WIDNES. The annual vestry was held on Monday evening, the Rev S A Spooner, incumbrut, presiding. There was a good at- tendance. The Chairman re-appointed Mr E Carey his warden, and on the proposition of Mr J Williams, seconded by Mr Mercer. Mr John Valentina was unattimously re- elected parishioners' warden. Mr Robert Riley, treasurer, submitted a stltement of accounts showing a small balance to the credit of the church. It was considered satisfactory, and adopted on the motion of Mr eallandar, seconded by Mr Goff The following sidesmen were appointed t—Mesers Bullough, Minton, Mercer, Goff, Riley, Geo. Neil, Callen- der, Smith, Hill, Upward, Carlile, Edwardson, 9 Kidd, H Glover, and Lea. Mr Riley consented to again accept the office of treasurer. HALTON PARISH CHURCH.

The annual vestry meeting was held in the schoolroom on Tuesday evening. The Rev J Lockwood, vicar, pro. sided, and there were present 'Messrs T F Acton, J Stokes, T Wright, Ratter, Jeacack, Haguley, W Stokes, Woodier, Lambert, T W Haddock, and A Povey (applrator) —Mr Joseph Stokes read the accounts, which showed that the ex- penditure had exceeded the receipts by £l6. including a balance of £lO on the wrong side last year —The Chairman said with reference to a charge of 10s 61 there were some pew rents in Whitley which were not collected. The Bishop's secretary advised him to put the bailiffs in one of the houses as a test case. He did not like to take the pro- ceedings recommended by the Bishop's secretary, but it was the only course open.—Mr J Stokes did not see why these persons would not pay, as they had previously done so to Mr C3x —The Vicar thought as a Parish Church in the country district they stood in a remarkably good position. In the first place they commenced the year with £lO on the wrong side, but they had thoroughly renovated the church, and he felt perfectly satisfied himself as to their present pecuniary position. He said he had great pleasure in in- forming them that his churchwarden for the ensuing year woull be Mr Rutter.—Mr Wm Stokes was appointed the parishioners' churchwarden.—A vote of thanks was accorded to Mr Acton for his services as oburchwarden.—Mr Acton said he was much obliged for the expressions towards btai,

and he would help Mr Rutter in every way he ' The following were appointed sidesmen :—Messirs John Ackerley, Albert Woodier. and William Nixon. Messrs T L Acton and J Stokes were appointed lay representatives. A vote of thanks was given to the lay reader, Mr Haddock.— The Chairman said he would like to suggest that in future the churchwardens attend in the vestry at Easter and re- ceive the pew rents.—This was agreed to.—Mr Acton pro. posed that the church of Halton be declared free and open, to rich and poor alike.—Mr Lambert seconded.—An amend- ment was moved by Mr J Stokes.—The Chairman said he would recommend Mr Acton to give notice of the subject for the next Easter vestry, so that the churchwardens could state it on the notice convening the meeting.—Nir A Povey seconded the amendment, which was put to the meeting and carried—seven, voting for the amendment and three against. —Votee of thanks were given to the choir and to the chair- man, and closed the meeting. _ _ GREAT SANKEY. _
On Monday the annual vestry meeting in connection with St Mary's Church, Great Sinkey, was held under the chair- manship of the Rev E Jackson. ST. PAUL'S, WARRINGTON.

The annual vestry meeting was held on Monday, the vicar, the Rev S Wilkinson, in the chair. Messrs Thomas Jolley (vicar's warden), Thomas Sutton (people's warden),: and other gentlemen were present. —The accounts for the past year, which showed the receipts to have been £l5l 9.s 3d and the expenditure £153 143 7d. wale passed on the motion of Mr Pollitt, seconded by Mr Finney. It was stated that from £20,t0 £3O were still owing for extraordinary expenses, such as repairs and alterations.—The ViCar re-appointed Mr Thomas Jolley as his warden, and Mr Thomas Batton j was re-elected people's warden. Messrs Ash arst, T Morris; D Janes, W Lawless, J Smethurst, and W Po/litt were ap- pointed sidesnaen, and Messrs D W Finney and W Richard- son lay representatives.—A discussion took place regarding the practicability of improving the churchyard and giving it a moreattractive appearance, and a committee was ap- pointed toconsider the matter and report to a future meeting of theparishioners. ST. ANNE'S, WARRINGTON.

The annual vestry meeting of this church was held on Tuesday morning. The Rev Jfi Richards presided, and there: were also present Messrs H 'Bretherton and Silk (late churchwardens), E Gibbon, James Baird, Dagnall, and II Woods (deputy vestry clerk.)—The Chairman said he was exceedingly sorry that their present wardens, who had been as. good wardens as they had ever had, had thought it neces- sary to give up their offices. But seeing that it was so he would appoint Mr John Baird, of Bewsey-street, as vicar's warden. Mr G Gleave was then appointed people's warden, and Messrs James Baird and E Gibbon sidesmen. Messrs Bretherton and E Gibbon having been appointed lay repre- sentatives at the ruri-decanal conference, a vote of thanks to the chairman brought the proceedings to a close. CHRIST CHURCH, LATCHFORD._ _ _ _
The vestry meeting of this 'church was held last night

in the schoolroom. the Vicar, the Rev B B Prescott, -oc- cluded the chair, and there were also present the Rev J M Prescott, MessrsJ White and R Gorton (wardens), and several parishioners.—Mr Gorton suSmitted the annual balance sheet, which showed as follows :—Receipts-Special offertories, £4B 15s 71 ; general offertories, £llB 4s iii; donations, £3O 5s 2d. Expenditure, £2lB lie std.' Balance due to wardens, £2l es sd.—ln answer to an inquiry, Mr White said the total voluntary offerings were less this year by about £lB than in the previous year. This, however, was partly accounted for by the fact that there had been font fewer Sundays between the Easter of this year and that of last year than in the year previous.—The accounts were passed.—Thp Chairman re-appointed Mr White to be his warden, and Mr Gorton was unanimously re-elected parishioners' warden for the ensuing year —Mr H Woods and Mr James Lowe were appointed lay representatives.— Oa the motion of Mr Gorton the organist's salary was again fixed At £2O per annum, with a gratuity of £lo. Mr White nominated Mr C S Burgess, and Mr Garton nom- inated Mr John Lee as eidesmen.—Votes Of thanks were passed to the choir, the churchwardens, and the Vicar, for their past set vices,

div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.
Several of the Roman Catholic Hierarchy, including Archbishop Crokeand Bishop Donnelly, have left Ireland for Rome. _ _ _

BNOCKING ACCIDENT TO A BM—James Gorman, sixteen years of age, was instantaneously killed at a ropewalk in Port Glasgow on Friday afternoon. He was attending a small locomotive, and while trying to cross the rails when the engine was in motion he was overtaken, knocked down, and killed. His holy was mangled in a fearful manner.

div.head: ROYAL VISIT TO IRELAND.
div.p: THE ROYAL VISIT TO IRELAND.

The drawing-room at Dublin Castle did not conclude until nearly two o'clock on Friday morning. The attendance of ladies was unprecedently large, numbering close upon eight hundred. The last to arrive had to wait in the carriages three hours before they reached the Castle Yard. The Prince of Wales on Friday re- ceived, at Dublin Castle, aidresses from various academic and other bodies of Irish citizens, who wished to welcome him to the country. The ceremony took place in St. Pat- rick's Hall, and was largely attended. In the afternoon the Prince received the honorary degree of music at the Royal Academy, and laid the foundation stone of the Science and Art Museum. In replying collectively to the addressee, the Prince of Wales espressed himsdf highly honoured at being welcomed in that historic hall by the leaders of the loyal administrations, chief magistrates, representatives of learn- ing, art, philanthropy, and education; and to receive their expressions of loyalty and devo ion to the Queen and the interests of their country. `"`Both himself and the Princess would entertain pleasast recollections of the country in which they hoped in the future to spend many happy days.

div.head: CANADTAN REVOLT.'
div.p: THE CANADTAN REVOLT.'

OrrawA. FRIDAY.—In yesterday's sitting of the Do- minion House of Commons, Sir John Macdonald, the Pre- mier, stated that be had received no confirmation of the reported movement of Indians from American to Canadian territory. He believed that the report was invented by in- terested parties. According to intelligence received thie morning from other sources, the Crows, Kooteray, and Gros Ventres Indians have sent a large lighting party via Bear's Paw,raountains in the United States to Cypress Hill on the Canadian side. The party is now encamped on the Milk River, which is on the way to Cypress Hill. The Indians in other districts are adopting an insolent attitude.
THE RUSSI)-AFGRA NT WAR

RUSSIAN VIEW OF THE SITUATION. Sr. PETERSBURG, FRIDAY.— Trio semi-011131a1 Journal de St Petersburg to-day commenting upon General Ko- maroff's despatch reporting the fighting on the Kushk River, rlvs the absence of precise details only permits of conj!cture at present regarding the origin, character, and bearing ot the conflict. The fact that General Komaroff, after having repulsed the Afghans, returned within his lines, is significant, and ..afforJs reasoa to suppose that the movement of the Russiau troops must have been caused by hostile acts on the part of the Afghans. On this supposi- tion the affair can only be regarded as an accidental con- flict, difficult to avoid in a situation so uncertain and strained considering the proximity of the two parties. We may, therefore, entertain the hope that it will in no way modify the negotiatious being carried on between the two Governments.

A Central New telegram from St Petersburgh this morning states that General Komaroff had no orders from his Government to advance or to occupy Penideb. After chastising the Afghans he retired without occupying the. territory in dispute, being unwilling to impede the progress. of the negotiations. M. De Wens is all for peace, but the war party and the press are very aggressive. Lord Dufferin and Sir Peter Lumsden are accused of provoking _war.

div.head: BISMARCK'S HOPES OF PEACE.
div.p: BISMARCK'S HOPES OF PEACE.

rAms, FRIDAY.—The Gau/ois publishes a telegram from Berlin stating that Prince Bismarck has assured a great benker that, ie spite of the Penjiela incident yesterday, the Emperor of Russia has serious hopes of establishing peace. RUSSIAN PROFESSIONS OF PEACE, AND ENGLISH PREPARATIONS FOR WAR.

The Central News says, compared with the panic which prevailed on Thursday, the excitement on the Stock Ex. change on Friday was neither general nor intense. The im- proved feeling was due to the belief that the statement made in the House of Commons at midnight by Mr Gladstone, foreshadowed an intention, on the part of the Government to throw a considerable portion of the responsibility for the conflict of March 30th upon the Afghans, who, it is con- sidered, certainly broke the rlreement by crossing the river Kushk. It is thought that General Komaroff will in con-- sequence be able to make a plausible explanation of his con- duct, and that the British government will, under the circumstances, accept an expression of regret by the Hamann government, and will then proceed with the negotiations for the final delineation of the frontier. This optimism howeYer, was almost confined to the city. In ether parts of the metropolis and in chief provincial centres the war- , like feeling is certainly predominant, and throughout the. country there are no signs of any appreciable abatement of I the popular excitement. During the day most of the ministers, with the exception of Lord Derby, who hao returned to Tunbridge, were .engaged at their offices. Lord Granville sent to and received several despatches from Sir E Thornt( n, at St Petersburg. His Lo-dship received a telegram from Sir Edward Thornton communicating the reply of the Russian Government to our demand the ex- planations, which was subsequently, communicated to the Rouse of Commons by Mr Gladstone. It cannot be said that either the substance or the manner of the. Premier's brief statement created a favourable impression, and its subsequent publication in the evening papers in no way re- lieved the public anxiety. The Central News is enabled to state, however,that M D Giers in communicating his formal reply to the British reiterates on behalf of himself and his Imperial Master the expression of an earnest hope that the conflict at Ptenideh may not interfere with the progress of the negociations for a peaceful settlement of the frontier delineation. At the same time the Russian Chancellor took occasion to intimate that be had no reason to doubt the sub- stantial aocuracy of General Komarofre version of the affair, andt hat further inquiry would prove that the Afghans were aggressors. Despite these assnranoes,the Government as a whole are understood to remain firm in the belies in the accuracy of the accounts of the con- flict furnished to them by Sir Peter Lurnadeu The first active move on the part of England will he the despatch to Herat of a number of British Engineer officers, to be quickly followed by a concentration of a Won fcx3e

at Canoebar. The naval and military preparations are in the meantime being vigorously proceeded with. At Wool- wich, Cheat-am, Portsmouth,and other important centres, at the present moment, there are some twenty or thirty vessels of various descriptions under orders to prepare for active service.

Rumours werecurrent on Friday evening to the effect that Lord Granville had been sounded as to the willingness of England to submit the dispute with Russia to arbitration. It is, however, considered extremely improbable that any of the Powers would interfere in such a delicate matter and at such a juncture. The F. and Ce. Steamers Ballarat and Income have been requeitioned to convey 600 and 400 troops respectively to India. Thirty officers of various corps left Charing Cross Station on Friday evening for tnzlia via. Brindiel. It is stated that the strength of the Army Reserves to be called up will be 60,000 men. The whole of the Militia will , be called up, and the Naval Reserve will be used for pur- poses of defence. . ADVANCE IN THE PRICE OF CORN. lAt the London corn market on, Friday an advance of 41 per quarter was paid for wheat. A Dover correspondent says that the price of corn has increased 2s al per quarter in that neighbourhood, and that farmers decline to sell in anticipation of a further advance. The effect of tha war news upon East Kent corn markets has been to raise the price of English wheat 2s a quarter. Glasgow underwriters are asking 10s extra to insure ships for San Francisco; 7$ 64 extra for sailing vessels to Calcutta; and 5s extra for steamers to Calcutta. The feeling, however, is that Russia cannot seriously injure us at sea.

RUSSIA AND THE DARDENELLES. FARIS, FRIDAY AFTERNOON. It is positively asserted that Russia will, at the Suez Canal Conference, raise the question of placing the Dardenelles under international control.

div.head: SOITDA_N CAMPAIGN. AN EGYPTIAN ARMY TO BE RAISED. ALEXANDRIA, FRIDAE 11-30 A ISf.—lt is reported here that the Government has ordered an Egyptian army of 30,000 men to be raised.
div.p: THE SOITDA_N CAMPAIGN. AN EGYPTIAN ARMY TO BE RAISED. ALEXANDRIA, FRIDAE 11-30 A ISf.—lt is reported here that the Government has ordered an Egyptian army of 30,000 men to be raised.

LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF COMMOINS.—FRIDAY. The House met at four o'clock. FRANCE AND CRISA.—Lord FiTzmarnicE, replying to a question said a claim had been put forward by France to search neutral vessels bound for Hong Kong, but it had not been admitted by the British Government. Communica• lions were proceeding on the subject. Lord Fitzmaurice, replying to Mr. Gourley, said the Government had received no °Metal intimation of the signing of the treaty of peace between France and China. They had, however, rea,,Jon to believe that the reports in circulation to that effect were true.

THE PROTECTION OF BRITISH SHIPPING. Mr. NOR. WOOD asked if provision was being made to protect British commerce in the Baltic and Black Seas.—Sir 'r. BRASSEY said the subject had engaged the careful attention of the admiralty. They would make adequate provision for any eventuality, bat he declined to give a detailed explanation. He also declined to give information as to the armatnent of certain transport cruisers purchased by the Government. ZEBEHR PASEA.--Mr. GLADSTONE, replying to Mr. Baxter, I said they had no confirmation of the intelligence that it was an emisevry of Zebebr who betrayed Khartoum and murdered General Gordon. THE BATTLE ON THE AFGHAN I RONTIER. Mr. GLADSTONE, replying to Sir Nor, cote, said a reply had been received to the communication he had stated had been addressed to the Russian Government yesterday. It stated that the Russian Government bad already called on General Komaroff for an explanation of his conduct. Replying ta other questions, he said the Rus- sians did not occupy Penjdeh. No communicaticn had yet been receiyed from the Viceroy. THE REDISTRIBU rION BILL. The House then went into Committee on the Redistribu- tion Bill. The consideration of an amendment, moved by Mr. SEX. TON, to the fifth schedule, for the purpose of increasing the area of Dublin was resumed.—Mr. HEALY supported the amendment. He said that they did not ask for an additional member for Dublin, but only for such an alteration of the boundaries as wood provide against the breaking up of the existing wards.—Sir C. DUKE opposed the amendment, and said he had nothing further to add to the statement he had already made on the debate on the proposal for an additional member for Dublin.—Mr. PAR- NELL supported the amendment.—Eventually the amend- ment was withdrawn and the schedule agreed to.—Mr. T P. O'Comion moved theamendment to the sixth schedulefor extending the Liverpool Exchange Ward, with the object ' as he stated, of securing to the Irish minority its due share of representation, and of putting the Irish voters more compactly together.—Sir C. • DILIIE svggested that the amendment should not be pressed at present, but that time should be given for consideration and the matter dealt with on report.—Mr. WHITELEY believed all classes in Liver- pool were fairly represented by the Bill as it stood.—Mr. Lawn BRIGHT hoped the amendment would be fairly con- sidered by the Government, and if possible adopted.—Lord CLAUD HAMILTON. believed the amendment, if adopted, would revive ill-feeling which was now happily drifting out in Liverpool.—The amendment, as suggested by Sir C Dilke, was withdrawn.—Mr. S. SMITH moved to substitute Central for Abercromby Ward, Liverpool.—Sir C. DUKE opposed the amendment and it was negatived.—Mt WEBSTER moved to omit Aberdeen from the schedule. He wished the addi- tional member to be given it as an individual borough.— Sir C BILEB opposed the amendment, which, he said, was contrary to the compact on which the bill was founded.— After a long discussion the amendment was rejected by 57 votes to 26.—Mr SEXTON, accepting the four members for Dublin and the boundary lines of the cify, moved an amend- ment altering the divisions as made by the Commissioner and retaining them as the four courts, Rotunda, St Patricks and College Green divisions. div.head: STEALING A KISS. AN EXTRAORDINARY CASE.
div.p: STEALING A KISS. AN EXTRAORDINARY CASE.

At Warrington Borough Court yesterday, a married woman named Mary Fairbanks, of Winwick-road, charged a married man named William Lee, also of Winwick-road , a master contractor of labour at Dallam Forge, with assault- ing her by kissing her against her will on the 4th inst.— Complainant said that she had returned home after taking her husband's breakfast to him at the Forge, where he worked, when defendant, who had accosted her on her way, came into the house by the front door and, having given her a kiss by force, asked her to give him one in return.— The Mayor (who presided) : He did not attempt to use any violence? No, sir.—The Clerk : Gave you one kiss and asked you to give him another? (Laughter.)—Witness, continuing, said that she did not mean to take out a sum- mons, but scandal had arisen through the affair, and she felt compelled to clear her character.—Mr Browne (who defended): I suppose he said "Good morning" to you ?- Yes, in a friendly manner.—And you were talking rather familiarly crossing the fields? No.—Was not a drive pro- ' posed ? Yes, he proposed a drive to me.—And did not you consent to it? No I did not.—You went in your backway and said "Good morning"? He came to the front door and asked me for a kiss. (Laughter.)—Did not you ask him to come in and look at your house ? No, he said " This is the house in which you live," and I said Yes." He walked straight in. (I aughter.)—Were you not at the door pulling your ulster off, and did not von aek him to come into the house? No, he walked in. —Did you not ask him to come and see whether your house was beautiful or not? No. You told him the lodger was coming downstairs? No.—Was not there a. lodger in bed ? I said there was alyeung man in the bouse.—How long was defendant in the house ? About ten mintnes.—You say he kissed you ? Yes.—Did you scream.? (Laughter.) Yes, I did.—Did the lodger hear you? I did not scream out anything, but he took me by force and made improper observations. In farther cross- examination witness admitted having, two years ago, brought a similar charge against another man, who gave her £1 to settle the case.—Mr Browne submitted that the case was one of extortion. His client had worked 34' years at Dallarn Forge and never had a complaint against him. On the morning in question he Saw complainant giving her husband his breakfast at the north gates. He put his stock book in the cabin at the gates, and in coming out saw com- plainant 30 or 40 yards in front. He was going across the gelds to his own home, near the complainant's, and when he got to Heybridge-Ironworks complainant was wait- ing for him, standing against the wall. She said " Good :morning," and be replied in the same manner. They began to talk familiarly, and he asked her if she would like a drive. She replied that she would. Defendant left her, and on going round to his own house she was wilting for him at the front door. She said " This is my house. I have heen beautifying 'it; will you come in and look at it? " Defendint did not admit kissing her, but he did admit putting his arm round , her.—The Mayor: You ad nit that he put his arm round her and that he is a married man ? Yes.—Living in such close proximity, ho knew she was a married woman? Yes. —The Mayor: Surely no one car: justify the impronriety I of his putting Ibis arm round a married woman's waist.— Questioned, complainant said she had taken out the Summoll4 because of the scandal, which, she alleged, had been set about by defendant.—Mr Thowne,.oo behalf of his client, denied that—The Mayer: By ycur own showing he com- mitted an assault ? It was a trivial one.—The Mayor: Surely it was an improper overture to ask a married woman to go for a drive. Nothing collie) justify that.—Mr Brewne Nothing could justify her waiting for him.—The Mayor: That Zs an a.ssamption. I think his object in the byst place must have been a very impure one to invite her to go for a drive, anti I am inclined to think if he could put his arm round her waist he would not hesitate to kiss her if be had the chance. (Laughtor.l-- Complainant said that she , simply desired to cleat; her character—The Bench I.).tand I defendant over in hit own recognisances to keep the peace for six months.

IN PARLIAMBNT—BESSION 1885. "DISTRICT OF HAYCOCK IN THE COUNTY OF L &BOASTER. RE "HE ST. HELENS AND ‘VIGAN JUNCTIONS RAILWAY BILL, 1885. NOTICE is HEREBY GIVEN, that at a Special Meeting of the Lccal Board for the district of Haydock, called in pursuance of the Act 35 and 38 Victoria, cap. 91, and held on Wednesday, the 11th day of February, 1885, the following re- solution was passed by an absolute majority of the whae dum- ber of the sad Lccal Board, that is to say : Resolved, by an absolute majority of the whole number of the Local Board for the district of Haydock, and present at this meeting, that in the judgment of the said Local Board as- sembled, being the governing body for the said district, it is expedient for such governing body to oppose a Bill in Parlia- ment to be pxomoted in the next Session, called "The St. Helens and Wigan Junctions Pallway Bill, 1885," and tl-at the said Local Bard, as such governing body of the said die- tt let do oppose the said Bill in hirliament, and for that pur- pose apply the general dis'rict fund and the general distrkt rate under the control of such governing bady or such portion thereof as may be nece sary for the payment of the costs and expenses attending the Fame. (eigned) JOSEPH EVANS, Chairman of the said Local Board.

ANANTLES.—Some Mantle Shops have a disreputable system of ticketing Mantles in the window much under va us. and this is often observed by ladies who purchase at the Mantle Co.'s Whol-sale Warehouse, which necessitates an ex- planation of this bad system. Ladies should know that Mantles prominently displayed, apparently under value, if secured might be bargains, but when marked under cost it is net intended they should be sold. These are made specially for the window as a draw, and probably so made as to fit no one, or are artfully changed for inferior copies hanging in readiness at the back of the window, of commoner materials and trimmings. in imitation of the one ticketed. This system Is carried on with Black Costumes also. The Mantle Co. chal- lenge competition; but this false window display ne.ds ex- posure. Ladles who patronise the Mantle Co.'s Warehouse are guaranteed every satisfaction, and are certain of saving a large retail profit —The MANTLE 00.'s RETAIL STOCKROOM is 33, PICCADILLY.
